item.title: Modal synthesis and metallic percussion in real time
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How real-time modal synthesis models metallic percussion: mallet strike exciters, banks of inharmonic second-order resonators, dispersive waveguides, and Chladni plates.
item.content:encoded:
Modal synthesis metallic percussion sound design simulates acoustic resonance by decomposing complex vibrating structures into independent resonant modes. Unlike acoustic strings and open cylindrical pipes, whose boundary conditions produce integer harmonic partials (such as 1f, 2f, 3f, and 4f), metallic objects like bells, struck rods, vibraphone bars, cymbals, and gongs exhibit strongly inharmonic frequency spectra.

When a mallet strikes a solid bronze bell or steel plate, energy distributes across dozens of vibrational modes simultaneously. Each mode oscillates at its own characteristic frequency, dissipates energy at a material-dependent decay rate, and responds to the hardness and velocity of the exciter.

In audiovisual modular environments like Infinite, physical modelling provides an expressive acoustic bridge between digital signal processing and procedural graphics. Because the underlying state variables (such as mode displacement, exciter velocity, and high-frequency dissipation) are calculated in real time on the audio thread, they can be routed directly into 3D mesh deformation, particle velocities, and shaders.

Here is an analysis of how real-time modal synthesis models metallic percussion, how mallet contact mechanics excite resonant structures, how second-order bandpass resonator banks are formulated, how dispersive waveguides reproduce high-frequency shimmer, and how to patch a complete metallic percussion synthesiser using native nodes.

What modal synthesis solves for struck metal

In acoustic percussion modelling, sound designers historically relied on two conventional techniques: sample playback and frequency modulation (FM) synthesis.

Sample libraries record acoustic instruments with fidelity, but they remain static snapshots. Sticking, damping, scraping, or striking an acoustic gong at varying distances from the rim requires dozens of velocity layers and round-robin samples. Even with extensive sample sets, phase cancellation and repetitive transients degrade acoustic realism during fast rolls or sustained strikes.

FM synthesis excels at producing metallic sidebands by modulating a sinusoidal carrier with another operator. However, FM sideband distribution follows Bessel functions of the first kind (J_n(beta)), where the partials are symmetrically spaced around the carrier frequency:

f_sideband = f_carrier +/- n * f_modulator

Real solid metals do not follow linear FM sideband symmetry. Their natural resonant frequencies arise from the physical stiffness and boundary conditions of elastic solids, producing wide, asymmetrical frequency spreads that sound unnatural when forced into FM operator ratios.

Modal synthesis resolves this by modelling the resonant body as a parallel bank of damped second-order resonators. Each filter represents one orthogonal physical vibrational mode. By configuring the frequency ratios, initial amplitudes, and decay times of each filter to match the analytical solutions of acoustic differential equations, modal synthesis reproduces the nuanced acoustic behaviour of struck metal with low computational overhead.

The acoustic physics of vibrating bars, plates, and bells

To model metallic percussion accurately, we must examine how acoustic waves propagate through different geometric structures: one-dimensional bars, two-dimensional plates, and three-dimensional bells.

Transverse vibrations in stiff bars (Euler-Bernoulli beam theory)

In an ideal flexible string, tension dominates restoring forces, producing harmonic overtones. In a stiff metallic bar (such as a glockenspiel or xylophone bar), shear stiffness and bending moments govern motion. The fourth-order Euler-Bernoulli partial differential equation describes this transverse displacement y(x, t):

rho * A * (d^2 y / dt^2) + E * I * (d^4 y / dx^4) = 0

Where rho represents material density, A is cross-sectional area, E is Young's modulus of elasticity, and I is the area moment of inertia.

For a bar with free ends, the boundary conditions require zero bending moment and zero shear force at both boundaries. Solving this eigenvalue equation yields the modal frequencies:

f_n = (pi / (2 * L^2)) * sqrt((E * I) / (rho * A)) * m_n^2

Where the modal constants m_n approximately equal:

m_1 = 3.0112,   m_2 = 5.0000,   m_3 = 7.0000,   m_4 = 9.0000

Normalising by the fundamental frequency f_1, the modal frequency ratios for an ideal free-free metallic bar become:

f_1 / f_1 = 1.000
f_2 / f_1 = (5.000 / 3.0112)^2 = 2.756
f_3 / f_1 = (7.000 / 3.0112)^2 = 5.404
f_4 / f_1 = (9.000 / 3.0112)^2 = 8.933
f_5 / f_1 = (11.00 / 3.0112)^2 = 13.344

Notice that the second mode is nearly 2.76 times the fundamental, and the third mode is over 5.4 times the fundamental. This progressive widening of partial spacing creates the bright, bell-like timbre of struck steel.

Two-dimensional circular plates and Chladni figures

When energy disperses across a circular bronze plate, cymbal, or gong, waves propagate radially and azimuthally. Ernst Chladni demonstrated that sand scattered on vibrating plates gathers along stationary nodal lines and nodal circles.

The governing equation for a vibrating thin plate of thickness h is Poisson's plate equation:

D * nabla^4 w + rho * h * (d^2 w / dt^2) = 0

Where D = (E * h^3) / (12 * (1 - nu^2)) is the flexural rigidity and nu is Poisson's ratio. In polar coordinates, the spatial mode shapes are given by combinations of ordinary and modified Bessel functions:

w_mn(r, theta) = [A * J_m(k * r) + B * I_m(k * r)] * cos(m * theta)

The modal frequencies correspond to the roots of the transcendental boundary equation. For a circular plate clamped at the centre and free at the edge (typical of a suspended cymbal or small gong), the resulting modal ratios deviate sharply from integer multiples:

f_01 / f_01 = 1.000   (fundamental mode)
f_11 / f_01 = 1.482   (one nodal diameter)
f_21 / f_01 = 2.045   (two nodal diameters)
f_02 / f_01 = 2.684   (one nodal circle)
f_31 / f_01 = 3.420   (three nodal diameters)
f_12 / f_01 = 4.250   (one diameter, one circle)

These clustered, closely spaced inharmonic ratios produce the dense shimmering wash and acoustic turbulence characteristic of cymbals and tam-tams.

The acoustic hierarchy of tuned church bells

Tuned bells (such as carillons and orchestral chimes) represent a specialised branch of acoustics. Bell founders shape the bronze casting profile so that five key partials align into a musically consonant structure:

  1. Hum tone (0.5 * f_0): One octave below the strike note.
  2. Prime (1.0 * f_0): The nominal pitch of the bell.
  3. Tierce (1.189 * f_0): A minor third above the prime, giving European bells their melancholic quality.
  4. Quint (1.5 * f_0): A perfect fifth above the prime.
  5. Nominal (2.0 * f_0): One octave above the prime, which governs the perceived strike pitch.

Higher modes (supernominal at 2.74x, octave nominal at 4.0x) decay rapidly, while the lower hum tone and prime ring for seconds.

Mallet excitation and transient contact mechanics

The sound of struck metal depends heavily on the exciter. Striking a bell with a hard brass rod produces a sharp transient rich in high frequencies. Striking the same bell with a soft felt mallet yields a rounded, deep resonance with minimal high-frequency content.

Raised-cosine contact model

In physical acoustics, mallet impact can be approximated as an elastic sphere contacting a surface. According to Hertzian contact mechanics, the contact duration tau varies inversely with strike velocity v_0:

tau proportional to v_0^(-1/5)

For real-time synthesiser architectures, a raised-cosine impulse function simulates the mallet contact force p(t) over contact duration T_c:

p(t) = 0.5 * [1 - cos((2 * pi * t) / T_c)]    for 0 <= t <= T_c
p(t) = 0                                       for t > T_c

The Fourier transform of this raised-cosine pulse exhibits spectral nulls at multiples of 1 / T_c:

P(f) = (sin(pi * f * T_c) / (pi * f * T_c)) * (1 / (1 - (f * T_c)^2))

When the mallet is hard, T_c is short (around 0.5 to 1.5 milliseconds), pushing the spectral cutoff well into the ultrasonic range and exciting every high mode. When the mallet is soft, T_c lengthens to 8 to 20 milliseconds, filtering out high frequencies before they reach the resonator bank.

In Infinite's Metallic node, the transient parameter controls both the mallet strike hardness and the injection of a micro-burst of band-limited noise into the resonators, simulating the physical scrape and impact of the mallet head.

Second-order inharmonic resonator bank formulation

To compute modal resonance efficiently on digital hardware, each mode is implemented as a two-pole digital bandpass filter.

Continuous to discrete transformation

The continuous-time transfer function of a single damped mechanical oscillator is:

H(s) = (omega_0 / Q) * s / (s^2 + (omega_0 / Q) * s + omega_0^2)

Applying the impulse invariant transform or matched z-transform yields the canonical second-order infinite impulse response (IIR) filter:

y[n] = 2 * r * cos(theta) * y[n-1] - r^2 * y[n-2] + b_0 * (x[n] - r * cos(theta) * x[n-1])

Where:

  • omega_0 = 2 * pi * f_mode / f_s is the normalised angular frequency at sample rate f_s.
  • r = exp(-pi * B / f_s) represents the pole radius, where B is the -3 dB resonance bandwidth in Hertz.
  • theta = omega_0 * sqrt(1 - 1 / (4 * Q^2)) is the pole angle.
  • b_0 = (1 - r^2) * sin(theta) normalises the peak gain to unity at the resonant frequency.

Mode decoupling and parallel execution

In real-time processing, evaluating 12 independent second-order filters in parallel offers numerical stability. Unlike cascade filters, where small coefficient roundoff errors can propagate and cause instability, parallel resonators run independently:

y_total[n] = sum_{m=0}^{M-1} g_m * y_m[n]

Where g_m is the excitation gain for mode m.

Frequency-dependent damping

In solid metals, high-frequency modes dissipate energy faster than low-frequency modes due to internal thermoelastic friction and acoustic radiation into the surrounding air. The decay time tau_m of each mode scales with frequency:

tau_m = tau_base * (f_0 / f_m)^alpha

Where alpha represents the material loss coefficient (typically 0.2 to 0.8 for metals, 1.2 to 1.8 for wood or ceramic). By applying this frequency-dependent damping curve across the resonator bank, high partials ring out quickly while the fundamental and lower modes sustain for several seconds.

Dispersive waveguides and allpass phase delay loops

While a 12-mode resonator bank accurately captures the discrete lower and middle partials of metallic bodies, dense high-frequency energy (above 6 kHz) requires hundreds of closely packed modes. Evaluating hundreds of discrete filters per voice strains CPU budgets.

To solve this, modal synthesis can be paired with an extended Karplus-Strong waveguide featuring allpass dispersion filters.

An ideal delay line recirculates audio with uniform delay across all frequencies. In a stiff metallic medium, however, wave propagation velocity increases with frequency:

v_phase(f) = sqrt(2 * pi * f) * ((E * I) / (rho * A))^(1/4)

Higher frequencies travel faster than lower frequencies. To model this dispersion in discrete time, a cascade of first-order allpass filters is inserted into the feedback loop:

A(z) = (a + z^-1) / (1 + a * z^-1)

The group delay tau_g(omega) of this allpass filter varies with frequency:

tau_g(omega) = - d(phi) / d(omega) = (1 - a^2) / (1 + 2 * a * cos(omega) + a^2)

When a > 0, high frequencies experience shorter phase delay through the loop than low frequencies. As the strike transient recirculates through the waveguide, the impulse stretches out into a dispersed chirp, creating the characteristic metallic ringing tail found in metal rods and sheet springs.

Material physics presets and acoustic modal ratios

Infinite's Metallic node packages these mathematical foundations into eight material presets, each defining distinct mode ratios, decay times, and dispersion strengths.

Preset comparison

  1. Steel (kSteel): Modeled on Euler-Bernoulli clamped bar ratios (1.00, 2.76, 5.40, 8.93, 13.34, 18.64...). Stiffness is set to 0.25, producing clear, bright overtones with moderate dispersion and clean harmonic decay.
  2. Bell Bronze (kBell): Incorporates tuned church bell ratios (hum 0.50x, prime 1.00x, minor third tierce 1.189x, quint 1.50x, nominal 2.00x, supernominal 2.74x). Delivers a long 3.5-second sustain with minor-third beating.
  3. Gong / Plate (kGong): Based on two-dimensional Chladni circular plate modes (1.00, 1.48, 2.05, 2.68, 3.42, 4.25...). Features high dispersion (0.70) and nonlinear detuning (0.012) to simulate modal collisions and wash.
  4. Cast Iron (kIron): Features heavy high-frequency loss (0.85) and short 1.2-second decay. Models heavy machinery, anvils, and thick industrial plates.
  5. Titanium (kTitanium): High stiffness (0.60) and minimal high-frequency damping (0.18). Produces an ultra-bright, piercing resonance with a 2.8-second decay.
  6. Glass / Crystal (kGlass): Extremely low high-frequency loss (0.12) with pure, crystalline modal ratios. Simulates struck wine glasses and crystal singing bowls.
  7. Ceramic (kCeramic): Rapid high-frequency decay (1.10) with dry, hollow wooden-metallic overtones resembling marimba bars or porcelain tiles.
  8. Vibraphone Bar (kVibraphone): Tuned bar with an undercut arch profile, aligning the second mode to the fourth harmonic (4.00x) rather than the standard 2.76x of uniform bars.

Audiovisual patching: coupling modal acoustics to 3D geometry

Because Infinite executes both audio DSP and 3D graphics inside a unified graph, physical modal parameters can modulate procedural geometry in real time.

[Note Sequencer] ---> (notes) ---> [Metallic] ---> (audio) ---> [Gain] ---> [Audio Output]
                                       |
                                       +---> [Audio Analyze]
                                                    |
                                          (rms / peak / pitch)
                                                    |
                                                    v
[Mesh (Plate)] ---> [Audio Displacement] <----------+
                           |
                           v
                      [Render 3D]

Visualising Chladni nodal figures in 3D

To visualise the acoustic modes directly on a procedural surface:

  1. Spawn a Metallic node and select the Bell Bronze or Gong / Plate material preset.
  2. Connect a Note Sequencer node to the notes input slot of Metallic to drive rhythmic strikes with varying velocity.
  3. Route the audio output of Metallic into an Audio Analyze node.
  4. Spawn a Geometry node set to a high-resolution subdivided cylinder or plane (representing the physical plate).
  5. Cable the geometry into an Audio Displacement node.
  6. Patch the spectralRms or mode outputs from Audio Analyze into the displacement amplitude and frequency slots.
  7. As the Metallic node sounds, the surface vertices deform along the theoretical Bessel nodal rings. High-velocity strikes create dramatic surface ripples, which smoothly settle into stationary nodal rings as the modes decay.

You can explore functional examples of physical modelling and geometry patching in the Infinite patch library.

Building a complete physical percussion instrument in Infinite

Here is the step-by-step procedure to construct a complete, playable metallic percussion instrument from scratch:

1. Exciter and sequencing setup

Create a Note Sequencer node. Set division to 1/16 sync and dial length to 16 steps. Program an uneven rhythmic pattern with varied velocity steps.

Add a Random modulator node. Set its distribution to Gaussian, rate to 1/8 bar, and smoothing to 45 ms. Route this random value into the transient parameter of Metallic. Each strike now hits with a slightly different mallet snap and contact duration, avoiding repetitive transients.

2. Tuning and material selection

Open the Metallic node. Select Bell Bronze for deep metallic resonance, or Steel for bright melodic percussion. Set frequency to 220 Hz (A3).

If controlling via an external keyboard or MIDI controller, patch a MIDI Notes node into the notes slot. Metallic supports up to 8 polyphonic voices, tracking pitch across standard MIDI note numbers while maintaining inharmonic modal ratios.

3. Spatialisation and dynamics

Route Metallic's stereo output into a Gain node. Attenuate the master gain by -3.5 dB to prevent clipping during dense polyphonic strikes.

Add an Audio Filter node configured as a subtle high-shelf cut around 12 kHz to emulate room acoustic absorption, or apply subtle saturation using Gain's soft drive.

4. Interactive scope monitoring

Metallic features an integrated real-time oscilloscope in its node body. By observing the trace during a strike, you can visually monitor how the initial mallet transient gives way to sinusoidal modal decay. The node publishes decimated peak waveforms directly to the UI thread via ReadScope, ensuring visual feedback without audio dropouts.

Real-time execution constraints and performance bounds

Physical modelling synthesis requires strict computational discipline to ensure glitch-free audio execution.

In Infinite's audio engine:

  • The 12-mode resonator bank runs inside the audio callback at 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz.
  • Filter calculations use SIMD vectorisation where available, updating 12 poles and zeros in parallel chunks.
  • Parameter updates (such as decay, stiffness, and frequency) are delivered from the UI thread to the audio thread via atomic mailboxes (ParamMailbox), avoiding thread locks or memory allocation.
  • Voice allocation is handled dynamically: idle voices whose energy drops below -96 dB are put to sleep, keeping CPU utilisation under 2.5% on modern processors.

By combining the mathematical precision of acoustic wave equations with real-time modulation, modal synthesis transforms metallic percussion from static sampled hits into responsive, living acoustic instruments.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/modal-synthesis-and-physical-modelling-of-metallic-percussion.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Delaunay triangulation and Voronoi geometry in real time
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How real-time Delaunay triangulation and dual Voronoi cells work in creative coding: empty circumcircles, Bowyer-Watson, polygon insetting, and audio-reactive 3D.
item.content:encoded:
In computational geometry and procedural graphics, delaunay triangulation real time algorithms provide a method to generate clean, dynamic 3D meshes directly from shifting point clouds. While static meshes rely on pre-baked vertex index buffers that remain rigid during performance, dynamic triangulation reconstructs the topological connectivity between vertices on every frame. When combined with its mathematical dual, the Voronoi diagram, artists can transform particle clouds, audio waveforms, and spatial simulations into fluid geometric surfaces, faceted crystalline shells, and organic cellular tessellations.

In real-time audiovisual environments like Infinite, dynamic triangulation links sound synthesis with procedural 3D form. Because audio signals can displace spatial coordinates at frame rates, recalculating Delaunay triangles and Voronoi cells on the fly allows the topology of a mesh to split, merge, and reform in direct response to acoustic energy.

Here is an in-depth examination of the mathematical principles behind Delaunay triangulation, the Bowyer-Watson cavity insertion algorithm, dual Voronoi cell generation with polygon insetting, 3D heightfield lifting, and how to patch an audio-reactive mesh using native nodes.

Dynamic topology versus static meshes in computer graphics

Most 3D models in computer graphics are defined by two arrays: a vertex array containing spatial positions (x, y, z), normals, and texture coordinates, and an index array containing triplets of integers that reference those vertices to form triangular faces. In standard rendering pipelines, the index array is static. When a vertex shader or physics engine deforms the model, the vertices move, but the edges between them remain fixed.

This rigidity works well for character meshes and rigid bodies, but it limits generative and reactive art. If a cloud of particles expands, contracts, or swirls under turbulent forces, stretching static triangles produces long, distorted needles known as slivers. Slivers cause severe rendering artefacts, including rasterisation bottlenecks, pixel flickering, and erratic surface normals under directional lighting.

Dynamic triangulation solves this by recomputing the triangle index buffer on every cook cycle. As points drift, separate, or enter the scene, the algorithm evaluates spatial proximity and reconfigures the edge connections. When two particles move apart, their connecting edge dissolves, and new edges form between closer neighbours. This produces a continuous, surface-like manifold that adapts to whatever spatial distribution the simulation generates.

The empty circumcircle criterion and Bowyer-Watson insertion

A triangulation of a planar point set P is a collection of non-overlapping triangles whose vertices are in P and whose union covers the convex hull of P. For any set of three non-collinear points in the Cartesian plane, there exists a unique circle that passes through all three points: the circumcircle.

In 1934, Boris Delaunay proved that a triangulation is optimal if and only if the circumcircle of every triangle contains no points of P in its interior. This condition is the empty circumcircle criterion:

For every triangle T(a, b, c) in the triangulation:
Distance(p, Centre(T)) >= Radius(T)  for all points p in P

The empty circumcircle property possesses a critical geometric consequence: it maximises the minimum interior angle of all triangles in the mesh. By avoiding skinny, acute angles, Delaunay triangulation produces the most equiangular, well-proportioned triangles possible for any given distribution of vertices.

Computing the circumcircle in double precision

Given three 2D vertices a, b, and c, we can translate vertex a to the origin:

bx = b.x - a.x,   by = b.y - a.y
cx = c.x - a.x,   cy = c.y - a.y

The circumcentre offset (ux, uy) from a is found by solving the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of sides ab and ac. The system determinant D is:

D = 2.0 * (bx * cy - by * cx)

If abs(D) is close to zero, the three vertices are collinear, and no finite circumcircle exists. Otherwise, using the squared lengths b2 = bx*bx + by*by and c2 = cx*cx + cy*cy, the circumcentre (cx_circ, cy_circ) and radius squared r2 are:

ux = (cy * b2 - by * c2) / D
uy = (bx * c2 - cx * b2) / D

cx_circ = a.x + ux
cy_circ = a.y + uy
r2 = ux * ux + uy * uy

A point (px, py) violates the Delaunay criterion for this triangle if:

(px - cx_circ)^2 + (py - cy_circ)^2 < r2 * (1.0 - 1e-12)

The small epsilon tolerance 1e-12 prevents numerical instability when points lie almost exactly on the circumcircle boundary.

The Bowyer-Watson incremental algorithm

The Bowyer-Watson algorithm (developed independently by Adrian Bowyer and David Watson in 1981) inserts points one by one into an existing Delaunay triangulation:

  1. Initialise with a super-triangle: construct an artificial, expansive triangle that completely encloses the bounding box of the point set. This guarantees that all real points fall within at least one valid triangle.
  2. Find bad triangles: when inserting point p, scan the existing triangle list and identify every triangle whose circumcircle encloses p.
  3. Form the cavity: delete all bad triangles. The union of these deleted triangles forms a star-shaped polygonal cavity containing p. The boundary of this cavity consists of all edges that belonged to exactly one bad triangle.
  4. Sew new triangles: connect each edge of the cavity boundary to the new point p, creating a set of new triangles that satisfy the empty circumcircle criterion.
  5. Remove super-triangle vertices: once all points are inserted, discard every triangle that shares any vertex with the initial super-triangle. The remaining triangles form the Delaunay triangulation of the input points.

To maintain real-time performance at 60 FPS, the implementation in Infinite sorts points along a grid-snake spatial curve prior to insertion. Because sequentially inserted points are spatially adjacent, the set of invalid triangles remains local, allowing rapid cavity extraction. Furthermore, dead triangles are periodically compacted in memory to prevent the traversal loop from scanning discarded entries.

Building the Voronoi dual and polygon insetting

Every Delaunay triangulation has a unique geometric dual: the Voronoi diagram (first studied by Georgy Voronoy in 1908). While Delaunay triangulation partitions space into triangles connecting neighbouring sites, the Voronoi diagram partitions space into convex polygonal cells, where each cell contains all spatial locations closer to its generating site than to any other site.

The duality between the two structures is exact:

  • Each circumcentre of a Delaunay triangle becomes a vertex of the Voronoi diagram.
  • Each edge in the Delaunay triangulation corresponds to a shared boundary edge in the Voronoi diagram, running perpendicular to the Delaunay edge.
  • Each site in the Delaunay triangulation is surrounded by a Voronoi polygon whose vertices are the circumcentres of the Delaunay triangles sharing that site.

Extracting Voronoi cells from triangle fans

To construct Voronoi cells from the triangulated mesh, the Voronoi Cells node in Infinite executes the following steps:

  1. Count edge usage: iterate through all Delaunay triangles and count how many times each undirected edge appears. Edges that appear exactly once form the convex hull of the point cloud.
  2. Prune hull vertices: sites that lie on the convex hull have unbounded Voronoi cells that extend to infinity. These are flagged and skipped so that only well-defined, closed interior cells are generated.
  3. Assemble triangle fans: for each interior site, collect the indices of all triangles meeting at that site.
  4. Sort circumcentres radially: calculate the circumcentre of each triangle in the fan and compute its polar angle relative to the site: angle = atan2(cy - site_y, cx - site_x). Sorting the circumcentres by angle arranges the vertices of the Voronoi cell in counter-clockwise order.
  5. Cap sliver circumcentres: triangles near the outer boundary can occasionally have circumcentres that lie far outside the cloud. The engine clamps the distance of any circumcentre to at most twice the maximum radius of the triangle, preventing spikes from rupturing the cell layout.

Polygon insetting for architectural and cellular aesthetics

A flat tessellation where all cells touch edge-to-edge can look monolithic. The Voronoi Cells node includes an inset parameter (ranging from 0.0 to 0.95) that scales each cell towards its generating site:

inset_vertex = site + (circumcentre - site) * (1.0 - inset)

When inset is zero, cells share mutual boundaries. As inset increases, channels open up between adjacent cells, revealing negative space. The node triangulates each inset cell by creating a central vertex at the site position and generating a fan of triangular faces connecting the centre to each pair of adjacent perimeter vertices.

This insetting mechanism enables diverse creative styles, ranging from stained-glass windows and architectural ceiling cassettes to cracked desert mud and microscopic cellular membranes.

Projecting planes and lifting back to three dimensions

While 2D Delaunay algorithms are mathematically robust and computationally tractable in real time, many generative audiovisual scenes require 3D geometry. Calculating true 3D Delaunay tetrahedralisation is substantially more expensive, $O(n^2)$ to $O(n^4)$, and yields solid 3D tetrahedra rather than a hollow, renderable 2D surface manifold.

To solve this, Infinite uses a 2.5D projection and lifting architecture in DelaunayMeshNode:

  1. Projection: the user selects a projection plane via the plane parameter (0: XY, 1: XZ, 2: YZ). The 3D coordinates (px, py, pz) of each site are projected onto the selected 2D plane:
  • For XY, the projected coordinates are (u = px, v = py), facing normal (0, 0, 1).
  • For XZ, the projected coordinates are (u = pz, v = px), facing normal (0, 1, 0).
  • For YZ, the projected coordinates are (u = py, v = pz), facing normal (1, 0, 0).
  1. Planar triangulation: the 2D projected coordinates are triangulated using the Bowyer-Watson engine. Texture coordinates (u, v) are normalised across the bounding box of the cloud to enable texture mapping.
  2. Elevation lifting: once the triangle topology is established, the original third unprojected coordinate is restored for each vertex.

When a point cloud has elevation, such as an audio-displaced particle grid or terrain heights, the 2D triangulation acts as a surface mesh lifted into 3D space. The resulting surface bends, folds, and undulates with the underlying simulation, creating an expressive terrain that never tears or overlaps unnaturally.

Patching an audio-reactive mesh in Infinite

Building a complete real-time audiovisual patch using Delaunay and Voronoi nodes involves connecting audio analysis, procedural point generation, geometry operations, and 3D rendering.

Here is a recommended node graph layout:

[Audio Input] -> [Audio Analyze]
                       |
               (FFT low / mid / high)
                       |
                       v
[Point Distribution] -> [Audio Displacement] -> [Delaunay Mesh] -> [Material] -> [Render 3D]
                                                     |
                                            (or [Voronoi Cells])

1. Generating the point cloud

Add a Point Distribution node to spawn the initial site positions. You can set the distribution mode to a 2D Poisson disc distribution or a random planar scatter. Alternatively, a Particle System node can be used to simulate floating particles driven by curl noise and velocity damping.

Set the point count to approximately 800 to 1,500 points. This provides high geometric detail while leaving headroom for other synthesis and graphics nodes on the canvas.

2. Audio displacement

Wire the audio output from a synth, sampler, or live audio track into an Audio Analyze node. The node extracts an 8-band FFT spectrum and transient onset detectors.

Patch the point cloud from Point Distribution into the geometry input of an Audio Displacement node. Map the low-frequency bass band to the vertical displacement axis. When a kick drum hits, the points push upward in world space.

3. Mesh construction with Delaunay Mesh

Connect the displaced points into a Delaunay Mesh node. Configure its parameters:

  • plane: select XZ so the triangulation occurs across the horizontal ground plane while the audio displacement lifts vertices along the Y axis.
  • aliveOnly: enable this toggle when using particles so that dead particles are excluded before triangulation.
  • maxPoints: set to 2000 to protect the rendering loop against unexpected particle bursts.

As the points move under the influence of the audio signal, the Delaunay engine dynamically recalculates the triangle indices. If you switch the node to Voronoi Cells and set inset to 0.20, the mesh transforms into an array of floating, isolated tiles that pulse and tilt with the sound.

4. Shading and rendering

Wire the mesh output into a Material node. Set the roughness to 0.3 and metallic to 0.8 to give the facets a reflective, polished finish.

Connect the material into a Render 3D node alongside a Directional Light and a Camera 3D. As the facets shift their orientation each frame, specular highlights glint across the changing edges, producing a visual response synchronized to the music.

For further exploration of shader uniforms and procedural deformation techniques, refer to our guide on procedural 3D geometry nodes and audio deformation and our walkthrough of audio-reactive particle systems in real time.

Computational complexity, spatial sorting, and point budgets

Understanding the computational performance of dynamic triangulation is essential for maintaining a stable 60 FPS frame rate in live performances.

Time complexity and memory compaction

A naive implementation of the Bowyer-Watson algorithm tests every inserted point against all existing triangles, resulting in an $O(n^2)$ worst-case time complexity. For 1,000 points, this requires approximately 1,000,000 circumcircle checks.

To optimise this for real-time operation, Infinite uses a grid-snake spatial sort. By sorting points into a 2D spatial grid prior to insertion, each point is placed into the mesh immediately adjacent to the triangles created by its spatial predecessor. This keeps the cavity search local and reduces average-case execution time towards $O(n \log n)$.

Furthermore, during cavity deletion, bad triangles are marked dead. In a long insertion loop, dead triangles can clutter memory and slow down linear scans. Infinite's core Delaunay implementation checks when the triangle array exceeds 4,096 entries and automatically compacts the array by copying live triangles into contiguous memory.

Practical point budgeting

For real-time graphics at 60 FPS, a frame budget is roughly 16.6 milliseconds. In a combined audiovisual patch, audio processing typically takes 1 to 2 ms, GPU shader passes take 4 to 8 ms, leaving approximately 3 to 5 ms for CPU geometry calculations.

Based on benchmark tests across Apple Silicon and x86_64 architectures:

  • 300 to 600 points: cook time is under 0.6 ms. This is ideal when multiple meshes are active simultaneously or when running complex GLSL post-processing effects.
  • 1,000 to 1,800 points: cook time is 1.2 to 2.4 ms. This produces dense, intricate geometric surfaces with crisp silhouette details.
  • 2,500 to 5,000 points: cook time reaches 4.5 to 9.0 ms. While viable on dedicated desktop machines, it approaches the limit of real-time responsiveness and should be used cautiously in live VJ contexts.

Infinite enforces a configurable maxPoints cap (defaulting to 2,000 points) on both Delaunay Mesh and Voronoi Cells. If an upstream particle emitter exceeds this threshold, the node systematically subsamples the sites to maintain real-time stability rather than dropping frames.

Practical creative workflows and aesthetic applications

Dynamic Delaunay and Voronoi geometry opens up distinct visual aesthetics that are difficult to achieve with standard polygonal modeling:

  • Low-poly crystalline landscapes: by displacing an XZ particle grid with Perlin noise and audio low-end, Delaunay triangulation forms a faceted, low-poly mountain range where polygons continuously adapt to the contours.
  • Shattered glass and Voronoi fracture: mapping an audio onset trigger to the inset control creates the illusion of an impact crater, where a smooth surface abruptly fractures into hundreds of receding tiles when a snare drum fires.
  • Cellular lifeforms and organic membranes: pairing Voronoi Cells with curl-noise particle flow simulates the movement of microscopic cells drifting under fluid currents.
  • Dynamic wireframe webs: extracting the edges of the Delaunay mesh and rendering them as geometric lines yields a retro-futuristic radar web that connects points when they approach each other and severs links when they diverge.

You can inspect ready-to-run audiovisual patches and templates in the Infinite Library, or explore the core architecture on the Infinite home page. Dynamic triangulation bridges the gap between chaotic point distributions and ordered 3D surfaces, turning raw mathematical coordinates into living generative visuals.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/delaunay-triangulation-and-voronoi-geometry-in-real-time.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Physical modelling string synthesis in real time
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How physical modelling string synthesis works: digital waveguides, Karplus-Strong delay loops, allpass dispersion, bow friction, and acoustic modal bodies.
item.content:encoded:
Physical modelling synthesis generates sound by simulating the actual physical mechanics of vibrating matter rather than playing static wavetables or filtering raw geometric waveforms. While traditional subtractive synthesis uses mathematical approximations like saw and square waves, and sample libraries replay pre-recorded audio recordings of instruments, physical modelling calculates the physical wave propagation, boundary reflections, internal material damping, and structural resonance of acoustic objects in code.

When you pluck, strike, or bow an acoustic string, its sonic timbre evolves dynamically across every note. The attack transient reflects the pick position along the string length, the mechanical stiffness produces subtle inharmonic frequency shifts across higher partials, and the wooden instrument body colours the acoustic radiation through dozens of coupled resonant modes.

In real-time audiovisual environments like Infinite, physical modelling provides an expressive foundation for both sound design and generative visuals. Because the underlying physical variables (such as string velocity, bridge displacement, and energy dissipation) are evaluated directly on the audio thread, they can be routed seamlessly into 3D geometry deformation and real-time shaders.

Here is an in-depth examination of how digital waveguide physical modelling operates, how fractional allpass filters maintain pitch accuracy, how dispersion creates natural inharmonicity, how exciter mechanics simulate plucking, striking, and bowing, and how to patch a complete physical modelling instrument using native nodes.

What physical modelling solves in computer music

The central challenge with electronic instruments is acoustic realism and continuous expressiveness. A sampled acoustic guitar or cello can capture the timbre of an isolated note, but it struggles with real-time articulation. When a performer alters bow pressure, slides between frets, or alternates between fingerpicking and a sharp plectrum, a sample library must crossfade between distinct recordings. This often creates phase cancellation, unnatural chorusing, or static, repetitive transients known as the machine-gun effect.

Subtractive synthesis offers continuous modulation through filters and envelopes, but its harmonic structure remains synthetic. An oscillator running through a resonant lowpass filter lacks the complex modal distribution and material losses of real wood and vibrating steel.

Physical modelling solves this by simulating the physical acoustic system from first principles. When you alter a parameter like string stiffness or bow velocity, you are not adjusting an artificial audio filter: you are modifying the physical differential equation governing wave motion. The resulting acoustic response reacts organically, producing natural transients, sympathetic resonance, and expressive feedback.

Digital waveguides: bidirectional delay lines and wave propagation

The foundation of modern string modelling is the digital waveguide, formulated by Julius O. Smith (1992) as an extension of the pioneering Karplus-Strong plucked string algorithm (1983).

The physical motion of an ideal vibrating string is governed by the one-dimensional acoustic wave equation:

d^2 y / dt^2 = c^2 * (d^2 y / dx^2)

Where y represents transverse displacement, t is time, x is the spatial coordinate along the string, and c is the wave propagation speed determined by string tension T and linear mass density mu (c = sqrt(T / mu)).

D'Alembert showed that any solution to this differential equation can be decomposed into two independent travelling waves moving in opposite directions:

y(x, t) = y_plus(t - x/c) + y_minus(t + x/c)

Here, y_plus represents a wave travelling to the right (towards the bridge), and y_minus represents a wave travelling to the left (towards the nut).

Discretisation into digital delay lines

In a computer simulation, continuous spatial wave propagation is discretised into two tapped delay lines. The total round-trip propagation time corresponds to the period of the fundamental frequency f_0:

Period T = 1.0 / f_0
Delay samples N = f_s / f_0

Where f_s is the digital sample rate (such as 44,100 Hz or 48,000 Hz).

At the string boundaries, the travelling waves undergo physical reflections:

  1. The nut (fret boundary): Assumed to be rigid. The string displacement must be zero at x = 0, forcing an inverting reflection with reflection coefficient R_0 = -1. The wave reflects with inverted phase.
  2. The bridge: The string terminates at a bridge that transfers energy to the resonant instrument body. The bridge reflection is modelled by an inverting reflection combined with a frequency-dependent loop filter H_loop(z) that accounts for energy loss and phase delay.

When a pulse is injected into the bidirectional delay loop, it travels back and forth between the nut and bridge. Each round trip corresponds to one cycle of the fundamental pitch, producing a rich harmonic spectrum.

Tuning and fractional delay: solving the phase allpass filter

In a naive digital delay line, the buffer length is constrained to integer sample counts N = floor(f_s / f_0).

This creates a serious musical problem: pitch quantization. For high notes, the integer rounding error causes severe out-of-tune intonation. For instance, at a sample rate of 48 kHz:

  • A note at 1000 Hz requires 48000 / 1000 = 48.0 samples.
  • The next semitone up (1059.25 Hz) requires 48000 / 1059.25 = 45.315 samples.
  • Rounding to 45 samples produces 1066.67 Hz, an unacceptable tuning error of over 12 cents.

To achieve exact microtonal and chromatic intonation, the delay loop must support fractional sample delays.

The first-order allpass filter

In the native String node in Infinite, fractional delay is implemented using a first-order allpass filter:

A(z) = (a + z^-1) / (1.0 + a * z^-1)

An allpass filter has a flat magnitude frequency response of exactly 1.0 across all frequencies, but its phase response introduces a controllable group delay without causing any artificial attenuation or damping in the loop.

The phase delay D(w) of the allpass filter at angular frequency w radians per sample is:

D(w) = - (atan2(-sin(w), a + cos(w)) - atan2(-a * sin(w), 1.0 + a * cos(w))) / w

Because delay decreases monotonically as coefficient a rises, the engine solves for the exact coefficient a using a numerical bisection solver across 40 iterations on every parameter update chunk:

double SolveAllpass(double delay, double w)
{
   double lo = -0.95, hi = 0.95;
   for (int it = 0; it < 40; it++)
   {
      const double mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi);
      if (AllpassDelay(mid, w) > delay)
         lo = mid;
      else
         hi = mid;
   }
   return 0.5 * (lo + hi);
}

By subtracting the fractional delay of the allpass filter and loop filter from the total delay requirement, the fundamental pitch f_0 remains mathematically exact, regardless of how other controls like decay, tone, and stiffness are adjusted.

Dispersion and stiffness: inharmonicity across higher partials

In a purely flexible, mathematical string, all harmonic partials are exact integer multiples of the fundamental frequency: f_k = k * f_0.

Real physical strings (such as piano wire, bass guitar strings, or harp strings), however, possess inherent bending stiffness. A stiff wire resists bending, introducing an additional restoring force governed by the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation:

d^2 y / dt^2 = c^2 * (d^2 y / dx^2) - kappa^2 * (d^4 y / dx^4)

Where kappa is the stiffness parameter.

The consequence of this fourth-order derivative is dispersion: higher-frequency waves travel along the string faster than lower-frequency waves. As a result, the higher partials are displaced upwards in frequency, following the inharmonicity formula:

f_k = k * f_0 * sqrt(1.0 + B * k^2)

Where B is the inharmonicity coefficient.

Modelling dispersion with allpass cascades

Without stiffness, a plucked digital string sounds sterile and electronic, resembling a simple comb-filtered pulse. When stiffness is introduced, the upper partials ring with the distinct metallic attack and organic complexity heard in real acoustic instruments.

In Infinite's String node, dispersion is implemented using a cascade of four first-order allpass filters placed directly in the feedback path of the bridge. Each allpass stage adds frequency-dependent phase delay, slightly advancing the arrival time of higher harmonics relative to the fundamental.

Modulating the stiffness parameter shifts the string character from a warm, flexible nylon classical guitar string to a taut, clanging steel piano wire or metallic bass string.

Exciter mechanics: pluck, hammer strike, and bow friction

A physical string model requires an excitation source to inject kinetic energy into the delay lines. The nature of this excitation dictates whether the instrument sounds plucked, struck, or bowed.

The String node features three distinct physical exciter models:

1. Pluck excitation

A plectrum or finger plucks a string by displacing it at a specific normalised position x_rel (from 0.0 at the bridge to 1.0 at the nut). When released, the initial triangular displacement splits into two identical half-amplitude pulses propagating in opposite directions towards the nut and bridge.

The point of excitation introduces comb filtering. Plucking near the bridge (position = 0.1) suppresses low frequencies and emphasizes sharp, nasal upper harmonics. Plucking near the centre (position = 0.5) eliminates even harmonics, producing a hollow, clarinet-like tone.

The hardness parameter controls the pulse duration. A hard pick generates an instantaneous sharp spike, exciting high-frequency energy up to the Nyquist frequency. A soft finger widens the pulse up to tenfold, naturally rounding and softening the transient attack.

2. Strike excitation

A strike models a piano or dulcimer felt hammer hitting the string. Unlike an instantaneous pluck, a felt hammer has physical mass and compliant elasticity.

The interaction is non-linear: a soft strike compresses the felt gently, resulting in a prolonged contact duration and a warm, mellow tone. A heavy strike compresses the felt rapidly into its dense wooden core, drastically shortening the contact duration and releasing a burst of bright, forceful upper partials.

In code, the pulse length scales dynamically with incoming note velocity:

pulseLen = max(2, round(sampleRate * (0.004 - 0.003 * velocity)));

3. Bow excitation (Smith's friction junction)

Bowing a string is a continuous, self-oscillating non-linear process driven by friction between sticky rosin-coated horsehair and the string.

The bow moves at a constant speed v_bow. The interaction alternates rapidly between two phases:

  • Stick phase: Static friction holds the string against the bow hair, dragging the string along with the bow until tension forces overcome friction.
  • Slip phase: The string breaks free and snaps backwards towards its resting point under dynamic friction.

This stick-slip mechanism is modelled using a non-linear friction characteristic curve:

F_friction(v_rel) = sign(v_rel) * (mu_dynamic + (mu_static - mu_dynamic) * exp(-c * |v_rel|)) * F_bow

Where v_rel = v_bow - v_string is the relative velocity between bow and string, and F_bow is normal bow pressure.

The String node implements bow friction with oversampled integration (up to 8x internal oversampling for high notes) to eliminate digital limit cycles. Modulating the pressure and noise parameters allows you to recreate authentic string scrapes, raspy rosin friction, and the smooth transition into pure sustained Helmholtz bowing.

Acoustic radiation: mode tables and modal bodies

An isolated vibrating string has very little surface area. In an acoustic instrument, virtually all audible sound radiates from the resonant wooden soundboard and body cavity (the body of a guitar, violin, or cello).

The instrument body acts as a complex acoustic filter with dozens of closely spaced resonant peaks. Rather than running a static graphic equaliser, Infinite couples the string output to a shared modal resonator bank (DenseBody).

The body simulation evaluates ten parallel second-order modal bandpass resonators, each configured with an exact centre frequency, bandwidth, and amplitude mode table:

y_body(t) = sum_{m=1}^{10} A_m * exp(-alpha_m * t) * sin(omega_m * t + phi_m)

Infinite includes five calibrated body profiles fitted from acoustic measurements of real instruments:

Body profileKey acoustic resonancesSonic character
BoxHelmholtz cavity (98 Hz) and primary plate mode (204 Hz)Small hollow acoustic box with dry, woody decay
GuitarAir mode A0 (99 Hz), top plate T(1,1) pair (199 Hz, 392 Hz)Warm, balanced acoustic dreadnought and classical guitar
HarpSoundboard resonance (211 Hz) and pillar modes (325 Hz)Open, airy, resonant decay with singing sustain
ViolinAir mode A0 (281 Hz), corpus corpus modes B1-/B1+ (445 Hz, 535 Hz)Focused, expressive acoustic projection with bite
CelloDeep cavity mode (105 Hz) and body resonances (199 Hz, 320 Hz)Rich, woody, authoritative low-frequency resonance

Because all active polyphonic voices feed into the same shared body filter, notes interact acoustically, vibrating the simulated soundboard and creating natural sympathetic depth.

Building an audiovisual physical modelling patch in Infinite

In Infinite, sound synthesis and visual rendering run on the same unified graph. You can patch an expressive physical modelling instrument and use its internal acoustics to deform 3D meshes in real time.

+----------------+      note       +------------------+      audio      +------------------+
| Note Sequencer | --------------> | String (Synth)   | --------------> | Resonator Bank   |
+----------------+                 +------------------+                 +------------------+
                                            ^                                    |
                                            | pressure mod                       | audio
+----------------+                          |                                    v
| LFO            | -------------------------+                           +------------------+
+----------------+                                                      | Audio Analyze    |
                                                                        +------------------+
                                                                                 |
                                                                                 | spectral RMS
                                                                                 v
+----------------+      mesh       +--------------------+      mesh     +------------------+
| Cylinder Wire  | --------------> | Audio Displacement | ------------> | Render 3D        |
+----------------+                 +--------------------+               +------------------+

Step 1: Create the note driver and exciter

  1. Add a Note Sequencer node to the canvas. Set division to 1/16 sync and program an arpeggiated melodic line.
  2. Add a String node. Connect the green note output of the Note Sequencer to the notes input of the String node.
  3. On the String node, select exciter: Bow and choose bodyType: Cello.
  4. Set decay to 2.4 s, stiffness to 0.30, and tone to 0.75.

Step 2: Add dynamic expressive modulation

  1. Add an LFO node. Set the shape to Triangle and tempo-sync the rate to 1/2 bar.
  2. Connect the LFO output cable to the pressure parameter of the String node. As the LFO oscillates, the simulated bow pressure increases and relaxes, moving naturally between gentle whispers and raspy, full-bodied string sustains.
  3. Add a second slow LFO (or an envelope follower) routed to position, moving the bowing point between the bridge (sul ponticello) and the fingerboard (sul tasto).

Step 3: Route through the modal resonator and analysis

  1. Connect the audio output of String to a Resonator Bank node to introduce room resonance and spatial depth.
  2. Connect the output to an Audio Analyze node. This extracts real-time amplitude envelopes, spectral RMS energy, and pitch tracking data on every audio buffer.

Step 4: Deform 3D geometry in Render 3D

  1. Add a Cylinder mesh primitive and set it to wireframe mode to represent a vibrating physical string.
  2. Add an Audio Displacement node. Connect the mesh output into its geometry input, and connect the spectralRms output from Audio Analyze to the displacement amplitude.
  3. Wire the resulting geometry into Render 3D.

When a note is bowed, the 3D string geometry physically vibrates with travelling wave deformations matching the exact frequency, damping, and decay of the acoustic digital waveguide.

Performance characteristics and real-time execution

Running complex numerical differential equations and allpass filter cascades in real time requires strict computational discipline:

  • Eight-voice polyphony: The String node supports up to 8 polyphonic voices. Unused voices are culled instantaneously when their decay envelope drops below -96 dB, conserving CPU cycles.
  • Chunked parameter updates: Heavy mathematical operations (such as the 40-iteration allpass phase solver and modal coefficient recalculations) run once every 32 samples (0.7 ms at 48 kHz). Sample-rate audio buffers interpolate these values using lock-free atomic parameter mailboxes, avoiding audio dropouts or zipper noise.
  • SIMD vectorisation: The modal body filter bank evaluates multiple biquad modes in parallel using AVX2 and ARM Neon vector instructions.
  • Zero dynamic memory allocations: All waveguide ring buffers, allpass delay lines, and mode state arrays are statically pre-allocated at startup. The audio thread executes without heap allocations or mutex contention.

By combining the physical mathematics of acoustic wave propagation with real-time modular execution, physical modelling synthesis delivers responsive instruments that feel alive under your fingers and on screen.

Explore native sound design and modular synthesis in the Infinite Library, inspect the full Node Reference, or read our deep dive on audio-reactive GLSL shaders.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/physical-modelling-string-synthesis-in-real-time.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Wave terrain synthesis: audio from 3D surfaces
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How wave terrain synthesis works: orbital trajectories, 3D surfaces, discrete Fourier transform anti-aliasing, and patching audio-visual synths in Infinite.
item.content:encoded:
Wave terrain synthesis is one of the most expressive, mathematically elegant methods for generating sound from visual geometry. Instead of reading through one-dimensional wavetables or computing traditional trigonometric oscillator formulas, a wave terrain synthesiser treats sound generation as a particle travelling across a three-dimensional topographic landscape.

As an orbital trajectory scans across the contours, ridges, and valleys of this surface at audio rates, the instantaneous height of the terrain produces an acoustic waveform. When the landscape shifts or the trajectory rotates, the harmonic spectrum morphs continuously, producing organic timbres that range from acoustic woodwinds to evolving crystalline drones.

Although conceptualised decades ago by researchers including Mitsuhashi and Curtis Roads, real-time wave terrain synthesis remained rare in traditional digital audio workstations. The technique requires simultaneous high-resolution two-dimensional image processing and sample-accurate numerical audio digital signal processing. In Infinite, audio synthesis and computer graphics share a single execution graph, making native wave terrain synthesis available directly on the modular canvas.

Here is an analysis of how wave terrain synthesis operates, the mathematics of two-dimensional orbital scanning, how discrete Fourier transform mip pyramids eliminate Nyquist aliasing, and how to patch an audio-visual wave terrain instrument using native nodes.

What is wave terrain synthesis

Traditional wavetable synthesis reads through a sequence of one-dimensional periodic arrays: $s(t) = W(\phi(t))$, where $\phi(t)$ represents the normalised phase accumulator advancing from zero to one. While wavetable position modulation allows timbral movement, the sound remains constrained to a linear path through pre-recorded cycles.

Wave terrain synthesis expands this concept into two spatial dimensions. A two-dimensional terrain function $z = T(u, v)$ defines a continuous surface over the normalised coordinate plane $(u, v) \in [0, 1] \times [0, 1]$. An orbital path generator computes a closed two-dimensional trajectory $(u(t), v(t))$ that repeats at the fundamental frequency $f_0$ of the played musical note:

s(t) = T(u(t), v(t))

The resulting audio waveform $s(t)$ depends on two independent factors:

  1. The topography of the terrain: The static shape or dynamic motion of the surface $T(u, v)$, including its gradients, crests, and saddle points.
  2. The geometry of the orbit: The shape, scale, centre offset, and orientation of the path $(u(t), v(t))$ traced across the surface.

This decoupling gives sound designers two distinct modulation axes. Modulating the orbit changes the harmonic balance and formant character of each note. Modulating the underlying terrain changes the underlying timbre and physical presence of the entire patch.

The mathematics of wave terrains: functions and image rasters

In mathematical theory, a wave terrain can be defined by explicit continuous equations, such as polynomials, sums of sine products, or saddle functions:

T(u, v) = cos(2π u) · sin(2π v) + 0.5 · sin(4π (u + v))

In modular creative coding environments like Infinite, terrains can also be derived directly from dynamic image textures. Video feeds, procedural noise, reaction-diffusion simulations, and generative pixel shaders can all serve as live wave terrains.

When an image texture supplies the terrain, the continuous coordinate $(u, v)$ must be sampled from a discrete raster of pixels with width $W$ and height $H$. To prevent steppy, noisy distortion when the orbit moves between discrete pixel centres, the synthesiser applies bilinear interpolation:

fx = u · W - 0.5
fy = v · H - 0.5

x0 = floor(fx),  x1 = x0 + 1
y0 = floor(fy),  y1 = y0 + 1

tx = fx - x0
ty = fy - y0

T(u, v) = (1 - tx)(1 - ty)c00 + tx(1 - ty)c10 + (1 - tx)ty c01 + tx ty c11

Here, $c_{00}, c_{10}, c_{01}, c_{11}$ represent the scalar values extracted from the four nearest neighbouring pixels. In Infinite's Wave Terrain node, the wtChan parameter determines how multi-channel colour data maps to surface elevation:

  • Luminance: Computes perceived brightness using standard colourimetric weighting: $0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B$. Smooth gradients produce warm, rounded harmonic spectra.
  • Red, green, blue, and alpha: Solos a single colour channel. Useful when complex multi-pass shaders encode distinct mathematical data into separate colour channels.
  • Edge magnitude: Computes the absolute gradient from median luminance: $|Luminance - 0.5| \times 2.0$. This mode isolates high-contrast boundaries in textures, generating bright, metallic overtones with punchy attacks.

Because texture coordinates wrap periodically, orbital paths that exceed the unit boundary seamlessly loop around the terrain edges without clicks or discontinuity.

Kinematic scanning: orbital trajectories in two dimensions

The path $(u(t), v(t))$ determines which contours of the terrain are read during each audio cycle. For a note with fundamental frequency $f_0$, the normalised phase $t$ advances across $[0, 1)$ at rate $f_0 / f_s$, where $f_s$ is the audio sampling rate (typically 48,000 Hz).

Infinite provides five distinct orbital geometries, each offering unique harmonic characteristics:

1. Elliptical orbits (kOrbitCircle)

The simplest trajectory is an ellipse centred at $(c_x, c_y)$ with radii $(r_x, r_y)$ and phase offset $\phi$:

u(t) = cx + rx · cos(2π t)
v(t) = cy + ry · sin(2π t + 2π φ)

When $r_x = r_y$ and $\phi = 0$, the orbit traces a circle. Increasing or decreasing the radii scales the amplitude of modulation across the terrain, acting similarly to the modulation index in frequency modulation synthesis. Small radii inspect local, gentle slopes, yielding warm sine-like tones. Large radii traverse steep peaks and troughs, producing complex spectra rich in high-order harmonics.

2. Lissajous figures (kOrbitLissajous)

Lissajous trajectories introduce harmonic ratio multipliers $\text{ratioA}$ and $\text{ratioB}$ on the horizontal and vertical axes:

u(t) = cx + rx · sin(2π t · ratioA + 2π φ)
v(t) = cy + ry · sin(2π t · ratioB)

When $\text{ratioA}$ and $\text{ratioB}$ form integer proportions such as 3:2, 4:3, or 5:4, the orbit loops through intricate figure-eight and braided geometries. Because the path revisits different parts of the terrain at sub-harmonic intervals, Lissajous orbits generate vocal formants and bell-like inharmonic overtones reminiscent of complex wavefolding.

3. Lemniscate of Bernoulli (kOrbitLemniscate)

The lemniscate traces a continuous infinity loop across the terrain:

denom = 1 + sin²(2π t)
u(t) = cx + rx · cos(2π t) / denom
v(t) = cy + ry · sin(2π t) · cos(2π t) / denom

The lemniscate features an inflection point at the centre of the loop where velocity reaches its maximum. When scanned across a non-linear terrain, this velocity profile creates rich acoustic asymmetry, producing hollow, woody resonances similar to acoustic clarinets and bowed strings.

4. Archimedean spirals (kOrbitSpiral)

The spiral trajectory expands outwards over multiple rotations before cycling:

rFactor = 0.2 + 0.8 · t
u(t) = cx + rx · rFactor · cos(2π t · turns)
v(t) = cy + ry · rFactor · sin(2π t · turns)

Spirals cross concentric contours, generating sweeping spectral motion even on static terrains.

5. Scanline rasterisation (kOrbitScanline)

The scanline orbit sweeps linearly across the horizontal axis while stepping the vertical coordinate across discrete frames. This produces biting, digital wavetable-style timbres ideal for aggressive basslines.

Eliminating aliasing: discrete Fourier transform mip levels

A major challenge in wave terrain synthesis is digital aliasing. When an orbit traces across sharp cliffs, high-frequency noise, or steep gradients on a terrain, the resulting waveform $s(t)$ contains harmonics that can extend far beyond the Nyquist limit ($f_s / 2 = 24,000\text{ Hz}$). Without band-limiting, these harmonics fold back across the Nyquist threshold, creating unmusical, harsh intermodulation distortion.

To solve this, Infinite's real-time digital signal processing engine uses a Cooley-Tukey Radix-2 fast Fourier transform (FFT) pipeline with an exact 10-level mip pyramid.

The 1024-point Radix-2 FFT pipeline

During preparation, the synthesiser pre-samples the selected orbit across 8 morph frames into 1024-sample wavetable buffers. Each buffer undergoes a forward discrete Fourier transform:

// Forward Cooley-Tukey Radix-2 FFT (N = 1024)
Radix2FFT::Instance().Forward(realBuffer, imagBuffer);

Once in the frequency domain, the spectrum consists of 512 discrete harmonic bins. The engine computes 10 band-limited mip levels, where each successive level halves the maximum allowable harmonic index:

  • Mip 0: Contains all 512 harmonics. Used for low bass notes ($20\text{ Hz} - 90\text{ Hz}$) where the 512th harmonic remains below 24,000 Hz.
  • Mip 1: Band-limited to 256 harmonics ($90\text{ Hz} - 180\text{ Hz}$).
  • Mip 2: Band-limited to 128 harmonics ($180\text{ Hz} - 370\text{ Hz}$).
  • Mip 3: Band-limited to 64 harmonics ($370\text{ Hz} - 750\text{ Hz}$).
  • ...
  • Mip 9: Band-limited to a single fundamental harmonic (pure sine wave) for high soprano registers above 10,000 Hz.

For each mip level, harmonics above the cutoff threshold are zeroed out, and an inverse FFT reconstructs a clean, alias-free time-domain cycle:

Radix2FFT::Instance().Inverse(realBuffer, imagBuffer);

During real-time voice rendering, the audio engine calculates the exact continuous pitch of the note, determines the fractional mip level, and blends between the two adjacent mip tables using cubic Hermite interpolation. This guarantees more than 80 dB of aliasing suppression across all 8 octaves of the keyboard.

Polyphony, unison voicing, and filtering

The Wave Terrain node in Infinite includes full performance architecture built into the DSP engine:

8-voice polyphony

The node maintains eight independent polyphonic voices. Each voice tracks its own MIDI note number, note frequency, phase accumulator, and four-stage ADSR envelope (attack, decay, sustain, release). When a chord is played, each voice samples the terrain at its own independent playback speed, preserving harmonic clarity across complex intervals.

Unison detuning and stereo spreading

For thick lead sounds and wide ambient textures, the engine supports up to 8 unison sub-voices per note:

  • Detune: Spreads unison voice frequencies apart by up to 100 cents using calibrated logarithmic detune curves.
  • Stereo width: Pans unison voice pairs symmetrically across the stereo field from -1.0 (hard left) to +1.0 (hard right).

Multi-mode resonant filter

After terrain evaluation and unison summing, the signal passes into an internal state-variable filter. The filter offers 12 dB, 24 dB, and 36 dB slopes in lowpass, highpass, bandpass, and notch modes, controllable via cutoff, resonance, and drive.

Patching wave terrain synthesis in Infinite

Connecting a wave terrain synthesiser on Infinite's canvas takes less than a minute. Because image cables, note cables, and audio cables all coexist on the same workspace, visual and acoustic nodes link directly together.

[Reaction-Diffusion] (texture) ──> (texture) [Wave Terrain] ──> [Audio Out]
                                          ▲
[Keyboard / Sequencer] (notes) ───────────┘

Step 1: Add the terrain source

Add a generative visual node to supply the landscape:

  1. Press Shift+A and select Visuals > Reaction-Diffusion.
  2. Set the algorithm parameters to generate organic Turing patterns: feed = 0.054, kill = 0.062.
  3. Adjust the simulation speed to 0.25 so the visual patterns slowly pulse and drift over time.

Step 2: Add the Wave Terrain synthesiser

  1. Press Shift+A and select Synths > Wave Terrain.
  2. Connect the out (picture) pin of Reaction-Diffusion to the texture input of Wave Terrain.
  3. Set wtOrbit to Lemniscate.
  4. Set wtChan to Luminance.
  5. Set unison to 3 and detune to 14 cents for subtle chorus movement.

Step 3: Trigger notes and monitor output

  1. Press Shift+A and select Notes > Keyboard (or Random Note Generator for automated generative playback).
  2. Connect the note output to the note input of Wave Terrain.
  3. Connect the audio output of Wave Terrain to an Audio Out node.

When you play notes, you will hear a rich, resonant tone. As the reaction-diffusion pattern morphs on the canvas, the acoustic timbre shifts in tandem.

Example patch file

Infinite saves patches in human-readable plain text .inf files. Here is the starting patch:

infinite-patch 1
rev 2
node 1 Visuals Reaction-Diffusion
  id rdiff
  pos 120 240
  param feed 0.054
  param kill 0.062
end
node 2 Notes Keyboard
  id keys
  pos 120 440
end
node 3 Synths Wave Terrain
  id wt
  pos 420 300
  param wtOrbit 2
  param wtChan 0
  param radiusX 0.45
  param radiusY 0.45
  param unison 3
  param detune 14
  param cutoff 8500
end
node 4 Audio Audio Out
  id out
  pos 740 300
end
cable rdiff texture -> wt texture
cable keys notes -> wt note
cable wt audio -> out in

Sound design recipes: evolving drones, aggressive bass, and ambient pads

Here are three practical production recipes using the Wave Terrain engine:

1. Organic morphing drone

  • Terrain source: Noise node with simplex noise and slow octaves evolution.
  • Orbit: kOrbitLemniscate with radiusX = 0.65, radiusY = 0.40.
  • Modulation: Connect a slow sine LFO (0.08 Hz) to the rotation parameter of Wave Terrain.
  • Filter: 24 dB lowpass with cutoff = 3200 Hz and subtle resonance.
  • Character: As the rotation rotates the infinity loop across the noise field, the harmonic overtone balance shifts without sudden timbre jumps, creating an evolving drone suitable for film scoring.

2. Aggressive industrial Reese bass

  • Terrain source: High-contrast geometric shapes from a Shape or Glitch node.
  • Orbit: kOrbitLissajous with ratioA = 3.0, ratioB = 2.0, and wtChan = Edge Magnitude.
  • Unison: 5 voices, detune = 28 cents, stereoWidth = 0.85.
  • Filter: 24 dB lowpass with moderate drive to saturate the summed unison output.
  • Character: The edge detection mode reads hard transitions as intense harmonic spikes. Coupled with the 3:2 Lissajous trajectory and unison detuning, this produces a ferocious, roaring bass sound with distinctive stereophonic movement.

3. Shimmering ambient glass pad

  • Terrain source: Live video feed from a webcam or liquid video loop via Video.
  • Orbit: kOrbitSpiral with radiusX = 0.85, radiusY = 0.85.
  • Envelope: attack = 1200 ms, release = 2400 ms.
  • Modulation: Route the high-frequency band from an Audio Analyze node back into radiusX, creating an acoustic feedback loop where brightness opens the spatial scan.
  • Character: Delicate, shimmering, crystalline pads that breathe dynamically in response to room sound and video luminance.

Summary and exploration

Wave terrain synthesis transforms the relationship between visual graphics and electronic sound. By viewing sound synthesis as spatial kinematics across topographic surfaces, artists can design instruments that are visually expressive and sonically complex.

With built-in 1024-point discrete Fourier transform anti-aliasing, eight-voice polyphony, and unison spreading, Infinite makes wave terrain synthesis reliable for live performance and studio composition.

Explore ready-to-run wave terrain patches in the Infinite Library, inspect the full control specifications in the Wave Terrain node documentation, or download Infinite to start sculpting sound from two-dimensional landscapes.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/wave-terrain-synthesis-in-real-time.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Audio-reactive 3D particle systems in real time
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How to build audio-reactive 3D particle systems: Euler physics, turbulent 3D noise force fields, spectral transient triggers, and GPU point rendering on a modular canvas.
item.content:encoded:
An audio reactive particle system transforms live musical transients and spectral frequencies into streams of kinetic points in three-dimensional space. From gentle dust motes drifting across an ambient soundscape to explosive shockwaves synchronised with sub-bass kick drums, particle systems provide an organic bridge between acoustic energy and computer graphics.

In real-time visual engines and audiovisual workstations like Infinite, audio and geometry share a unified execution graph. Rather than rendering pre-baked animations or relying on loose open sound control messages across network sockets, simulation nodes evaluate physical differential equations directly alongside audio-rate buffers. This enables deterministic, frame-accurate responses to rhythm and spectral timbre.

Here is how real-time particle mechanics operate under the hood, how numerical integration handles drag and velocity, how procedural 3D turbulence vector fields create fluid motion, and how to patch an audio-reactive particle pipeline using native nodes.

What makes particle systems feel musical

A common pitfall in generative music visualisation is mapping raw audio volume directly to particle count or size. When overall loudness drives everything, the visual output becomes a muddy, fluttering cloud that feels detached from the rhythmic structure of the music.

Musicality in a particle system requires separating three physical aspects of sound:

  1. Rhythmic transients: Sudden bursts of energy (such as kick drums, snare rimshots, and hi-hat attacks) should trigger discrete physical events: spawning a cluster of new particles or imparting an instantaneous impulse shockwave.
  2. Harmonic spectral balance: Sustained tonal components (such as basslines, synth pads, or vocals) should influence persistent environmental force fields: shaping gravity, drag, curl noise turbulence, and orbital attraction.
  3. Temporal decay and resonance: Particle lifetimes and trail lengths should correspond to musical tempo divisions, ensuring kinetic movement breathes in sync with the song rather than piling up into visual noise.

By decoupling instantaneous onset triggers from continuous vector fields, particles behave like physical matter reacting to sound waves propagating through a medium.

Numerical physics: fixed-step Euler integration

At the core of any particle engine is numerical integration: advancing position and velocity forward across discrete steps in time.

In Infinite, the Particle System node maintains an internal state array of particle records. Each particle stores position, velocity, remaining lifetime, initial lifetime, and scalar seed data.

To prevent simulation instability when frame rates vary during heavy rendering passes, the physics simulation runs on a fixed timestep:

kFixedStep = 1.0f / 120.0f;  // 120 Hz internal physics update

If a frame takes longer than usual (for example, during a window resize or shader compilation), the accumulator advances in discrete 120 Hz sub-steps up to a hard cap, preventing explosive time-step jumps.

The equations of motion

For each active particle at time t, the simulator computes acceleration by summing directional gravity g, external atmospheric forces, and fluid turbulence:

F_total = g + F_turbulence + F_external

The updated velocity v(t + dt) applies acceleration and accounts for atmospheric drag:

v(t + dt) = (v(t) + F_total * dt) * (1.0 - drag * dt)

Position p(t + dt) then advances along the newly computed velocity vector:

p(t + dt) = p(t) + v(t + dt) * dt

Linear drag acts as a damping factor: without it, particles in an active turbulence field would continuously gain kinetic energy until flying off to infinity. Setting drag between 0.05 and 0.2 creates a natural terminal velocity reminiscent of smoke particles or underwater sediment.

3D turbulence and procedural vector force fields

Static directional gravity produces predictable fountain effects. To create organic, swirling motion where particles dance like embers or schooling fish, simulations apply procedural 3D noise vector fields.

Rather than sampling expensive perlin noise textures across memory, real-time particle kernels compute value noise and pseudo-curl fields analytically:

inline float Noise3D(float x, float y, float z)
{
    const float v = std::sin(x * 12.9898f + y * 78.233f + z * 37.719f) * 43758.5453f;
    return (v - std::floor(v)) * 2.0f - 1.0f;
}

In the Particle System node, turbulence is evaluated in three spatial dimensions:

float nx = Noise3D(p.x * turbScale, p.y * turbScale, p.z * turbScale + time);
float ny = Noise3D(p.x * turbScale + 19.1f, p.y * turbScale, p.z * turbScale);
float nz = Noise3D(p.x * turbScale, p.y * turbScale + 31.7f, p.z * turbScale);

F_turbulence = Vec3(nx, ny, nz) * turbulenceAmount;

When turbulence is modulated by an audio feature (such as spectral flux or mid-frequency energy), complex vortex structures suddenly twist and expand whenever an instrument enters the mix, returning to laminar flow during quiet breakdowns.

Isolating audio transients for explosive particle bursts

To create tight rhythmic synchronisation, incoming audio must pass through envelope extraction before reaching the particle emitter.

In a modular graph, the Audio In node captures multi-channel audio from your interface, system sound, or DAW routing. This feeds directly into an Audio Analyze node, which divides the audio spectrum into frequency bands and tracks both peak amplitudes and transient envelopes:

  1. Sub-bass band (20 Hz to 120 Hz): Isolates kick drums and bass stabs. Connecting this output to the particle emitter's rate / sec parameter creates explosive bursts on downbeats.
  2. Spectral flux: Measures the rate of change across frequency bins. A sudden brass chord or snare strike produces a high spectral flux value, ideal for driving turbulence or spread.
  3. High-frequency envelope (6 kHz to 16 kHz): Tracks hi-hats, shakers, and cymbal sizzle. Modulating particle start size or speed random with high frequencies adds crisp kinetic shimmer to rapid rhythmic passages.

Because modulation values update at UI and block intervals without latency, particle emission synchronises tightly with what the audience hears.

Point trails, ribbon geometry, and GPU rendering

Individual floating points can look sparse on large display projections. To give particles visual weight and continuity, Infinite pairs the Particle System with downstream geometry generators and compositing nodes.

Turning points into continuous ribbons with Point Trails

The Point Trails node samples point positions across successive frames and extrudes them into continuous triangle strips. As particles whip through turbulent vortices, their trajectories form luminous ribbons through space.

Key controls in Point Trails include:

  • trail length: Determines the historical sample depth (from 4 to 64 steps). Shorter trails produce comet tails; longer trails create intricate calligraphic ribbons.
  • ribbon width: Defines the cross-sectional geometry size in world space.
  • fade alpha: Tapers opacity exponentially towards the tail so older segments dissolve smoothly into the background.

Point sprite rendering in Render 3D

Both raw particles and ribbon meshes connect directly into the Render 3D node. For dense point clouds containing tens of thousands of elements, Render 3D uses hardware-accelerated point sprites. Rather than drawing individual quad polygons, a single vertex shader call computes screen-space point sizes while fragment shaders evaluate circular alpha falloffs and depth fading.

Adding a Bloom node downstream extracts specular highlights from high-density particle clusters, wrapping them in a natural optical glow. A subtle Color Adjustments pass allows fine-tuning contrast and grading the colour palette to match the mood of the performance.

You can also explore how audio-reactive shaders compare to geometric pipelines in our guide to audio-reactive GLSL shaders.

Complete example patch
