Here is a complete, reproducible Infinite patch demonstrating an audio-reactive 3D particle system. It sets up an audio input, transient analysis, a high-capacity particle generator, point trails, a 3D camera renderer, optical bloom, and screen output.

You can paste this plain text directly into an .inf file or inspect it to understand the node connections:

infinite-patch 1
rev 2
# Audio-Reactive 3D Particle System: transient bursts, curl turbulence, and bloom

node 1 Audio Audio In
  id audio_in
  pos 120 280
end

node 2 Audio Audio Analyze
  id analyze
  pos 380 280
end

node 3 Modulator LFO
  id lfo_sway
  pos 380 460
  param shape 0
  param frequency 0.15
end

node 4 3D Particle System
  id particles
  pos 700 280
  param max_particles 30000
  param rate 180
  param shape 1
  param radius 0.25
  param lifetime 3.5
  param speed 1.8
  param spread 0.45
  param dir_y 1.0
  param gravity_y -1.2
  param drag 0.12
  param turbulence 2.2
  param turb_scale 1.4
  param start_size 0.05
  param end_size 0.01
end

node 5 3D Point Trails
  id trails
  pos 1020 280
  param length 18
  param width 0.03
  param fade 0.85
end

node 6 3D Render 3D
  id renderer
  pos 1320 280
  param fov 45.0
  param cam_dist 4.2
  param shading 1
end

node 7 Image Bloom
  id bloom_fx
  pos 1600 280
  param threshold 0.60
  param radius 2.0
  param intensity 1.4
end

node 8 Image Color Adjustments
  id color_grade
  pos 1860 280
  param contrast 1.15
  param saturation 1.25
end

node 9 Utility Output
  id out_screen
  pos 2120 280
end

# Wiring
cable analyze 0 audio_in 0
cable particles 1 analyze 1        # Kick transient envelope -> Particle Emit Rate
cable particles 11 analyze 2       # Spectral flux -> Turbulence intensity
cable particles 9 lfo_sway 0       # Slow LFO -> Gravity Y drift
geo trails 0 particles
geo renderer 0 trails
cable bloom_fx 0 renderer 0
cable color_grade 0 bloom_fx 0
cable out_screen 0 color_grade 0

When live audio plays through Audio In, kick transients trigger dense bursts of new points while spectral changes continuously alter the curl turbulence, causing the trails to swirl in synchrony with the music.

Performance and buffer limits

Running tens of thousands of particles in real time alongside audio DSP requires keeping CPU and GPU overhead predictable:

  • Particle capacity: On modern hardware, Particle System comfortably simulates 20,000 to 50,000 particles at 120 frames per second. If your project targets portable laptops or high-resolution multi-projector setups, keeping max particles between 15,000 and 25,000 ensures plenty of GPU headroom for post-processing shaders.
  • Lifetimes and garbage collection: Shorter particle lifetimes (between 2.0 and 4.0 seconds) cycle dead particles out of the buffer quickly, preventing memory bloat during prolonged high-tempo sections.
  • Trails depth: Point Trails creates geometric triangle meshes for each particle. If particle counts exceed 30,000, consider reducing length to 8 or 12 points to minimise vertex memory bandwidth.

For ready-to-run templates, generative synths, and community visual rigs, visit the Infinite library. You can download Infinite for macOS, Windows, and Linux from the download page and begin patching generative audiovisual instruments immediately.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/audio-reactive-particle-systems-in-real-time.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Drum and bass Reese bass sound design in modular synthesisers
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Master drum and bass Reese bass sound design in modular synthesisers: detuned saw phase movement, multi-band filter splits, distortion, and audio-reactive visuals.
item.content:encoded:
Few sounds define underground electronic music as completely as the Reese bass. Originating on the Casio CZ-1 synthesiser under Kevin Saunderson's Reese moniker in 1988, the patch became the sonic cornerstone of jungle, drum and bass, techstep, and neurofunk. Producers from Renegade Soundwave to Ed Rush, Optical, Dillinja, and Noisia transformed what began as a simple pair of detuned oscillators into an evolving, multi-band instrument of pressure and texture.

Achieving authentic drum and bass Reese bass sound design requires understanding the acoustic physics of phase cancellation, harmonic saturation, and multi-band routing. In conventional digital audio workstations, setting up this architecture requires dozens of plugin windows, complex auxiliary buses, and clunky phase-alignment utilities.

In Infinite, the entire signal path lives directly on a unified node canvas. You can route audio, control voltages, and real-time graphics without latency penalties or auxiliary routing bottlenecks. Here is a step-by-step engineering breakdown of how to construct a professional, club-ready Reese bass from scratch.

Acoustic foundations of the Reese bass

At its core, a Reese bass is generated by the physical phenomenon of acoustic beating. When two periodic waveforms with nearly identical frequencies f_1 and f_2 are summed together, their phase relationship continuously shifts between constructive interference and destructive interference.

The resulting composite waveform pulsates at a beat frequency determined by the absolute difference between the two oscillators:

f_beat = |f_1 - f_2|

If an oscillator plays an F1 note at 43.65 Hz and a second oscillator is detuned sharp by +9 cents (approximately 43.88 Hz), the beat frequency is:

f_beat = |43.88 - 43.65| = 0.23 Hz

This 0.23 Hz differential produces a slow, hypnotic swelling cycle every 4.3 seconds. If the detune is widened to +25 cents, the beating accelerates into an aggressive growl.

The sub-bass phase cancellation trap

While acoustic beating sounds rich across the midrange, it introduces a severe physical defect in the sub-bass register below 90 Hz. When the two detuned saw waves drift into anti-phase (180 degrees apart), their fundamental frequencies cancel each other out completely.

On a large club sound system, this cancellation causes the low end to collapse periodically. The dancefloor feels a momentary drop in kinetic weight every time the waveforms cross zero. To build a Reese bass that translates powerfully across large subwoofers, you must decouple the sub fundamental from the detuned mid band using multi-band frequency splitting.

Dual oscillator core in the Analog node

The foundation of the patch begins with the Analog node. Rather than using pre-recorded wavetables or sample loops, Infinite generates anti-aliased analogue waveforms in real time using band-limited step correction.

[ Note In ] ---> pitch ---> [ Analog Node ]

Oscillator configuration

  1. Oscillator 1: Set the waveform to Sawtooth. Set the octave to 0 and the coarse pitch to 0 semitones. This oscillator serves as our pitch reference.
  2. Oscillator 2: Set the waveform to Sawtooth. Set the coarse pitch to 0 semitones and the fine tune control to +8.5 cents. The subtle pitch disparity creates our primary acoustic beating.
  3. Sub oscillator: Configure the internal sub oscillator to a pure Sine wave, pitched exactly -1 octave down (-12 semitones). We will extract this pure sine during the band-split phase to serve as our mono sub anchor.
  4. Phase mode: Ensure phase sync is disabled so both oscillators run free. Synchronising oscillator phase on every note-on event produces an artificial, static attack. Free-running oscillators guarantee that every note triggers with a slightly different phase alignment, mimicking vintage analogue hardware.
  5. Glide and legato: Set polyphony to Mono Legato and dial in a glide time between 35 ms and 55 ms. Smooth pitch portamento between notes is essential for drum and bass basslines.

You can inspect pre-configured synthesiser templates in the Infinite Library to see how monophonic glide circuits are wired into note graphs.

Multi-band crossover: isolating the sub fundamental

To resolve the phase cancellation dilemma, we split the output of the Analog node into two discrete frequency bands at 110 Hz:

  1. Sub band (20 Hz to 110 Hz): Contains only the solid, monophonic fundamental frequency. This band bypasses all distortion, modulation, and spatial effects to remain completely mono and phase-stable.
  2. Grit band (110 Hz to 20 kHz): Contains the rich detuned saw harmonics. This band is aggressively saturated, filtered, and widened.

We implement this split using two Filter nodes operating in parallel.

                     +---> [ Filter: Lowpass 110 Hz ] ---> (Sub Bus: Mono)
                     |
[ Analog Output ] ---+
                     |
                     +---> [ Filter: Highpass 110 Hz ] ---> [ Distortion Node ]

Configuring the crossover filters

  • Sub filter: Set filter topology to 4-pole Butterworth Lowpass (24 dB per octave rolloff). Set the cutoff frequency to 110 Hz with zero resonance (Q = 0.707).
  • Grit filter: Set filter topology to 4-pole Butterworth Highpass (24 dB per octave rolloff). Set the cutoff frequency identically to 110 Hz with zero resonance (Q = 0.707).

Because both filters share matching 24 dB per octave Butterworth responses at identical corner frequencies, their phase shifts align smoothly at the crossover point without phase cancellation or comb-filter notches across the 110 Hz boundary.

Nonlinear waveshaping and harmonic saturation

With the sub fundamental safely isolated, we can subject the highpassed grit band to heavy nonlinear processing without compromising the low end.

We patch the highpass output directly into the Distortion node. In drum and bass production, clean saw waves sound thin and dated. Squeezing them through asymmetric clipping generates complex odd and even harmonics that fill out the 300 Hz to 4 kHz frequency band.

The mathematics of asymmetric saturation

A standard symmetric waveshaper clips positive and negative signal peaks identically:

f(x) = tanh(k * x)

Symmetric clipping generates only odd harmonics (3rd, 5th, 7th), resulting in a hollow, square-wave tonality. To produce the snarling, guttural character characteristic of neurofunk, we introduce a DC bias offset before saturation. This asymmetry generates prominent even harmonics (2nd, 4th, 6th):

f(x) = tanh(k * (x + bias)) - tanh(k * bias)

Parameter settings in the Distortion node

  • Drive: Increase drive to +14 dB to push the detuned saw beating into hard saturation. As the beating waveforms periodically crest, the distortion unit saturates them into dense square-like plateaus.
  • Mode: Select Asymmetric Tube Fold.
  • Bias: Set bias to +0.22. This introduces even-order harmonic sweetness.
  • Oversampling: Engage 4x oversampling. Hard nonlinear distortion creates harmonic energy that can exceed the Nyquist frequency (24 kHz at a 48 kHz sample rate). 4x oversampling suppresses aliasing artifacts, preserving high-frequency clarity.
  • Post-tilt equaliser: Add a gentle +2.5 dB high-shelf boost starting at 2.2 kHz to compensate for high-frequency energy lost during saturation.

For a deeper exploration of custom mathematical waveshaping kernels, consult our technical guide on per-sample DSP audio kernels in Field language.

Formant sweeps with modulated twin notch filters

The signature vocal quality of modern Reese basses is created by sweeping notch and comb filters across the saturated spectrum. When an audio signal with dense harmonic content passes through narrow rejection notches, human ears perceive vowel-like vocal formants (such as "ow", "ah", and "ee").

We insert a second Filter node after the distortion stage, configured in twin-notch rejection mode.

[ Distortion Out ] ---> [ Filter: Twin Notch ] ---> [ Chorus Node ]
                               ^
                               |
                        [ Modulator LFO ]

Wiring the modulator LFO

To bring the sound to life, we patch a Modulator node to animate the filter cutoff frequency:

  1. Modulator shape: Select a morphed triangle-to-sine wave or a slow chaotic random walk.
  2. Sync rate: Synchronise the LFO to the global transport, selecting 1/2 bar or 1/4 dotted divisions.
  3. Slew rate: Set a 12 ms slew filter on the LFO output to prevent abrupt parameter jumps from causing audible clicks.
  4. Modulation depth: Map the LFO output to the notch filter cutoff parameter with a modulation depth of 65 percent. As the bassline sustains, the notches sweep dynamically between 400 Hz and 3.2 kHz, producing the iconic moving vowel resonance.

Stereo widening and mono compatibility on club systems

In professional sound design, width creates perceived size. However, spreading low frequencies across the stereo field is catastrophic in club venues, where subwoofer arrays are driven in mono. If out-of-phase low-frequency information reaches a mono subwoofer summing amplifier, the sound cancels itself out in the room.

Because we established a multi-band split earlier in our patch, we can apply aggressive stereo expansion exclusively to the highpassed grit band, leaving the sub fundamental completely untouched in mono.

[ Sub Filter: Lowpass 110 Hz ] ------------------------+---> [ Audio Out: Left (Mono Sum) ]
                                                       |
[ Grit: Saturated & Notched ] ---> [ Chorus Node ] ---+---> [ Audio Out: Stereo Width ]

Configuring the Chorus node

  1. Haas delay spread: Introduce a small micro-delay between the left and right channels (0.0 ms on the left channel, +14.2 ms on the right channel). This exploits the psychoacoustic Haas effect to stretch the perceived stereo image far beyond the physical speaker positions.
  2. Modulation depth: Keep chorus modulation gentle (rate at 0.28 Hz, depth at 25 percent) to avoid disorienting pitch warble.
  3. Dry and wet balance: Set wet mix to 60 percent.

Verifying phase correlation with the Audio Meter

To ensure our stereo width does not cause phase issues when summed to mono, we connect the master output into an Audio Meter node.

The Audio Meter displays a real-time goniometer and phase correlation coefficient:

  • +1.0: Perfect mono correlation (identical left and right channels).
  • 0.0: Wide stereo separation with healthy decorrelation.
  • -1.0: Total anti-phase cancellation (summing to mono will result in complete silence).

With our band-split architecture, the phase correlation meter remains pinned between +0.88 and +0.96. The sub-110 Hz foundation is completely vertical and mono, while the high-frequency grit spreads wide across the stereo perimeter.

Audio-reactive visual modulation on the unified canvas

One of Infinite's most compelling design capabilities is that audio synthesis and real-time graphics share the same underlying execution engine. In standard production workflows, synchronising visuals to a bassline requires rendering an audio file, importing it into TouchDesigner or Blender, running an offline FFT, and tweaking sensitivity curves by hand.

In Infinite, we can tap the exact modulation signals driving our Reese bass and route them straight into visual shaders and 3D geometry nodes in real time.

                           +---> [ Filter: Twin Notch ] ---> [ Audio Out ]
                           |
[ Modulator LFO ] ---------+
                           |
                           +---> [ Audio Texture ] ---> [ Render 3D: Mesh Displacement ]

Patching audio-reactive graphics

  1. Audio Texture node: We cable the output of the highpassed grit band directly into an Audio Texture node. The node converts the instantaneous audio waveform and frequency spectrum into a 512x1 floating-point GPU texture buffer.
  2. Render 3D node: We pipe the Audio Texture into a Render 3D node to displace the vertices of a high-density geometric icosphere or wireframe terrain.
  3. Direct beat coupling: Because the visual vertex shader samples the actual audio waveform buffer at 60 frames per second, the 3D geometry pulses and ripples in physical lockstep with the acoustic beating frequencies of the detuned saw waves. Every time the oscillators slip into constructive interference, the geometry expands.

To learn more about bridging sound and procedural visuals, read our companion guide on making your first audio-reactive visual in Infinite.

Summary parameter reference and routing checklist

Here is a quick reference table of every node, parameter, and cable connection in this Reese bass architecture:

Node nameParameterValuePurpose
AnalogOscillator 1Sawtooth (0 st, 0 ct)Pitch root reference
AnalogOscillator 2Sawtooth (0 st, +8.5 ct)Acoustic beating generator
AnalogOscillator 3Sine (-12 st, 0 ct)Pure sub fundamental anchor
AnalogPortamentoMono Legato (45 ms)Authentic glide between bassline notes
Filter (Sub)Topology4-pole Lowpass (110 Hz)Isolates monophonic low end
Filter (Grit)Topology4-pole Highpass (110 Hz)Extracts midrange for saturation
DistortionDrive & Bias+14.5 dB Drive, +0.22 BiasAsymmetric even/odd harmonic fold
DistortionOversampling4x Polyphase IIRPrevents Nyquist aliasing harshness
Filter (Notch)TopologyTwin Notch (Q = 4.8)Dynamic vocal formant resonances
ModulatorRate & Shape1/2 Bar Sync, Slew 12 msSweeps notch filters smoothly
ChorusHaas Offset+14.2 ms Right ChannelWide stereo imaging on high band
Audio MeterCorrelationMinimum +0.85 TargetConfirms mono club sound safety
Audio TextureBuffer512x1 Float16 GPU BufferBridges acoustic beat into visual shaders

Engineering limits and practical considerations

When deploying complex multi-band synthesis graphs in production, keep the following practical engineering guidelines in mind:

  1. Headroom management: Asymmetric distortion and resonant notch filtering introduce gain peaks. Always leave at least -3 dBFS of digital headroom on the Reese track before it hits the master limiter. Excessive peak levels into the master bus can trigger inter-sample clipping when converted to lossy streaming formats like AAC or MP3.
  2. Crossover frequency tuning: While 110 Hz is the standard crossover frequency for drum and bass, adjust this boundary based on your track's root key. For tracks in F (fundamental at ~43 Hz, second harmonic at ~87 Hz), 100 Hz to 110 Hz works cleanly. For tracks in A (fundamental at ~55 Hz, second harmonic at ~110 Hz), shift the crossover down to 85 Hz to prevent the second harmonic from splitting awkwardly across both filters.
  3. Equaliser carve for kick drums: A dense Reese bass occupies significant energy between 80 Hz and 200 Hz. Use an envelope or sidechain compressor keyed to your kick drum to duck the Reese by 4 dB to 6 dB during the initial 40 ms of the kick transient.

By building your bass sound design on a unified modular graph, you eliminate plugin latency drift, retain absolute control over low-end phase integrity, and create instruments that bridge sound and visuals into a single cohesive performance.

Explore ready-to-run synthesiser patches and creative coding instruments in the Infinite Library, or review our tutorial on sub bass, pluck, and ambient pad sound design.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/drum-and-bass-reese-bass-sound-design.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: L-system procedural 3D branching and fractal generation
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Build procedural 3D trees and fractals using L-system branching, 3D turtle geometry, mesh extrusion, and real-time audio modulation in Infinite.
item.content:encoded:
An l-system procedural 3d branching architecture brings the algorithmic elegance of formal rewriting grammars into real-time computer graphics and modular audiovisual performance. In traditional generative design, procedural geometry often relies on explicit loops, mathematical trigonometric functions, or Perlin noise fields. While noise produces organic displacement and sine waves yield predictable oscillation, neither method captures the developmental morphology of living organisms: structured self-similarity, hierarchical vascular branching, and recursive form unfolding across space and time.

In modular workstations like Infinite, the Lindenmayer system bridges formal language theory, three-dimensional geometry, and live sound design. By evaluating production rules inside a native L-System node, creative coders can grow intricate botanical canopies, generate procedural coral and crystal formations, and modulate geometric growth parameters live using incoming audio frequencies.

Here is how Lindenmayer grammars operate, how three-dimensional turtle geometry navigates space, how branch strands are swept into watertight polygonal tubes, and how to patch audio-reactive procedural trees on a unified canvas.

Formal grammars and parallel rewriting

The mathematical foundation of Lindenmayer systems was developed in 1968 by Hungarian theoretical biologist and botanist Aristid Lindenmayer. Originally formulated to study the growth patterns of multicellular algae, mosses, and vascular plants, L-systems belong to the family of formal rewriting grammars.

In classical Chomsky grammars used across compiler design, production rules are applied sequentially, replacing one non-terminal symbol at a time. In contrast, an L-system applies its replacement rules in parallel across every symbol in the string simultaneously. This parallel replacement reflects biological cell division, where multiple biological structures grow and divide at the same physical instant.

A deterministic context-free L-system (known formally as a DOL-system) is defined by three components:

  1. Alphabet: A finite set of formal symbols V containing characters that can be replaced or walked by a geometry interpreter.
  2. Axiom: An initial seed string omega of symbols chosen from V that defines the starting state of the organism.
  3. Production rules: A mapping P that associates predecessor characters with successor replacement strings.

Consider the canonical branching plant grammar:

Axiom: X
Rules: X = F+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X; F = FF

During generation zero, the system state consists solely of the axiom X. In the first generation, the production rule replaces X with its successor:

Generation 0: X
Generation 1: F+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X
Generation 2: FF+[[F+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X]-F+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X]-FF[-FFF+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X]+F+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X

As iterations advance, the length of the string increases exponentially. In the native L-System node inside Infinite, string expansion is governed by safety caps:

  • The maximum number of generations is bounded by kMaxIterations = 10.
  • The total rewritten symbol buffer is capped at kMaxSymbols = 200000.

If a grammar expands beyond the symbol limit, rewriting terminates cleanly and issues a diagnostic notification. This safety ceiling guarantees that complex grammars never exhaust host memory or block real-time rendering during live performances.

Turtle geometry in three dimensions

Once a string of symbols is rewritten, it must be translated into spatial form. This translation is performed by a three-dimensional turtle geometry interpreter, extending Seymour Papert's original two-dimensional Logo turtle into Cartesian space.

The turtle maintains an internal state consisting of a spatial position (px, py, pz) and three mutually orthogonal unit vectors that form an orthonormal frame in three dimensions:

  • Heading vector H: points in the direction the turtle is currently facing and moving forward.
  • Left vector L: points to the local left side of the turtle.
  • Up vector U: points along the local normal vector perpendicular to the heading and left vectors.

The orientation triad satisfies the cross-product relationship:

H x L = U

As the interpreter parses the rewritten symbol string from left to right, each character commands the turtle to move or reorient its local frame:

  • F: Move forward by the current step length while drawing geometry.
  • f: Move forward by the current step length without drawing geometry, creating intentional structural gaps.
  • +: Turn left by the branching angle, spinning vectors H and L around axis U.
  • -: Turn right by the branching angle, spinning vectors H and L in the opposite direction around axis U.
  • &: Pitch down by the branching angle, spinning vectors H and U around axis L.
  • ^: Pitch up by the branching angle, spinning vectors H and U in the opposite direction around axis L.
  • \: Roll left by the branching angle, spinning vectors L and U around axis H.
  • /: Roll right by the branching angle, spinning vectors L and U in the opposite direction around axis H.
  • |: Reverse direction by 180 degrees, inverting the heading vector.

Because repeated floating-point matrix rotations accumulate subtle numerical errors over thousands of symbols, Infinite executes an orthonormal renormalisation step following each rotation:

void Renormalize(Turtle& t)
{
   float* v[3] = { t.h, t.l, t.u };
   for (float* x : v)
   {
      const float len = std::sqrt(x[0] * x[0] + x[1] * x[1] + x[2] * x[2]);
      if (len > 1e-6f)
         for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
            x[i] /= len;
   }
}

This normalisation guarantees that the turtle orientation vectors never shear or collapse, maintaining geometric fidelity across deep recursive iterations.

Branching stacks and hierarchical state

Botanical forms require branching structures where subsidiary twigs diverge from parent boles while preserving the original growth trajectory. In L-systems, this hierarchy is encoded through pushdown automata symbols:

  • [: Push the current turtle state onto a lifo stack. The saved state includes spatial coordinates (px, py, pz), orientation frame vectors H, L, U, current branch radius, and current step length. The branch radius is then multiplied by radiusScale, and the step length is multiplied by lengthScale.
  • ]: Terminate the active branch and pop the saved turtle state from the stack, restoring the parent branch position, frame orientation, radius, and step length.

Through this stack mechanism, a single linear string encodes complex tree canopies with nested sub-branches of proportional thickness and length.

Tube extrusion and branching radii

Drawing wireframe polylines produces an informative schematic, but visual rendering demands solid three-dimensional geometry with surface normals, cross-sectional volume, and UV mapping for material shaders.

The native L-System node solves this by sweeping each continuous branch strand into a watertight polygonal cylinder via MeshOps::TubeAlong.

Strand points -> Cylindrical cross-sections -> Triangular quad strips -> Watertight mesh

Key physical parameters govern this mesh synthesis:

  • sides: Controls the radial polygon count of the cross-sections, adjustable between 3 (producing low-poly crystalline trunks) and 24 (producing smooth organic boughs).
  • radius: Sets the absolute base radius of the primary trunk.
  • radiusScale: The geometric multiplier applied to radius each time a sub-branch is pushed with [. A value of 0.75 ensures parent limbs are sturdier than daughter branches, mirroring Leonardo da Vinci's botanical rule of trees.
  • taper: Governs linear narrowing along the length of each strand segment, ensuring branches taper toward their terminal buds rather than ending abruptly as blunt cylinders.
  • length and lengthScale: Control the physical reach of the primary trunk and the rate at which daughter twigs shorten toward the perimeter.

To prevent GPU memory saturation during live performances, Infinite enforces a hard cap of kMaxStrands = 6000 extruded tubes. Any additional branches beyond this limit remain present in the polyline curve but are excluded from polygonal mesh extrusion.

Dual mesh and polyline representations

A distinctive design decision of the L-System node is its dual output contract: it concurrently provides both a three-dimensional polygonal Mesh and a continuous three-dimensional Polyline.

L-System Node
  ├── GetMesh()  -> Watertight 3D polygonal geometry (tubes, vertices, normals, UVs)
  └── GetCurve() -> Continuous 3D polyline path (reconstructed traversal points)

This dual pipeline opens versatile creative workflows:

  1. Polygonal mesh rendering: The mesh connects directly to standard 3D rendering pipelines, accepting PBR materials, casting shadow maps, and responding to scene lighting.
  2. Path tracking and camera choreography: The Polyline output connects to the Path node. Because the turtle traverses the tree in deterministic order, a Camera 3D can be constrained to glide along the polyline path, flying smoothly through the interior vascular channels of the fractal tree canopy.
  3. Particle flow guides: Downstream simulation nodes can distribute emitters or flow particles along the polyline curve, creating glowing sap rising through procedural veins.

Real-time audio modulation and kinetic foliage

Because Infinite evaluates its node graph in real time, the parameters of the L-System node can be dynamically modulated by audio analysis or control signals. Unlike pre-rendered 3D assets, a procedural grammar can breathe and pulse in direct synchronisation with music.

Consider the following audio-reactive modulation pairings:

Modulating branching angles with frequency bands

By connecting the low-frequency band of an Audio Analyze node to the angle parameter of L-System, the physical divergence of the tree branches expands and contracts in response to bass transients:

  • At quiet moments (angle = 18.0), branches align closely with the primary trunk, producing a slender, dormant cypress form.
  • On heavy kick drum or bass hits (angle = 38.0), branches fan outward into an open, blossoming canopy.

Because changing the branching angle preserves the total number of vertices and triangles, angle modulation incurs zero memory allocation overhead, running at full display frame rates without dropped frames.

Modulating length and scale with melodic envelopes

Connecting mid-range or high-frequency energy to lengthScale dynamically alters the density of the outer foliage. When a synth arpeggio or percussion roll plays, outer branches extend outward and recoil, giving the tree an organic breathing kinetic presence.

Modulating growth iterations across musical sections

The iterations parameter governs structural complexity. Routing a slow step sequencer or an arrangement automation curve to iterations allows a seed to sprout at generation 1 during an ambient intro, expand to generation 3 in the first verse, and erupt into a fully unfurled generation 5 fractal canopy at the musical drop.

Composing procedural scenes in Infinite

To assemble a finished audiovisual composition, the L-System node is wired into the standard 3D rendering graph alongside lighting and camera nodes.

Audio In ──────────> Audio Analyze ──[Low Band]──> Math ──> L-System (angle)
                                                               │
                                                         [Mesh Output]
                                                               │
Light 3D ──> Scene 3D ─────────────────────────────────────> Material ──> Render 3D ──> Viewport
                                                                            ▲
Camera 3D ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Here is the step-by-step assembly process:

  1. Add the audio chain: Place an Audio In node, wire it into Audio Analyze, and extract the low output band. Route this through a Math node to map incoming zero-to-one signal ranges into the desired angular span, such as 20.0 to 40.0 degrees.
  2. Add the generator: Place an L-System node. Connect the scaled audio signal into the angle parameter input. Set the axiom to X and rules to X=F+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X;F=FF. Set iterations to 4 or 5.
  3. Apply materials: Wire the mesh output into a Material node. Assign a deep organic albedo colour, set roughness to 0.65 for natural wood scattering, and configure a subtle emissive tint modulated by high-frequency audio energy.
  4. Set up lighting and camera: Connect the material into a Render 3D node. Add a Camera 3D positioned at (0.0, 1.5, 4.0) targeting the centre of the tree canopy. Add two Light 3D nodes: a warm directional key light and a cool cyan rim light to highlight branch contours against the dark ground.
  5. Combine with shaders: In Infinite, you can pair 3D geometry with 2D post-processing. Take the render output and composite it with background gradients or real-time GLSL shaders for depth of field and atmospheric haze.

To explore pre-configured templates and community patches featuring procedural geometry, visit the patch library.

Algorithmic variations and botanical grammars

The flexibility of Lindenmayer systems lies in their grammatical versatility. By modifying the axiom and replacement rules, the exact same node architecture generates fundamentally distinct natural forms.

Classic 3D bush

This classic grammar produces balanced spherical shrubbery with uniform outward branching:

Axiom: A
Rules: A = [&+F[A]][&-F[A]][^+F[A]][^-F[A]]; F = FF
Angle: 28.0

The four-way branch split combines pitch (&, ^) and yaw (+, -) rotations, producing full three-dimensional volumetric foliage.

Monopodial pine tree

For coniferous trees where a dominant central trunk continues upward while subordinate whorls emerge at regular intervals:

Axiom: !(1)F(100)/(45)A
Rules: A = [&(30)B]F(10)/(45)A; B = [&(30)F(20)]F(10)/(45)B
Angle: 25.0

Here, the primary trunk maintains vertical dominance while lateral branch clusters spiral radially around the central stem.

3D Hilbert space-filling curve

L-systems are not limited to biological plants; they also describe space-filling fractals and recursive mathematical curves:

Axiom: X
Rules: X = ^\XF^/XFX-F^//XFX&F+//XFX-F/X-
Angle: 90.0

When evaluated with 90-degree turning angles, this grammar weaves a single continuous polyline through every sub-cube of a three-dimensional lattice. When swept into tubes and modulated with audio, it creates intricate kinetic geometric sculptures.

For broader techniques combining mathematical deformation with procedural meshes, see our guide on procedural 3D geometry nodes.

Summary

L-system procedural 3D branching provides an expressive bridge between theoretical linguistics, computer graphics, and live music performance. By encoding complex natural structures into concise symbolic grammars, artists can generate organic botanical forms that remain entirely deterministic, mathematically pure, and lightweight.

Through Infinite's native L-System node, these formal grammars live inside an interactive modular graph. Artists can manipulate branch cross-sections, route geometry along motion paths, and modulate angles and lengths in real time to the rhythm of incoming audio. The result is a procedural instrument where mathematics, sound, and visual form grow together on a single canvas.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/l-system-procedural-3d-branching-fractals.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Granular synthesis in modular audio: soundscapes and grain clouds
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Explore granular synthesis in modular audio: grain clouds, window functions, time-stretching, stochastic spray, and feature sorting in Infinite.
item.content:encoded:
Granular synthesis in modular audio transforms continuous recorded sound into swarms of microscopic acoustic quanta. Rather than playing back an audio recording as a fixed linear timeline, granular synthesis deconstructs source audio into tiny acoustic fragments called grains, typically lasting between 5 and 100 milliseconds. By controlling the density, duration, pitch transposition, spatial distribution, and playback position of hundreds of simultaneous grains, sound designers can stretch time to infinity, dissolve field recordings into shimmering ambient clouds, or restructure rhythmic loops into completely new acoustic textures.

In Infinite, granular processing is not confined to an isolated plugin window or a static offline bounce. Granular processing operates directly on the real-time node canvas, where per-sample DSP, modulation signals, and GPU graphics interact within a single unified graph. Audio from microphones, live instruments, or loaded audio samples can be continuously streamed into granular buffers, modulated by low-frequency oscillators and rhythmic sequencers, and patched simultaneously into spatial delay networks and reactive visual shaders.

This guide explores the technical foundations of real-time granular synthesis, the mathematics of grain windowing and energy normalisation, the architecture of Infinite's native Granular and Grain Molder nodes, and practical routing recipes for experimental sound design.

Principles of micro-sound and granular synthesis

The physical concept of micro-sound originates in the pioneering work of physicist Dennis Gabor and composer Iannis Xenakis, later formalized by Curtis Roads in Microsound. Gabor demonstrated that any continuous acoustic signal can be represented as a two-dimensional matrix of time-frequency quanta, analogous to quantum wave packets in quantum mechanics.

A single isolated grain lasting 20 milliseconds is too short for the human auditory system to perceive as a continuous musical tone. When heard alone, a micro-grain sounds like a dry click or brief tap. However, when dozens or hundreds of grains are scheduled in rapid succession or layered simultaneously, a psychoacoustic transformation occurs:

  1. Quasi-synchronous grain streams: when grains are emitted at strictly regular periodic intervals, the repetition rate introduces a perceived fundamental pitch equal to the emission frequency ($f_0 = 1 / \Delta t$). At low rates (1 to 20 Hz), the listener hears a rapid train of distinct impulses or rhythmic ratchets. As the emission density exceeds 30 to 40 Hz, the individual grains fuse into a continuous pitched tone, a phenomenon known as pulsar synthesis.
  2. Asynchronous grain clouds: when grain onset times, durations, and read positions are perturbed by stochastic jitter, the periodic pulse dissolves. The ear no longer tracks individual events or synthetic pitch pulses; instead, it perceives a diffuse, textural acoustic cloud. By modulating the variance of read offsets (position spray) and pitch jitter, a sound designer can smoothly transition from pristine sample playback to lush, cinematic drones.
Time-domain representation of grain emission:

Periodic Train (Pulsar):
  +---+     +---+     +---+     +---+     +---+
  | g |     | g |     | g |     | g |     | g |     --> Perceived fundamental pitch
  +---+     +---+     +---+     +---+     +---+
  |<-- Delta t -->|

Stochastic Cloud (Asynchronous):
     +-----+         +---+
     | g1  |         |g3 |       +------+
     +-----+         +---+       |  g5  |           --> Diffuse ambient texture
        +-------+          +--+  +------+
        |  g2   |          |g4|
        +-------+          +--+

Controlling this transformation requires precise real-time scheduling. In traditional tape-based composition, cutting and splicing thousands of microscopic fragments was a laborious manual task. In modern digital audio environments, digital signal processors generate, interpolate, envelope, and accumulate hundreds of active grains per audio buffer without latency or dropouts.

Anatomy of a grain: windows and envelopes

Extracting a raw slice of digital audio creates abrupt discontinuities at the start and end boundaries. If a grain begins or ends away from a natural zero-crossing, the instantaneous voltage step creates high-frequency spectral splatter, perceived as harsh clicks and buzzing.

To eliminate boundary clicks, every grain must be multiplied by a smooth windowing envelope $w(t)$ over its normalized lifespan $t \in [0, 1]$. The shape of this window determines both the temporal attack and the harmonic colour of the grain cloud:

Window function comparison:

Hann:            Gaussian:        Exponential Decay:
    .-'-.            .---.            |\
  .'     '.        .'     '.          | \
 /         \      /         \         |  \..__
'-----------'    '-----------'        '-------'
Smooth spectrum  Optimal focus        Snappy strike

Infinite provides five distinct window functions within its native granular DSP engine:

1. Hann window

The raised cosine window is the standard choice for smooth time-stretching and ambient texture generation:

$$w(t) = 0.5 \cdot (1 - \cos(2\pi t))$$

The Hann window provides gentle attack and release slopes, with spectral sidelobes falling off at 18 dB per octave. It eliminates all transient clicks while preserving the harmonic purity of melodic source material.

2. Gaussian window

The Gaussian curve offers optimal mathematical localisation in both the time and frequency domains:

$$w(t) = \exp\left(-8 \cdot (2t - 1)^2\right)$$

Because the Gaussian curve approaches zero smoothly without abrupt truncation, it produces minimal spectral smearing. Grains windowed with a Gaussian envelope retain focused transient clarity, making it ideal for vocal textures and acoustic instruments.

3. Triangle window

The Bartlett or triangular window applies symmetric linear ramps:

$$w(t) = 1 - 2 \cdot |t - 0.5|$$

With sharper transitions at the apex and boundaries, the triangle window introduces subtle high-frequency harmonic edge, lending a bright, crystalline character to dense grain clouds.

4. Exponential decay window

Unlike symmetric windows, the exponential decay window mimics natural acoustic impact envelopes:

$$w(t) = \sin(\pi t) \cdot \exp(-3t) \cdot 2.3$$

This envelope combines a rapid, snappy onset with a curved decay tail. When applied to granular playback, it transforms sustained audio buffers into percussive micro-bursts, rain droplets, and metallic scatter.

5. Trapezoid window

The trapezoid window features steep linear attack and decay slopes (12% of total grain duration) flanking an 88% flat sustain plateau:

$$w(t) = \max\left(0, \min\left(1, \min\left(\frac{t}{0.12}, \frac{1 - t}{0.12}\right)\right)\right)$$

This envelope preserves the natural uncoloured amplitude of the source material for the majority of the grain duration, applying brief micro-fades only at the boundaries. It is particularly effective for granular loop slicing and stutter effects.

High-order fractional interpolation

When grains are pitch-shifted or played back at arbitrary speed ratios, the read position rarely aligns with discrete integer sample indices. Truncating to the nearest sample or using simple linear interpolation introduces noticeable aliasing and high-frequency noise.

Infinite's granular engine employs 4-point, 3rd-order Hermite cubic interpolation (ReadSampleHermite) for every sample lookup. Hermite interpolation fits a smooth cubic polynomial across four neighbouring sample points ($y_{-1}, y_0, y_1, y_2$), matching both position and first-order derivatives. This ensures continuous, artifact-free playback across pitch transpositions spanning multiple octaves.

Real-time engine architecture in Infinite

Executing granular synthesis in real time requires strict concurrency control and zero-allocation memory discipline. In Infinite, the granular subsystem separates duties between two core components:

  1. GranularNode (main UI thread): manages sample loading, waveform cache rendering, start and end trim markers, parameter serialisation to .inf patch files, and user interaction.
  2. AudioGranularNode (real-time audio thread): executes inside the high-priority OS audio callback, advancing the master scan playhead, spawning active grains, computing Hermite interpolation, and accumulating stereo output buffers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           MAIN THREAD                           |
|                                                                 |
|  [GranularNode]                                                 |
|         |                                                       |
|         +---> Sample file loading (.wav, .flac, .aif)           |
|         +---> Waveform peak cache generation                    |
|         +---> Visual start/end trim drag handles                |
|         +---> ParamRef registration for modulation cables       |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
                                |
                   Lock-free SampleSlot & Atomic Params
                                |
                                v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                          AUDIO THREAD                           |
|                                                                 |
|  [AudioGranularNode]                                            |
|         |                                                       |
|         +---> Live recording stream from Audio In pin           |
|         +---> Master scan playhead accumulator                  |
|         +---> Pre-allocated Grain pool (kMaxGrains = 64)        |
|         +---> Stochastic RNG for jitter & pitch spray           |
|         +---> Hermite 4-point cubic interpolation               |
|         +---> Power-preserving energy normalisation             |
|         +---> Constant-power stereo panning                     |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
                                |
                   Lock-free Visual Snapshot Ring
                                |
                                v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                         VIEWPORT / UI                           |
|                                                                 |
|  Real-time grain dots rendering at 60 fps over waveform         |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+

Pre-allocated grain pools and zero allocation

The audio thread must never allocate heap memory (malloc or new) or block on mutexes. Infinite pre-allocates a fixed pool of grain structures (kMaxGrains = 64) when the node is instantiated. When the spawn timer expires, the engine scans the pool for an inactive slot or reclaims the oldest finished grain.

If a new audio file is loaded during playback, the audio thread swaps sample buffers via an atomic lock-free SampleSlot. The old buffer is safely released on the background thread only after the audio thread has released its reference, preventing audio glitches.

Power-preserving energy normalisation

In granular synthesis, changing grain density or grain length dramatically alters the number of overlapping grains. At low density (e.g. 5 grains per second of 20 ms duration), overlap is minimal. At high density (e.g. 80 grains per second of 300 ms duration), twenty or more grains may sound simultaneously.

Summing twenty overlapping grains without compensation causes severe digital clipping and distortion. Conversely, dividing the output by the maximum theoretical grain count leaves sparse grain streams inaudibly quiet.

Infinite solves this using automatic power-preserving energy normalisation. For each spawned grain, the engine calculates the overlap factor based on duration and spawn interval:

$$\text{overlapFactor} = \max\left(1.0, \frac{\text{totalFrames}}{\text{intervalFrames}}\right)$$

$$\text{grainGain} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\text{overlapFactor}}}$$

By scaling each grain inversely by the square root of the overlap factor, the engine maintains constant root-mean-square (RMS) acoustic energy across radical density and length automations.

The Granular node: clouds, spray and freeze

The native Granular node provides a complete suite of controls for sculpting micro-sound clouds:

Playhead positioning and scan speed

  • position [0.0 to 1.0]: sets the base playback read position within the sample buffer. When patched to an external modulation source, such as an LFO or envelope, this acts as a precision scrubbing control.
  • scan [-2.0x to +2.0x]: enables autonomous playhead movement. Positive values scrub forward at fractional or accelerated speeds; negative values scrub backward. When set to 0.0, the playhead remains stationary, sustaining a micro-slice indefinitely.
  • start and end [0.0 to 1.0]: visual trim markers that constrain grain emission to a specific region of interest. When loop is active, the scan playhead and spawned grains wrap seamlessly between these boundaries.

Dispersion and stochastic jitter

Uniform grain emission sounds robotic and synthetic. To create organic, living textures, Granular provides dedicated dispersion controls:

  • randomPos (Position spray): adds Gaussian stochastic jitter to the spawn position of each grain. Small amounts (5% to 15%) introduce subtle acoustic shimmer; large amounts (50% to 100%) scatter grains across the entire buffer, dissolving temporal structure into an ambient wash.
  • randomLength: introduces random variation to individual grain durations, preventing repetitive flutter rhythms.
  • randomPitch [0 to 24 semitones]: applies random pitch transposition to each grain. Setting this to 12 semitones produces wide harmonic octave clouds; micro-tuning settings (0.2 to 0.5 semitones) create lush natural chorusing.
  • randomPan and width: scatters grains across the stereo field using constant-power equal-energy panning ($pan_L = \cos\theta, pan_R = \sin\theta$).
  • reverseProb [0.0 to 1.0]: sets the probability that an individual grain will play backward. Mixing 20% to 30% reverse grains adds ethereal spectral backwards tails without reversing the master playback direction.

Freeze mode and live buffer capture

Toggling freeze halts advancement of the master scan playhead. The engine continues spawning overlapping grains from the current position with all active spray and pitch jitter parameters intact. This captures an infinite, stationary drone from any transient sound.

Additionally, Granular includes a dedicated audio input pin (record in). Sound designers can route live microphone signals, modular synth patches, or drum tracks directly into the node. Toggling record captures incoming audio into the internal ring buffer in real time, allowing immediate granular manipulation of live performance inputs.

The Grain Molder node: topological sorting and scrambling

While standard granular engines process audio chronologically, the Grain Molder node introduces a radically different paradigm: time-domain grain sorting.

Grain Molder slices incoming audio buffers into overlapping grains (10 to 500 ms) and evaluates an acoustic metric for every slice:

  1. Level (RMS amplitude): calculates the root-mean-square energy of each grain. Sorting by level arranges the audio from quietest grains to loudest grains, or vice versa.
  2. Brightness (Spectral centroid): calculates the high-frequency energy distribution or zero-crossing rate. Sorting by brightness groups dark, low-frequency segments together, transitioning progressively into sharp, bright transients.
  3. Random: generates a deterministic, seed-based pseudo-random permutation of grain indices.
Grain sorting process in Grain Molder:

Original chronological order:
[G1: quiet] [G2: loud] [G3: medium] [G4: peak] [G5: silent]

Sorted by Level (ascending order):
[G5: silent] [G1: quiet] [G3: medium] [G2: loud] [G4: peak]  --> Natural riser

The Amount control: continuous order interpolation

The defining control of Grain Molder is the amount slider [0.0 to 1.0]. Rather than snapping abruptly between original playback and sorted order, amount provides a continuous morph:

  • At 0.0, the buffer plays back in its original chronological sequence.
  • At 1.0, the buffer plays back in strictly sorted metric rank order.
  • At intermediate values (e.g. 0.45), grains undergo continuous partial scrambling, introducing subtle rhythmic dislocations while preserving the overarching melodic contour.

When applied to complex acoustic material such as acoustic drum loops or orchestral recordings, automating the amount slider from 0.0 to 1.0 over four bars produces a natural, glitch-free build-up or riser without requiring volume automation or pitch risers.

Modular routing: modulation, effects and visuals

The power of granular synthesis expands exponentially when connected to Infinite's modular canvas. Because parameters in Infinite are exposed as typed ParamRef targets, any slider can be modulated by external control signals.

Modular canvas signal flow:

  [Audio In] --------> (record in)
                           |
  [LFO / Random] ----> (position)
                           |
  [Step Sequencer] --> (pitchShift)
                           |
                     [ Granular ]
                           |  (Stereo Audio Out)
                           +------------------------+
                           |                        |
                           v                        v
                    [ Stereo Delay ]        [ AudioTexture ]
                           |                        |
                    [ Reverb ]              [ AudioDisplacement ]
                           |                        |
                    [ Audio Out ]           [ Render 3D ]

Patch 1: Ambient orchestral shimmer cloud

  1. Drop an audio sample containing acoustic strings or piano into a Granular node.
  2. Set grainLength to 140 ms, density to 35 Hz, and select the Gaussian window shape.
  3. Set scan to 0.05x for ultra-slow forward progression.
  4. Set randomPos to 20%, randomPitch to 12 semitones, and randomPan to 85%.
  5. Wire a slow sine LFO (0.05 Hz) into position to gently wander across the sample.
  6. Connect the stereo audio output of Granular into a Stereo Delay node, followed by a lush Reverb.
  7. Engage freeze during dense chords to lock the texture into an infinite, evolving ambient pad.

Patch 2: Granular drum break scrambler

  1. Load a classic breakbeat into a Grain Molder node.
  2. Set grainMs to 60 ms and choose the Level sorting mode.
  3. Wire a synchronized ramp LFO running at 1/2 bar into the amount parameter.
  4. As the LFO ramps from 0% to 100%, the break progressively reassembles itself from quiet ghost notes into clustered snare and kick peaks, creating an automated rhythmic fill.
  5. Route the output into an AudioMeter to observe peak levels, ensuring the mix sits cleanly inside your master bus.

Patch 3: Synaesthetic granular audiovisuals

Granular synthesis produces intricate acoustic micro-transients that are ideally suited for driving real-time computer graphics. In Infinite, audio and visuals share the same memory space:

  1. Tap the stereo audio cable exiting Granular and patch it into an AudioTexture node.
  2. The AudioTexture converts time-domain grains and spectral bands into a dynamic GPU texture.
  3. Connect the texture into an AudioDisplacement node deforming a high-density Mesh Sphere.
  4. As grains trigger and scatter across the stereo field, the 3D sphere ripples and pulses in direct synchronisation with individual grain windows.
  5. Pipe the deformed geometry into a Render 3D node to view the resulting particle mesh in the live viewport.

For broader procedural routing possibilities, explore Infinite's node library and our companion architectural guide on node-based DAW workflows.

Comparing granular synthesis and spectral stretching

While both granular synthesis and spectral processing manipulate audio in non-linear ways, they operate on different mathematical principles:

ParameterGranular Synthesis (Granular)Spectral Stretching (PaulStretch)
DomainTime-domain windowed micro-quantaFrequency-domain STFT phase randomisation
Grain duration5 ms to 1000 ms2048 to 65536 FFT sample bins
Pitch manipulationPer-grain Hermite rate transpositionSpectral bin frequency shifting
Transient responsePreserves micro-attacks with tight windowsDiffuses all transients into glassy pads
Memory modelLock-free sample ring buffersOverlap-add IFFT synthesis buffers
Primary applicationClouds, texture scatter, live glitch, stutterExtreme ambient stretching (10x to 1000x)

For extreme time-stretching exceeding 50x duration, spectral algorithms such as PaulStretch excel at eliminating all perceived grain repetition. For rhythmic manipulation, micro-sound scattering, and interactive live performance, real-time granular synthesis remains unmatched.

Technical limits and performance considerations

When authoring complex granular patches in Infinite, several practical engineering limits apply:

  1. Voice ceiling and CPU load: the AudioGranularNode engine tracks up to 64 simultaneous active grains (kMaxGrains). Each active grain performs four Hermite cubic sample reads and window evaluation calculations per sample. On modern Apple Silicon and x86_64 multi-core processors, running two to four granular engines consumes less than 3% CPU. However, pushing multiple instances to maximum density (100 Hz with 1000 ms length) will saturate the pre-allocated grain pool.
  2. Buffer capacity: the live recording buffer captures up to 60 seconds of uncompressed 32-bit floating point audio at 44.1 or 48 kHz. Recording beyond this duration sets the internal overflow flag and halts writing to prevent memory exhaustion.
  3. Stand-alone and host architecture: Infinite is a standalone application and modular plugin host; it does not ship as an AAX plugin for Avid Pro Tools. It hosts native VST3 and AU plugins, routes MIDI and audio bidirectionally, and exports rendered compositions headless via its command-line interface.

Summary

Granular synthesis bridges the gap between micro-sound physics and musical sound design. By combining high-order Hermite interpolation, flexible window envelopes, stochastic spray generators, and topological metric sorting within a unified modular canvas, Infinite provides an expressive platform for real-time acoustic exploration.

To begin building your own granular clouds, download the latest release of Infinite, open the canvas, and patch an audio sample into Granular.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/granular-synthesis-modular-audio-sound-design.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Modular VST3 host: route plugins, MIDI and CV on an open canvas
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Explore modular VST3 host architecture in Infinite: patch audio and MIDI between plugins, route CV automation across an open canvas, and isolate plugin crashes.
item.content:encoded:
A modular VST3 host breaks audio plugins out of linear channel strips and fixed insert slots. In conventional digital audio workstations, instrument and effect plugins reside inside vertical tracks, where signal flows strictly from top to bottom. Routing one synthesiser into multiple parallel filter chains, tapping intermediate sidechain signals, or modulating plugin dials with external mathematical operators requires awkward aux buses, dummy tracks, or complex routing matrices. For electronic musicians and sound designers exploring generative composition, a dedicated vst3 host modular environment offers an entirely different workflow: plugins exist as free-floating nodes on an open canvas, connected by typed cables that carry stereo audio, frame-accurate MIDI, and continuous control voltage.

In Infinite, native VST3 and Audio Unit plugin hosting is built directly into the core node graph. Rather than isolating third-party instruments inside hidden track panes, each loaded plugin is represented by a Plugin node. Audio, note events, and automation signals enter and exit via explicit pins, making complex parallel processing, feedback loops, and cross-plugin modulation visible and editable at a glance.

This article details the technical architecture of Infinite's modular plugin host, explaining how the engine maintains real-time safety, dispatches sample-accurate note events, maps modulatable parameters, compensates for latency, and protects the canvas against third-party plugin crashes.

Architecture of a modular plugin host

Hosting arbitrary binary plugins inside a real-time audio graph introduces demanding concurrency constraints. Third-party plugins execute compiled machine code that may perform non-trivial DSP operations, allocate memory during initialisation, or communicate with native window managers. To maintain steady buffer playback without dropouts or audio glitches, Infinite isolates plugin execution using a strict two-thread design.

The hosting architecture separates duties between two distinct objects:

  1. The main-thread coordinator (AudioPluginNode): runs on the UI thread, managing plugin discovery, bundle loading, parameter mapping, preset state, and native editor windows.
  2. The audio-thread processor (AudioPluginAudioNode): executes inside the high-priority audio callback, pulling audio buffers, dispatching scheduled MIDI events, and invoking the plugin's render function.

Connecting these two halves is the plugin handle itself, stored as an atomic pointer (std::atomic<Platform::PluginHandle*>). The main thread prepares, configures, and parameterises the plugin instance before exposing it to the audio loop. When the audio engine evaluates the graph topology, the audio thread loads the atomic pointer with acquire semantics and calls the platform rendering wrapper (Platform::PluginRender).

+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           MAIN THREAD                           |
|                                                                 |
|  [AudioPluginNode]                                              |
|         |                                                       |
|         +---> Window Management (Native Win32 / Cocoa / X11)    |
|         +---> Preset State Serialization (Base64 chunk to .inf) |
|         +---> Parameter Mapping (32 positional modulation pins) |
|         +---> Touch-to-Learn Parameter Discovery               |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
                                |
                   atomic<PluginHandle*> (Acquire / Release)
                                |
                                v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|                          AUDIO THREAD                           |
|                                                                 |
|  [AudioPluginAudioNode]                                         |
|         |                                                       |
|         +---> Pull upstream AudioCable & NoteCable buffers      |
|         +---> Package frame-offset MIDI events into VST3 queue  |
|         +---> PluginCrashGuard::Scope breadcrumb journaling     |
|         +---> Invoke Platform::PluginRender                     |
|         +---> Advance Plugin Delay Compensation (PDC) line      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+

When swapping or unloading a plugin on the canvas, the old handle is never freed immediately on the main thread. Instead, it is retired across an engine generation boundary. This discipline ensures that if an in-flight audio callback is actively executing inside the third-party binary, the pointer remains valid until the callback concludes and the topology advances.

Lock-free parameter delivery and modulation

One of the defining advantages of a modular VST3 host is the ability to modulate any plugin parameter with external control signals. In Infinite, low-frequency oscillators (LFO), envelope generators (Envelope), chaos modulators (Random), and audio envelope followers (Audio Analyze) can patch directly into a plugin's parameter pins.

Most native nodes in Infinite deliver automation to the audio thread via a 64-slot parameter mailbox (ParamMailbox). However, complex VST3 plugins frequently expose hundreds or thousands of automatable parameters. Funnelling these through fixed mailbox slots would quickly exhaust thread communication buffers. Furthermore, modern VST3 instruments incorporate their own internal parameter smoothing algorithms.

To resolve this, Infinite implements an Ableton-style parameter configuration model with positional mapping slots:

[Note Sequencer] ---> [Plugin: Poly Synth] ===> [Plugin: Reverb] ---> [Audio Out]
                             |                         ^
                             |                         |
                      (Cutoff Parameter)        (Mix Parameter)
                             ^                         ^
                             |                         |
                          [LFO]                 [Envelope]

A user clicks the Configure toggle on the Plugin node body and touches any control inside the plugin's native graphical interface. Infinite's parameter-learn routine queries PluginVST3PollLearned to capture the parameter's 64-bit address, display title, and minimum and maximum bounds. It then assigns the control to one of 32 positional mapping slots (AudioPluginNode::Mapping).

Each mapped parameter appears on the node body as a horizontal slider equipped with an input modulation pin. When a modulation cable lands on the pin, modulation values sum with the base slider position. During graph evaluation (CookIfNeeded), the main thread pushes updated values directly into the plugin instance via Platform::PluginSetParameter.

Crucially, mapping slots are positional and are never compacted when an entry is removed. Modulation bindings in Infinite are keyed by the node index and parameter index. If a user unmaps an earlier parameter, the slot remains as an inactive placeholder rather than shifting subsequent indices, ensuring existing modulation cables never jump to unintended destinations.

Frame-accurate MIDI note scheduling

When hosting virtual instruments, timing jitter destroys the groove and transient clarity of sequenced parts. A modular canvas must deliver note-on, note-off, velocity, and pitch-bend events with sample accuracy.

In Infinite, musical events travel along dedicated note cables (NoteCable). Generative nodes such as the Note Sequencer, Arpeggiator, or Chorder output event queues containing note values, velocity layers, duration gates, and integer sample offsets relative to the start of the current processing block.

When the Plugin node processes its inputs, it inspects its note pin. If a note cable is connected, the audio thread converts each pending event into a standard three-byte MIDI packet and passes it to the VST3 event dispatcher:

// Conversion of internal NoteCable events to VST3 frame-offset events
for (const NoteEvent& ev : noteBuffer)
{
    unsigned char midiBytes[3];
    int length = 0;

    if (ev.type == NoteEventType::NoteOn)
    {
        midiBytes[0] = static_cast<unsigned char>(0x90 | (ev.channel & 0x0F));
        midiBytes[1] = static_cast<unsigned char>(std::clamp(ev.pitch, 0, 127));
        midiBytes[2] = static_cast<unsigned char>(std::clamp(static_cast<int>(ev.velocity * 127.0f), 1, 127));
        length = 3;
    }
    else if (ev.type == NoteEventType::NoteOff)
    {
        midiBytes[0] = static_cast<unsigned char>(0x80 | (ev.channel & 0x0F));
        midiBytes[1] = static_cast<unsigned char>(std::clamp(ev.pitch, 0, 127));
        midiBytes[2] = 0;
        length = 3;
    }

    if (length > 0)
    {
        Platform::PluginVST3ScheduleMIDIEvent(handle, ev.frameOffset, midiBytes, length);
    }
}

The underlying VST3 wrapper populates the plugin's IEventList interface, preserving the exact frameOffset within the block. Whether the audio buffer size is set to 64 samples or 512 samples, instruments respond to note triggers at the exact microsecond intended by the sequencer, preventing the phase flammability and rhythmic smearing typical of un-timestamped message loops.

Flexible audio routing, sidechaining and splitting

Traditional mixers route signals through rigid master channels and auxiliary returns. On a modular canvas, audio paths are completely fluid. A stereo output from a Plugin node can connect simultaneously to ten different downstream effect chains, or feed an audio-reactive visualiser while continuing into hardware outputs.

Consider a dynamic sidechain compression setup. In hardware racks or modular rigs, patching a kick drum into a vocal or bass compressor requires dedicated patch cables. In Infinite, the Plugin node detects whether a loaded plugin exposes sidechain audio buses by querying PluginVST3SidechainChannels. When auxiliary inputs exist, the node dynamically exposes an additional sidechain input pin:

  • Slot 0: main stereo audio input (in)
  • Slot 1: note event input (notes, visible when the plugin accepts MIDI)
  • Slot 2: sidechain stereo input (sidechain, visible when sidechain buses exist)

To set up rhythmic ducking, a musician patches the audio output of a kick drum synthesiser into both the master Mixer node and the sidechain pin of a downstream compressor Plugin. Both connections exist simultaneously without duplicating tracks or setting up complex bus sends.

Furthermore, because audio connections in Infinite carry multi-channel floating-point data, users can insert utility nodes like Splitter, Gain, and Blend Audio at any point in the signal chain. Splitting a synthesiser output into three frequency bands using high-pass, band-pass, and low-pass filters allows different third-party distortion and delay plugins to process each frequency band independently before summing back into a master bus.

Plugin delay compensation across modular topologies

When effect plugins utilise lookahead limiters, spectral fast Fourier transforms, or heavy convolution algorithms, they introduce processing latency. Without compensation, combining a dry audio signal with a delayed processed signal results in comb filtering, phase cancellation, and hollow transients.

Infinite incorporates automated Plugin Delay Compensation (PDC) across arbitrary modular topologies. Each processing cycle, every Plugin node queries its underlying instance using PluginVST3LatencySamples. The audio engine's topological sorter analyses latency across all converging paths in the patch:

                     +----------------------------+
                     |        Audio Source        |
                     +----------------------------+
                               /        \
                              /          \
               Zero Latency  /            \  512 Samples Latency
                            /              \
                           v                v
                 [Dry Delay Line]       [Lookahead Limiter VST3]
                 (PDC: +512 samples)    (Reports: 512 samples)
                           \                /
                            \              /
                             v            v
                     +----------------------------+
                     |         Summing Bus        |
                     +----------------------------+

When two cables converge at a mixer or summing node, Infinite calculates the difference between their accumulated upstream latencies. The engine allocates an internal circular delay line (CompensationDelay) on the faster path, retarding the dry audio by the exact number of samples reported by the plugin.

Crucially, zero-latency paths allocate no delay memory whatsoever. The PDC mechanism is verified headless using automated impulse response checks, confirming that summed transients arrive on identical sample indices without attenuation or phase distortion.

Crash isolation and recovery

Because VST3 plugins run within the host's memory space, an unhandled exception or null pointer dereference inside a third-party plugin could bring down the entire application. Losing an unsaved modular patch during a live performance or studio session is unacceptable.

Infinite mitigates this vulnerability through its PluginCrashGuard subsystem. Before invoking any third-party render call on the audio thread, the engine enters an execution scope:

{
    PluginCrashGuard::Scope guard(pluginIdentifier.c_str());
    Platform::PluginVST3Render(handle, inBuffers, 2, outBuffers, 2, frames, &transport, scBuffers, scChannels);
}

The guard stores a pointer to the active plugin's identifier in a thread-local variable, requiring only a single pointer write with zero dynamic memory allocation, making it safe for real-time audio threads.

If the plugin triggers a fatal segmentation fault or hardware trap, Infinite's platform crash handler executes. Because the thread was inside an active Scope, the crash handler extracts the offending plugin's identifier and writes an async-signal-safe breadcrumb marker to disk before terminating.

Upon the next launch, Infinite reads the crash journal:

  • Audio Units: the crashed plugin is automatically quarantined and loaded out-of-process via the macOS Audio Unit hosting service, ensuring future crashes mute the single node rather than crashing the DAW.
  • VST3 Plugins: because the VST3 standard lacks an operating-system-level out-of-process daemon, Infinite marks the node on the canvas, bypasses processing, and displays an informative banner naming the plugin that failed. The user can safely remove the offending plugin or update its binary without losing the rest of their patch cords, macros, or synthesizer configurations.

When a plugin behaves reliably, running it directly in-process eliminates inter-process memory copies, preserving minimal latency and peak CPU efficiency.

Patch format and state persistence

Saving and reloading complex modular setups must restore every third-party plugin to its exact preset state, including custom sound banks, sample tables, and internal GUI configurations.

Infinite stores patches as human-readable plain text .inf files. When saving a patch, the main thread calls PluginVST3SaveState on each active handle. The plugin serialises its complete internal data block into an opaque binary stream, which Infinite encodes into standard Base64 text.

In the .inf patch file, the plugin entry is written alongside its canvas coordinates, pin connections, and mapped controls:

node 4 Plugin x=-140.0 y=85.0
  set identifier "com.u-he.diva"
  set name "Diva Lead"
  set bypass 0
  map 0 1024 "Cutoff" 0.0 1.0 0.65
  map 1 1025 "Resonance" 0.0 1.0 0.42
  state "VkVTVDMBAAAAfAAAA...[Base64 chunk]..."
cable 2:0 4:1 notes
cable 4:0 7:0 audio
cable 4:1 7:1 audio
mod 1:0 4:0 0.35

When reopening the patch, Infinite instantiates the plugin, restores its binary state via PluginVST3RestoreState, and reconnects all audio and modulation cables. Because parameter mapping slots remain stable, external LFOs and sequencers immediately resume driving the synthesiser's internal filters without manual re-patching.

Step-by-step: building a modular plugin patch

To experience the power of a modular VST3 host, consider constructing a dynamic patch combining native algorithmic note generation, an external synthesiser, and audio-reactive modulation:

  1. Spawn a Note Sequencer node. Set the step division to 16th notes and configure an eight-step generative sequence with varying velocity levels.
  2. Add a Plugin node and select your favourite VST3 instrument from the picker. Connect the output of the Note Sequencer into the notes pin of the Plugin node.
  3. Patch the stereo audio outputs of the Plugin node into an Audio Out node to hear the synthesiser output.
  4. Click Configure on the Plugin node and adjust the synthesiser's filter cutoff dial in its native interface. A new slider labelled Cutoff appears on the node body with its own modulation pin.
  5. Spawn an LFO node. Set its shape to sine and rate to 1/4 bar. Cable the output of the LFO into the newly created Cutoff modulation pin on the Plugin node. Adjust the modulation depth dial to hear the filter sweep in tempo.
  6. Split the synthesiser's audio into an Audio Analyze node. The 8-band fast Fourier transform extracts low, mid, and high energy envelopes. Cable the high-frequency band into an external reverb plugin's decay time or into a Field Pixel shader node to render synchronised visual art.

By uniting virtual instruments, audio effects, generative sequencing, and parameter modulation on one unified canvas, a modular VST3 host unlocks expressive creative possibilities that conventional track-based digital audio workstations cannot match. Discover ready-made templates and patch ideas in the Infinite patch library.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/modular-vst3-host-audio-routing-and-modulation.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Linux DAW workflows: modular audio, VST3 hosting and live visuals
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Explore modular music production on Linux with Infinite: a Linux DAW to route synthesiser graphs, host Linux VST3 plugins, and patch audio into live visuals.
item.content:encoded:
Selecting a Linux DAW has historically required choosing between two compromises: rigid timeline workstations ported from commercial platforms, or specialised open-source modular environments that excel at algorithmic sound but lack unified visual workflows. Traditional workstations organise music production around horizontal tracks, channel strips, and aux sends. While this paradigm serves multi-track recording well, it creates unnecessary friction for electronic musicians, generative composers, and creative coders who treat audio routing, parameter modulation, and visual synthesis as interconnected elements of a single performance.

In Infinite, modular audio routing, synthesiser sound design, Linux VST3 hosting, and live GPU graphics share one node graph. Instead of segregating audio processing to one application and routing control data or textures over inter-process bridges, every signal flows across typed patch cables on an open canvas. This guide examines how to construct a complete production setup within a modern Linux DAW, covering audio server integration, low-latency device scheduling, native plugin hosting, generative MIDI note pipelines, and audio-reactive visual synthesis.

Architecture of a Linux DAW on an open canvas

Conventional workstations evaluate signal flow through a fixed hierarchy: audio clips sit on tracks, tracks process insert effects, and buses sum channels into master outputs. In contrast, Infinite models entire musical compositions and visual presentations as a directed acyclic graph.

Signal flow occurs through typed connection pins:

  • Audio pins: Transmit multi-channel 32-bit floating-point audio buffers evaluated at the hardware sample rate (such as 48 kHz or 96 kHz).
  • Note pins: Carry polyphonic note events, gate states, velocity values, and microtonal pitch offsets.
  • Modulation pins: Provide floating-point control values, envelope contours, and low-frequency oscillations updated per audio block.
  • Visual pins: Stream GPU texture references, 3D geometry meshes, camera matrices, and shader parameters.

At the beginning of each audio block, Infinite sorts the graph topologically to determine execution order. Nodes without audio dependencies compute first, passing output buffers forward to downstream processors. This explicit data flow eliminates invisible bus latency and enables parallel processing across multi-core processors. You can examine this topology in depth in our node-based DAW guide.

Low-latency audio with PipeWire and ALSA

Reliable audio performance on Linux depends on clear interaction with audio subsystems. Infinite provides native backend support designed for modern Linux audio environments:
