  1. ALSA direct hardware access: For dedicated audio interfaces in studio environments, Infinite can interface directly with ALSA. Bypassing intermediate system daemons yields predictable buffer timing and allows running low buffer sizes, such as 64 or 128 samples at 48 kHz, without dropouts.
  2. PipeWire integration: On modern Linux distributions where PipeWire manages system-wide audio routing, Infinite connects seamlessly through PipeWire ALSA and PulseAudio compatibility layers. Audio streams route alongside other system applications while maintaining stable clock synchronisation.

The audio engine runs its DSP computation inside a dedicated real-time audio thread. When system security configurations permit (such as through standard audio group limits in /etc/security/limits.d/audio.conf), the audio thread requests real-time scheduling priority (SCHED_FIFO). This isolates audio buffer generation from GUI rendering, file indexing, and background tasks, preventing audible xruns during intensive live sets.

Native Linux VST3 plugin hosting and modulation

The availability of high-quality software instruments on Linux has grown significantly. Open-source synthesiser projects such as Surge XT and Odin 2, alongside professional commercial plugins from developers like u-he and Vital, provide native Linux binaries.

Infinite features a native 64-bit VST3 hosting container via the Plugin node. On Linux, the host scans standard module locations:

~/.vst3/
/usr/lib/vst3/
/usr/local/lib/vst3/

Plugins distributed in standard Linux VST3 bundle format:

PluginName.vst3/Contents/x86_64-linux/PluginName.so

When you drop a Plugin node onto the canvas and load a synthesiser or effect, Infinite queries the plugin descriptor and exposes its parameters. Unlike traditional digital audio workstations where parameter automation requires drawing curves into hidden automation lanes, the Plugin node makes automation parameters available as modulatable input pins directly on the node face.

You can connect native canvas modulators, such as the LFO, Envelope Follower, or Random Note Generator, straight into filter cutoff, resonance, or delay time pins. If you wish to learn more about native sound generators, read our synthesiser sound design guide.

Generative sequencing with note graphs

Because note generation in Infinite is modular, you are not restricted to static piano roll loops. You can assemble complex generative sequencers using dedicated note processing nodes:

  1. Euclidean Sequencer: Generates polyrhythmic triggers based on the Euclidean rhythm algorithm. By varying step lengths (such as 16 steps with 7 distributed pulses), you create organic rhythmic counterpoints.
  2. Random Note Generator: Emits algorithmic pitch sequences with controlled randomness, drift probability, and octave constraints.
  3. Quantizer: Snaps continuous or arbitrary note pitches to musical scales (such as Minor Pentatonic, Dorian, or Hirajoshi).
  4. Note Sequencer: Provides classic step sequencing with velocity, gate duration, and pitch controls per step.

These note streams connect directly into internal synthesiser nodes. For example, route a polyrhythmic sequence into Analog for warm subtractive basslines, send a second stream into FM for crystalline bell tones, and trigger custom rhythmic percussion kits using Drum Sequencer. Because note cables carry discrete event packets, branching one sequencer into three separate instruments takes a single mouse drag.

Cabling audio directly into GPU shaders and 3D scenes

In conventional live performance workflows, synchronising visuals with sound requires running two separate programs and transmitting audio levels via OSC, MIDI, or virtual audio loops. This introduces latency, buffer jitter, and configuration complexity.

Infinite unifies audio DSP and graphics rendering within the same application process:

  • Audio Analyze: Computes an 8-band FFT spectrum and transient onset detectors directly from any audio node output cable. It provides immediate float values for sub-bass, low, mid, and high frequency energies.
  • Field Pixel: Implements custom GLSL fragment shaders evaluated directly on the GPU. You can declare uniforms with the param keyword and cable Audio Analyze frequency outputs directly into shader parameters.
  • Render 3D: Renders real-time 3D geometry meshes, point clouds, and procedural materials. Audio modulation can deform vertex displacements, drive camera orbit speeds, or modulate lighting colours.

Because audio analysis and shader rendering share the same memory space, visual reactions occur on the exact frame the audio transient occurs. For practical shader examples, explore our audio-reactive GLSL shader guide.

Headless audio rendering and automation on Linux

A key advantage of Linux in audio production is automation and scriptability. Infinite provides a comprehensive headless command-line interface that allows musicians and developers to render, validate, and inspect patches without launching a desktop window.

To validate an audio patch from a terminal:

infinite --validate --patch my_song.inf

To render an audio and video export on a headless Linux server or continuous integration runner:

xvfb-run -a infinite --render --patch my_song.inf --frames 1800 --out output.mp4

To extract an audio summary and verify peak levels:

infinite --audio-summary --patch my_song.inf

This capability makes it straightforward to automate album rendering, generate audio-reactive visual videos from automated cron scripts, or build headless generative music installations.

Hardware limits and platform considerations

Maintaining clear expectations about platform capabilities ensures dependable operation:

  1. Headless hardware inputs: In headless batch rendering mode, live hardware audio inputs (such as system microphones) and video cameras are refused, returning exit code 4. Offline batch rendering operates on deterministic file sources and synthesiser graphs.
  2. Display server requirements: Running headless rendering on headless Linux systems requires a virtual framebuffer, such as xvfb-run -a, because GPU shader passes require an active OpenGL context.
  3. Plugin compatibility: Infinite on Linux hosts 64-bit native Linux VST3 plugins. Windows VST binaries wrapped in wine bridges are not natively managed, and proprietary formats such as AAX are not supported.

By uniting modular audio graphs, low-latency Linux audio drivers, native VST3 plugin hosting, and GPU visual synthesis, Infinite provides a coherent, open-source foundation for creative music production on Linux.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/linux-daw-modular-audio-and-generative-visuals.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Generative visuals in live performance: audio, nodes and GPU
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Build robust generative visuals for live performance with audio FFT analysis, GPU shaders, procedural geometry, and stable feedback loops in Infinite.
item.content:encoded:
Designing generative visuals live performance systems requires balancing organic computational complexity against absolute stage reliability. Video loops pre-rendered to disk are predictable, but they cannot respond to improvisational tempo changes, unexpected beat drops, or the dynamic energy of a live crowd. Writing raw graphics code in standalone frameworks provides procedural freedom, but building custom audio routing, MIDI mapping, and projection calibration from scratch during show preparation introduces significant friction.

Infinite bridges this divide by providing a unified, node-based workstation where audio synthesis, digital signal processing, real-time GPU fragment shaders, and 3D procedural geometry execute within a single graph. Because audio and graphics share memory space, modulation runs without operating system inter-process latency.

This guide details the technical architecture needed to build robust generative stage visual rigs that respond accurately to incoming music while maintaining locked 60 fps rendering.

Latency budgets and audio-reactive signal chains

The primary failure mode of reactive stage visuals is phase latency: visual pulses hitting the projection screen after the audience has already heard and felt the acoustic transient through the sound system. In club environments and festival stages, human perception detects audiovisual offsets greater than 20 milliseconds as disconnected.

To maintain tight synchronisation, the signal pipeline must minimise buffer delays at every stage:

  1. Audio ingestion: Live sound enters through an Audio In node connected to the venue mixer booth monitor feed, or is generated internally using synthesiser nodes such as Analog or Sampler.
  2. Frequency decomposition: The signal connects to an Audio Analyze node. Rather than relying on simple root-mean-square amplitude, this node computes an 8-band fast Fourier transform filterbank alongside dedicated transient onset detection.
  3. Lock-free modulation transfer: Audio runs on real-time worker threads at 48 kHz in blocks of 128 or 256 samples (2.67 to 5.33 ms of latency). Visual render passes query analysis results through lock-free ring buffers immediately before cooking a frame, ensuring that graphics update within the same display refresh cycle.

The Audio Analyze node exposes specific pins designed for musical modulation:

  • low: Energy below 250 Hz, isolating sub-bass and kick drum attacks.
  • mid: Frequencies between 250 Hz and 4 kHz, tracking synth stabs, snares, and vocal phrases.
  • high: Frequencies above 4 kHz, capturing percussion sizzle and open hi-hats.
  • onset: Single-frame impulse triggers generated by high-frequency spectral flux, suitable for resetting phase counters or switching visual states.

Raw FFT signals often produce harsh, jittery modulation. Routing low or mid through a Smooth node or a Range To Range node dampens jitter, converting spiky numbers into smooth, continuous envelope sweeps.

Real-time fragment shaders with Field Pixel

While pre-built filter nodes handle standard video adjustments, unique visual aesthetics often demand custom GPU algorithms: reaction-diffusion patterns, raymarched distance fields, gyroids, and recursive domain warping. In Infinite, performers write these routines directly on the canvas using the Field Pixel node.

Field compiles high-level mathematical expressions into native GLSL fragment shaders executing on the graphics processor. Controls declared with the param keyword expose animatable input pins on the node body, allowing live audio signals to modulate shader constants.

Here is a complete, stage-ready domain-warping shader kernel designed for the Field Pixel node:

// Declared modulation inputs exposed as node pins
param bass_drive  = 0.45;
param warp_speed  = 1.20;
param complexity  = 3.50;
param colour_drift = 0.80;

// Normalised canvas coordinates
vec2 uv = (fragCoord - 0.5 * resolution.xy) / resolution.y;

// Audio-reactive domain warping
vec2 q = uv;
q.x += sin(uv.y * complexity + time * warp_speed) * 0.25;
q.y += cos(uv.x * complexity + time * warp_speed) * 0.25;

// Distance estimation
float dist = length(q) - (bass_drive * 0.6);
float rings = sin(dist * 18.0 - time * 2.0);
float edge = smoothstep(0.02, 0.0, abs(rings));

// Procedural cosine colour palette
vec3 tint_a = vec3(0.08, 0.10, 0.20);
vec3 tint_b = vec3(0.65, 0.70, 0.95);
vec3 tint_c = vec3(1.00, 0.42, 0.21);
vec3 col = tint_a + tint_b * cos(6.28318 * (colour_drift * q.xyx + vec3(0.0, 0.33, 0.67)));
col += edge * tint_c;

fragColor = vec4(col, 1.0);

When patched, connecting Audio Analyze (low) to bass_drive expands the central geometric core on every kick drum strike, while Audio Analyze (high) wired to colour_drift cycles the colour palette on open hats. For an in-depth review of fragment shader techniques, explore the audio-reactive GLSL shaders guide.

Procedural geometry and 3D instancing

Two-dimensional pixel shaders gain substantial depth when combined with procedural 3D structures. Rather than importing rigid polygonal assets from external modelling software, generative stage visual sets often use mathematical primitives deformed in real time.

In Infinite, 3D pipelines assemble using modular geometry nodes:

  1. Primitive sources: Nodes such as Cube, Sphere, Torus, or Cylinder generate parametric vertex meshes with configurable subdivisions.
  2. Procedural replication: The Array node duplicates geometry across three-dimensional Cartesian grids, concentric rings, or Fibonacci spirals without issuing multiple draw calls.
  3. Real-time vertex deformation: The Audio Displacement and Field Modifier nodes manipulate vertex positions P and surface normals N along mathematical functions or audio waveforms before rasterisation.
  4. Rendering: The Render 3D node collects instances, evaluates a virtual Camera, applies lighting models, and outputs a 2D texture buffer into the compositing tree.

By driving the rotation angles of Render 3D with an LFO node and modulating mesh displacement with live audio frequencies, performers create evolving architectural forms that breathe in tempo with the performance.

Stable feedback loops for live performance

Optical feedback is a foundational technique of live visual art. By feeding a rendered frame back into the input of a compositing chain with subtle scale, rotation, and colour offsets, static shapes evolve into fluid, self-organising cellular structures.

However, unconstrained digital feedback loops quickly suffer from instability: values either blow out to peak white within seconds or fade out into complete blackness.

A dependable stage feedback network requires three explicit stages:

  • Attenuation: Every iteration must decay slightly. A Blend node operating in Multiply or Screen mode, or an Opacity node set to 0.92 to 0.96, prevents energy from accumulating beyond display limits.
  • Spatial transformation: A Transform node placed inside the loop introduces slight zoom (for example, 1.015x) or rotation (0.3 degrees). This pushes old frame content outward toward the display borders, creating tunnel or vortex motion.
  • Temporal persistence: A Trails node preserves trailing light paths while dampening abrupt visual discontinuities.

Because Infinite manages texture buffers natively on the GPU, feedback loops execute without memory copy overhead between the graphics card and host CPU.

Stage control, MIDI mapping and multi-screen projection

A generative patch must remain steerable during a live show. Relying solely on automated sound analysis risks visual monotony across a ninety-minute set. Physical hardware control allows performers to introduce sudden breakdowns, adjust overall complexity, or transition between aesthetic themes.

Infinite supports direct hardware integration:

  • MIDI In: Binds physical knobs, faders, and rotary encoders to any parameter on the canvas. Assigning faders to feedback decay, shader warp frequency, and master brightness gives physical tactility to digital generative structures.
  • OSC Receive: Accepts Open Sound Control network packets over UDP from external sequencing apps, mobile control interfaces, or digital audio workstations.
  • Projection: The final output node provides four-corner perspective homography warping, keystoning, and grid-based mesh calibration for mapping angled projector outputs onto geometric stage surfaces.
  • Zero-copy interconnects: For multi-application stage configurations, Syphon Out (on macOS) and Spout Out (on Windows) stream GPU textures directly to lighting servers, media software, or broadcasting rigs without dropping frames.

Production checklist for stage reliability

When performing in front of an audience, technical failures cannot be negotiated away. Preparing a generative patch for live performance requires strict verification:

  1. Headless validation: Test patch syntax and node integrity from the command line using infinite --validate patch.inf. This verifies that all connections, modulation bindings, and shader kernels parse cleanly without syntax errors.
  2. Fixed resolution budgets: Target 1920x1080 at 60 fps for standard projection systems. Avoid arbitrarily oversized framebuffers that consume excessive fill-rate bandwidth without visible audience benefit.
  3. Thermal headroom: Confirm that your graphics processor maintains sustained frame rates under warm stage conditions. Monitor cook times in the performance matrix; an efficient generative graph should complete its graphics pass in under 4 milliseconds per frame.
  4. Safety fallbacks: Always patch a master fader mapped to an auxiliary hardware slider that can fade the entire visual output to black or crossfade into an ambient background if an incoming booth audio cable is disconnected.

Where to go next

Generative visual systems reward ongoing experimentation and iteration. To explore practical working patches, download free example setups from the Infinite Library, or consult the Field language manual to begin authoring bespoke mathematical shaders. By combining real-time DSP analysis with GPU-accelerated node pipelines, you can build responsive, instrument-grade visual instruments tailored specifically for live performance.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/generative-visuals-live-performance.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Open source VJ software: real-time visual performance in Infinite
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Build real-time generative visuals, map live audio frequencies, and drive stage projection with Infinite, an open source VJ software workstation for performers.
item.content:encoded:
Live visual performers, video artists, and VJs often find themselves caught between expensive proprietary suites and fragmented coding environments. Traditional VJ tools frequently rely on restrictive licensing dongles, fixed video playback paradigms, or separate audio analysis applications linked through fragile network protocols. Meanwhile, creative coding frameworks require writing low-level windowing and graphics boilerplate before rendering a single frame.

Infinite approaches live visual performance from a different direction. It is a free, MIT-licensed audiovisual workstation that brings audio synthesis, real-time video compositing, hardware modulation, and GPU fragment shaders together on a single canvas. As an open source VJ software platform running on macOS, Windows, and Linux, Infinite allows performers to build modular visual rigs that react directly to acoustic signals with sub-millisecond precision.

Whether you are performing generative visual sets alongside live electronic music, mixing live camera feeds at club nights, or projection mapping multi-screen stage environments, Infinite provides the building blocks for expressive real-time visuals.

Architecture of a real-time visual workstation

Standard video software treats audio and visuals as disconnected media tracks. An image mixer might read sound from an auxiliary sound card input, process amplitude through an operating system audio queue, and hand numbers over to a rendering loop several frames later. In high-tempo club environments or rhythmically intricate live electronic sets, this round-trip latency creates a noticeable disconnect between percussive attacks and visual impacts.

Infinite solves this through a shared engine architecture:

  1. Lock-free modulation queues: The audio engine operates on dedicated real-time worker threads at 48 kHz, while the graphics engine runs on the display refresh loop. Analysis values pass between these domains through lock-free ring buffers.
  2. Synchronous evaluation: When a video node cooks, it samples modulation values updated by the most recent audio block. The modulation pass evaluates immediately before the frame cooks, ensuring that picture updates track incoming sound rather than the previous frame.
  3. GPU-centric pipeline: Video textures, generative shaders, and compositing blend modes execute entirely within OpenGL framebuffers, avoiding unnecessary memory transfers between graphics memory and system RAM.

This unified design gives performers the immediacy of hardware modular synthesisers combined with the graphical flexibility of modern shader programming.

Ingesting live audio with Audio Analyze

Audio reactivity is central to modern visual performance. In Infinite, incoming acoustic signals enter the graph through either an Audio In node capturing line-level signals from a DJ mixer, an Audio File player, or internal synthesis nodes such as Analog.

To convert sound into visual modulation, route the audio signal into an Audio Analyze node. The node performs continuous fast Fourier transform analysis and envelope tracking across several dedicated outputs:

  • low: Energy below 250 Hz, isolating kick drums and sub-bass transients.
  • mid: Frequencies between 250 Hz and 4 kHz, tracking vocal presence, snare snaps, and melodic synths.
  • high: Energy above 4 kHz, capturing hi-hats, cymbals, and percussive sizzle.
  • level: Instantaneous root-mean-square amplitude across the full audible spectrum.
  • onset: Transient detection spikes that fire when sudden percussive strikes occur.
  • band0 through band7: An 8-band spectral filterbank providing granular frequency separation.

Connecting a cable from the low pin of Audio Analyze to a visual parameter allows basslines to pump canvas geometry, scale textures, or modulate colour lookup tables with zero perceptible latency.

Procedural shader generation in Field Pixel

Pre-rendered video clips consume substantial storage and can feel repetitive over a three-hour live set. Infinite incorporates generative graphics directly into the node graph through the Field Pixel node.

Field Pixel compiles concise mathematical expressions into GPU fragment shaders. Performers can declare modulatable parameters using the param keyword, which instantly exposes corresponding input pins on the node body:

param float bass = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0];
param float mid = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0];
param float speed = 1.0 [0.1, 4.0];
param float feedback_amount = 0.85 [0.0, 1.0];

# Centre coordinates and correct aspect ratio
vec2 p = (uv - 0.5) * vec2(aspect, 1.0);
float dist = length(p);
float angle = atan(p.y, p.x);

# Generate dynamic geometric rings modulated by audio
float wave = sin(dist * 24.0 - t * speed * 3.0 + angle * 4.0);
float pulse = smoothstep(0.04, 0.0, abs(wave) - 0.15 - bass * 0.35);

# Construct a luminous duotone colour gradient
vec3 c_deep = vec3(0.05, 0.06, 0.12);
vec3 c_accent = vec3(1.0, 0.42, 0.21);
vec3 c_signal = vec3(0.65, 0.69, 1.0);

col = mix(c_deep, c_accent, pulse);
col += c_signal * mid * smoothstep(0.4, 0.0, dist);

Because declared parameters become interactive pins on the canvas, you can patch low into bass and an LFO into speed. The shader recompiles in milliseconds whenever code changes, making live shader coding practical during rehearsals and shows.

Live video compositing with Blend and Feedback

Live VJing requires layering multiple visual streams: live camera feeds, generative shader patterns, 3D geometry renders, and typographic overlays. Infinite provides a suite of 2D compositing nodes designed for live video manipulation:

Multi-layer compositing with Blend

The Blend node takes two input textures (inA and inB) and combines them using approximately 30 compositing modes, including Normal, Multiply, Screen, Add, Overlay, Difference, and Exclusion.

Unlike conventional software that computes blending in non-linear gamma space, Infinite provides a linear toggle for physically accurate light accumulation, as well as headroom preservation so bright highlights do not clip prematurely. The mix slider controls crossfading between sources and can be modulated by hardware MIDI sliders or audio envelope followers.

Temporal recursion with Feedback and Trails

Spatial echoes and recursive feedback loops are classic staples of live visual performance. Infinite includes two purpose-built nodes for temporal processing:

  • Feedback: Captures its upstream image once per frame and introduces a single-frame delay. This safe delay allows cables to patch downstream results back into upstream nodes without causing infinite recursion errors during graph cooking.
  • Trails: Accumulates previous frames with adjustable decay and threshold controls, generating silky motion blur, liquid light trails, and phosphor persistence effects behind fast-moving visuals.

When combined with an upstream Transform node, a Feedback loop can continuously rotate, scale, or displace images, producing infinite zoom tunnels and kaleidoscopic generative textures.

Hardware control via MIDI CC and modulators

Performing without a physical interface can feel sterile. Infinite connects directly to external MIDI controllers, foot pedals, and fader boxes through dedicated input nodes:

  • MIDI CC: Listens for continuous controller messages from physical knobs, rotary encoders, and faders. Each incoming CC channel maps directly to any parameter in the graph.
  • MIDI Trigger: Translates incoming pad strikes and note-on events into instantaneous triggers, useful for strobing visuals or advancing clip banks.
  • LFO: Generates periodic modulation waveforms (Sine, Triangle, Saw, Square, Sample and Hold) with tempo synchronisation locked to musical divisions.
  • Audio to CV: Converts raw audio waveforms into smoothed control voltages with adjustable attack and release ballistic curves.

By mapping a MIDI controller fader to the mix parameter of a Blend node, while assigning rotary encoders to shader parameters, performers gain hands-on physical mastery over their generative visual environment.

Multi-display projection mapping and Syphon routing

Delivering visuals to audiences involves stage surfaces, projectors, and external LED walls. Infinite provides robust output routing options for professional venue configurations:

Projection mapping with the Projection node

The Projection node provides hardware-accelerated keystone correction, corner pinning, and mesh grid warping within a single render pass. Performers can choose between two primary warping modes:

  1. CornerPin: Provides 4-corner perspective homography, allowing operators to align rectangular visuals onto angled projection surfaces, fabric screens, or stage flats.
  2. MeshGrid: Subdivides the projection surface into an adjustable grid of control points, making it straightforward to map onto curved surfaces, architectural columns, or domes.

To speed up on-site projector alignment, the Projection node includes built-in test patterns, such as alignment crosshairs, coordinate grids, and calibration colour bars.

Inter-application video routing with Syphon and Spout

In complex multi-software setups, VJs often need to send visual streams between Infinite, Resolume Arena, OBS Studio, MadMapper, or TouchDesigner. Infinite supports zero-copy GPU texture sharing:

  • On macOS, the Syphon Out node broadcasts textures with zero CPU overhead, while Syphon In receives external camera streams or media playback feeds.
  • On Windows, the same nodes transparently utilise Spout2 for high-speed DirectX/OpenGL inter-process texture sharing.

For artists exploring stage setups and automatic show rigs, our guide to automatic visuals for DJ sets provides additional recipes for booth audio integration. Visual artists can also explore dedicated workflows on the VJs page.

Honest constraints and technical boundaries

Infinite is an evolving open-source project. Operating transparently about current capabilities helps artists plan their live production rigs reliably:

  • Headless mode limitations: While Infinite includes a comprehensive command-line interface for offline video rendering and patch validation, hardware devices (such as live webcams, capture cards, and microphone inputs) are refused in headless execution. Live VJ performances must be conducted within the interactive GUI application.
  • Linux texture sharing: While macOS provides Syphon and Windows provides Spout, Linux does not currently support inter-process GPU texture sharing in Infinite. Linux performers should use the Video In node with Video4Linux2 capture cards, local media files, or network streaming rather than Syphon/Spout nodes.
  • Plugin formats: Infinite hosts native AU and VST3 instruments and effects on macOS and Windows, but proprietary Avid AAX format plugins are not supported.

By maintaining clean separation between audio and graphics processing, eliminating licence restrictions, and providing direct access to low-level shader math, Infinite delivers a capable open-source VJ software environment for artists who value modular creative freedom.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/open-source-vj-software.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Automatic visuals for DJ sets: hands-free live visuals in Infinite
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Generate hands-free, audio-reactive visuals for DJ sets in Infinite using live audio analysis, frequency-split modulation, and hardware projection.
item.content:encoded:
Performing an electronic music set demands constant attention. Selecting tracks, adjusting equalization, matching phrasing, and monitoring booth levels leave no spare hands for triggering video clips or operating complex VJ software. Many performers resort to running pre-rendered video loops on a thumb drive. While convenient, looping video files quickly grow repetitive and fail to react when a track drops into an extended breakdown or changes tempo.

Creating automatic visuals for DJ sets solves this disconnection. By running an autonomous visual patch that listens to the master output of your DJ mixer, extracts rhythmic and spectral features in real time, and synthesises generative graphics on the GPU, you achieve synchronised club visuals that adapt to every transition without manual intervention.

In Infinite, audio processing and real-time graphics run inside the same unified canvas. Rather than stringing together separate audio hosts and VJ applications over networked video protocols with variable latency, Infinite shares memory between its low-latency audio engine and GPU rendering pipeline. This guide explains how to construct a robust, hands-free audiovisual patch for live DJ performance, from signal conditioning and frequency decomposition to generative shader synthesis and projector output.

Hardware setup and audio capture

The foundation of responsive generative visuals is a clean, low-latency audio feed from your performance hardware. Relying on an ambient room microphone produces muddy transients and room reverberation that blur beat detection.

To set up a reliable signal path:

  1. Connect the secondary master output, booth monitor output, or dedicated record output from your DJ mixer or club interface into a stereo line input on your audio interface.
  2. In Infinite, open audio settings and select your input device. Configure the hardware buffer size to 128 or 256 samples at 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz. At 48 kHz, a 128-sample buffer introduces under three milliseconds of capture latency, ensuring visual hits land on the exact transient of each kick drum.
  3. Add an Audio In node to the canvas. Verify that input gain levels peak between -6 dB and -3 dB during loud sections. Consistent headroom prevents digital clipping, which can distort high-frequency energy measurements.

Note that in Infinite, hardware audio capture requires running the application with its user interface. The headless command-line interface deliberately refuses microphone and live audio input patches with exit code 4 to prevent background processes from holding hardware audio device locks.

Frequency decomposition and onset detection

Raw audio waveforms fluctuate too rapidly to be cabled directly to visual parameters. A direct connection causes high-frequency flickering that strains the eyes and lacks rhythmic clarity. Instead, incoming sound must be decomposed into musically meaningful frequency bands and transient events.

Wire the stereo outputs of Audio In into an Audio Analyze node. The Audio Analyze node inspects 48 kHz audio buffers and separates the incoming spectrum into distinct frequency domains:

  • low: Energy below 250 Hz, isolating kick drums and sub-bass foundation.
  • mid: Energy between 250 Hz and 4 kHz, capturing vocal hooks, snare bodies, and synth leads.
  • high: Energy above 4 kHz, tracking hi-hats, cymbals, percussion sizzle, and vocal sibilance.
  • level: The instantaneous root-mean-square amplitude across the entire audible spectrum.

In addition to continuous frequency energy, Audio Analyze performs onset detection. By measuring rapid increases in spectral flux, the node outputs discrete trigger impulses whenever an acoustic transient occurs. These triggers allow your visual patch to register sudden tempo changes, snare hits, or unexpected drops.

Smoothing transients with envelope followers

While frequency splitting separates bass from treble, raw spectral energy still jumps abruptly from buffer to buffer. To turn these values into fluid, organic motion, route each frequency pin through signal conditioning before connecting them to graphics nodes.

The ideal tool for this smoothing is an Envelope Follower or an inline smoothing formula in the audio-reactive GLSL shader pipeline. An envelope follower applies asymmetrical attack and release times to incoming modulation values:

  • Fast attack (1 to 5 milliseconds): Allows visual elements to react immediately to the initial strike of a kick drum or crash cymbal, preserving rhythmic punch.
  • Controlled release (80 to 250 milliseconds): Prevents the parameter from dropping to zero between musical beats. The value decays exponentially, producing smooth physical recoil rather than jarring digital stepped changes.

For sub-bass frequencies, set a release time around 120 milliseconds. This timing allows geometric pulses to breathe in sync with typical 120 to 135 BPM dance music tempos. For high frequencies, a shorter release of 40 milliseconds keeps hi-hat shimmers crisp and articulate.

Designing generative visuals with Field Pixel

With smoothed frequency bands available as modulation sources, add a Field Pixel node to generate real-time visuals directly on the GPU. The Field Pixel node compiles mathematical Field expressions into native GLSL fragment programs.

Declare input parameters at the top of your kernel using the param keyword. Each declared parameter automatically exposes an input pin on the node body:

param float bass = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0];
param float mid = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0];
param float treble = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0];
param float energy = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0];
param float speed = 0.5 [0.0, 2.0];

Inside the kernel, map these parameters to visual geometry. A reliable starting point for club visuals is a polar tunnel or radial raymarcher. Normalized coordinates uv are centred and corrected for aspect ratio:

vec2 p = (uv - 0.5) * vec2(aspect, 1.0);
float r = length(p);
float a = atan(p.y, p.x);

// Bass drives radial deformation and pulse expansion
float tunnel = fract(2.0 / (r + 0.05 * bass) + t * speed);

// Treble modulates high-frequency geometric ridges
float ridges = sin(a * 8.0 + sin(tunnel * 12.0)) * 0.5 + 0.5;
ridges = pow(ridges, 3.0) * (0.2 + 0.8 * treble);

// Mid frequencies control luminous glow and core radius
float core = smoothstep(0.3 + 0.2 * mid, 0.0, r);
vec3 base_col = vec3(0.1, 0.15, 0.35);
vec3 pulse_col = vec3(1.0, 0.42, 0.21);

col = mix(base_col, pulse_col, tunnel * ridges + core * energy);

Because the shader recalculates every pixel in parallel on the GPU, complex mathematical forms render at a stable 60 frames per second without burdening the CPU threads responsible for audio analysis.

Adding motion trails and temporal depth

A common issue with procedural visuals in live venues is visual emptiness during breakdown sections. When the kick drum cuts out, a purely reactive shader may collapse into a flat, motionless background.

To maintain visual interest across quiet passages, pipe the output of your Field Pixel node into a Feedback node paired with a Blend node:

  1. Connect the shader output to the primary input of Blend.
  2. Connect the output of Blend into a Feedback node.
  3. Cable the output of Feedback through a subtle transform (such as a slight zoom of 1.01 or a minute rotation of 0.2 degrees) and route it back into the secondary input of Blend.
  4. Set the blend mode to Screen or Lighten, with opacity set between 0.85 and 0.92.

This feedback loop stores previous frames in texture memory and decays them over time. When intense drops occur, bright bursts leave radiant trails that echo outwards. When the music strips down to an ambient synth pad, the feedback buffer gently circulates the remaining visual energy, creating atmospheric smoke and fluid drift until the rhythm returns.

Evolving scenes across an hour-long set

To prevent audience fatigue during a sixty or ninety-minute performance, visuals must evolve over macro timescales. An audience will notice if a single shader pattern loops without variation for an entire hour.

You can introduce macro evolution autonomously using slow modulators:

  • Slow LFOs: Add an LFO node set to a Sine or Triangle shape at an ultra-low frequency, such as 0.005 Hz (one cycle every three minutes). Cable this LFO to camera rotation, tunnel depth, or geometric twist. The audience perceives a constantly shifting environment without sudden disjointed cuts.
  • Dynamic colour ramps: Route a slow noise signal from a Noise node into a Color Ramp node. Instead of fixed RGB values, the colour palette gradually glides from deep midnight blues and indigos into warm ember and amber hues over ten to fifteen minutes.
  • Breakdown detectors: Use a comparison node to monitor overall level. If overall audio amplitude drops below a threshold for more than four seconds, automatically trigger a slow fade into an expansive, floating particle field. When the onset detector registers a sudden peak in low energy, switch back to high-impact geometric pulses.

You can explore pre-configured generative patches and modulation recipes in the Infinite node library.

Routing low-latency video to stage projectors

Once your patch is generating responsive visuals, route the video stream to the venue display system:

  • Direct projector output: Connect an HDMI, DisplayPort, or USB-C cable to the club projector or LED processor. In Infinite, add a Projection node. In the node inspector, select the external display and enable full-screen presentation. Infinite renders borderless output to the selected screen while keeping the node canvas accessible on your laptop display.
  • Inter-application video sharing: If the venue uses visual mapping software such as Resolume Arena or broadcast tools like OBS, use Infinite's native video sharing nodes. On macOS, add a Syphon Out node; on Windows, add a Spout Out node; for networked rigs, use NDI Out. These protocols share GPU texture handles directly across memory without copying pixels back to system RAM, maintaining full frame rates with zero added latency.

Performance checklist and live limits

When preparing an autonomous visual rig for a live performance, follow these stability guidelines:

  1. Cap display refresh rates: Enable vertical synchronisation (VSync) or set a maximum frame limit of 60 frames per second in application preferences. Rendering at uncapped frame rates (such as 240 fps) heats your laptop graphics chip unnecessarily, increasing the risk of thermal throttling during long sets.
  2. Audio buffer safety: Keep your audio buffer at 128 or 256 samples. Avoid setting buffer sizes below 64 samples unless using a dedicated audio interface with robust proprietary drivers. A buffer underrun in the audio thread will momentarily disrupt feature extraction.
  3. Prevent operating system sleep: Ensure system energy saver settings prevent screen sleeping and disk spindown when the laptop lid is closed or unattended.
  4. Clean line inputs: Always request a dedicated booth or record output from the house sound technician rather than tapping an auxiliary headphone jack with unstable volume controls.

By combining low-latency audio capture, frequency-split envelope followers, and GPU fragment shaders, you can build an expressive, automatic visual accompaniment that elevates your live DJ sets while keeping your hands entirely focused on the music.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/automatic-visuals-for-dj-sets.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Node-based DAW workflows: modular audio routing on an infinite canvas
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Explore node-based DAW workflows in Infinite: wire synths, route MIDI into generative sequencers, and patch audio directly into live visual shaders.
item.content:encoded:
Conventional digital audio workstations structure musical composition around a rigid metaphor: horizontal timeline tracks flowing into vertical mixer channel strips. This architecture has powered music production for decades, yet it imposes artificial boundaries when working with complex generative systems, non-linear modulation, or multi-sensory performances. Routing a synthesiser output into an effects send, tapping intermediate filter states, or modulating an external parameter requires creating auxiliary buses, sidechain configurations, and hidden routing matrices.

A node based DAW replaces track strips with an open visual canvas. Instead of confining sound generators and processors to sequential channel slots, every element exists as an independent node whose inputs and outputs can be freely cabled together. Signals branch, merge, feedback, and modulate across arbitrary topologies without requiring dedicated bus channels.

In Infinite, this modular paradigm extends beyond audio. Audio DSP kernels, MIDI generators, VST3 plugin instruments, and real-time GPU shaders share the same sample-accurate graph. This architecture allows electronic musicians and creative coders to build generative soundscapes and responsive visuals within a single environment.

The architecture of a node-based DAW

Traditional audio workstations evaluate signal paths hierarchically: individual clips schedule events along a timeline, tracks accumulate instrument and insert plugin outputs, and aux channels sum multiple track streams into master stems. In contrast, a node-based DAW represents your entire project as a directed graph.

Every node in the graph exposes typed connection pins:

  • Note pins: Carry polyphonic note events, timing ticks, velocity values, and microtonal pitch offsets.
  • Audio pins: Stream multi-channel 32-bit floating-point audio buffers evaluated at the hardware sample rate (such as 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz).
  • Modulation pins: Transmit continuous control values, envelope followers, and low-frequency oscillations evaluated per block or per sample.
  • Visual pins: Pass GPU texture handles, 3D geometry buffers, and shader uniforms.

During each audio engine block, Infinite topologically sorts the graph to establish execution order. Nodes with zero incoming audio dependencies render first, pushing their buffers forward along output cables to downstream processors. Because routing is explicit, parallel signal paths execute concurrently on multi-core processors without phase drift or unintended latency penalties.

Generative MIDI note routing and transformation

In a linear DAW, polyphonic note data typically originates from a recorded MIDI clip or an external keyboard controller assigned to a single track. In a node-based environment, note streams become dynamic data pipelines that can be divided, filtered, and transformed mathematically before reaching an instrument.

Consider building an evolving ambient arpeggio. Instead of hand-drawing notes on a piano roll, you can construct a generative note network:

  1. Place a Note Sequencer node to establish a rhythmic pulse. Set the clock division to a sixteenth-note division with subtle swing.
  2. Cable the note output into a Random Note Generator set to a Markov chain drift algorithm. Constrain the output to a specific musical scale, such as D Dorian or F Lydian.
  3. Branch the resulting note stream into two parallel paths:
  • The first path cables directly into a Keyboard or Note Filter node set to pass only root notes and fifths down to a bass voice.
  • The second path routes through an Arpeggiator and a Quantizer node, shifting pitches across two octaves to generate floating melodic lines.

Because notes travel along visual patch cables, adding a Note Delay or Note Strum node requires only dropping the module between pins. You can inspect the active pitch and velocity data at every junction without digging through nested inspector menus. For a comprehensive walkthrough of available sequencing modules, consult our generative sequencing guide.

Multi-timbral sound generation and VST3 hosting

Once MIDI note streams are generated, they route directly into sound sources. Infinite provides native sound generators alongside full support for third-party instruments:

  • Analog: A dual-oscillator subtractive synthesiser featuring continuously morphable saw, pulse, and triangle waveforms, followed by a resonant 4-pole lowpass ladder filter and soft-clipping saturation.
  • FM: A multi-operator frequency modulation engine capable of generating bright metallic textures, complex bell spectra, and punchy electric basslines.
  • Wavetable: A multi-frame wavetable synthesiser supporting spectral scanning and custom wave extraction.
  • Granular and PaulStretch: Spectral time-stretching and granular sample scrubbers for ambient sound design.
  • Plugin: A native 64-bit VST3 and AU hosting container that opens external commercial synthesiser instruments and effects.

Unlike conventional plugin wrappers that conceal parameter automation inside automation lanes, the Plugin node exposes its internal controls directly as patch pins. If you host a complex synthesiser such as Surge XT or Vital, you can expose controls such as filter cutoff, wavetable position, and delay feedback as modulatable inputs on the node face. Any native modulator on your canvas can then drive those parameters directly.

To explore the sonic architecture of each built-in instrument, read our detailed Infinite sound design guide.

Complex modulation topologies without aux buses

Modulation routing in traditional workstations is often restricted. LFOs and envelopes are usually trapped inside the instrument that generated them, while DAW-level parameter automation requires tedious point-and-click curve editing.

In a node-based DAW, modulators are first-class canvas citizens. A single LFO node can branch its output cable to twenty destinations at once. You can route an LFO to:

  • Modulate the filter cutoff of an Analog synth.
  • Sweep the wavetable index of a Wavetable node.
  • Modulate the delay time parameter of a hosted VST3 chorus plugin.
  • Adjust the camera distance of a 3D visual render.

Furthermore, modulators can modulate other modulators. Routing a slow, non-synchronised Random noise node into the rate pin of an LFO creates organic, non-repeating movements that mimic analogue hardware instability. Passing an envelope through a Math node enables arithmetic operations: invert the curve, multiply by a depth scalar, or add a constant bias before reaching the destination pin.

Multi-segment envelope generators (MSEG) provide complex multi-breakpoint modulation curves that can be triggered by note events or looped freely as custom LFO shapes.

Crossing the boundary: audio directly into live shaders

The most distinctive capability of a unified node-based DAW is the elimination of the barrier between music production and live visual art.

In typical audiovisual production rigs, an artist runs Ableton Live or Bitwig Studio on one computer, transmits audio or MIDI over an interface, and captures it inside TouchDesigner, Resolume, or Notch on another machine. This split creates latency, requires managing multiple software licences, and restricts cross-talk between sound and image.

Infinite unites both worlds on a single canvas. The same engine that computes audio blocks also manages GPU rendering. You can take an audio cable directly from the output of an Analog synthesiser, an Audio Analyze FFT node, or an envelope follower and plug it directly into a visual parameter:

  1. Add a FieldPixel node to the canvas.
  2. In the Field language code editor, declare modulatable parameters:

``glsl param float bass = 0.0 [0, 1]; param float resonance = 0.0 [0, 1]; ``

  1. Cable the low-frequency output of Audio Analyze into bass.
  2. Cable the filter envelope of your synthesiser into resonance.

The GPU compiles the Field expression into native GLSL shaders that execute at 60 frames per second. Visual geometries deform in exact synchronisation with acoustic transients. Because audio analysis happens in-process within shared memory, visual reaction occurs on the exact frame of the audio onset. To learn more about authoring GPU fragment shaders in Field, consult our tutorial on audio-reactive GLSL shaders.

Practical patching: building an ambient generative patch

To experience the speed of node-based music creation, follow this five-minute patching workflow:

Step 1: Note generation

Create a Clock node set to 110 BPM. Cable its output into a Note Sequencer. Configure an 8-step sequence using notes from the C minor pentatonic scale (C3, Eb3, F3, G3, Bb3). Connect the output to a Note Strum node to add subtle timing humanisation.

Step 2: Dual synthesis engines

Add an Analog node and a FM node. Split the note cable from Note Strum into both synthesisers.

  • On Analog, select a warm saw oscillator with a warm 12 dB lowpass filter.
  • On FM, set operator frequency ratios to 1:2 to produce glass-like harmonic overtones.

Step 3: Spatial effects and summing

Add a Mixer node with four stereo channels. Route the audio output of Analog into Channel 1, and FM into Channel 2. Adjust pan positions slightly left and right to build stereo width.

Route the mixer master output into a Field Effect node loaded with an algorithmic stereo delay script. Set delay times to dotted eighth and dotted sixteenth intervals, with 45 percent feedback.

Step 4: Canvas modulation

Add an LFO node set to a slow sine wave at 0.1 Hz. Cable its output to:

  • Channel 1 filter cutoff on Analog.
  • FM modulation index on FM.
  • Delay feedback on Field Effect.

Your patch now breathes autonomously, shifting between warm analogue bass tones and crystalline FM chimes.

Step 5: Visual feedback

Finally, add an Audio Analyze node connected to the master output. Route the low band output into a FieldPixel generative visual tunnel. Route the final graphic to an Output node to project the visual in full screen on an external display or projector.

You can download ready-made modular patches, synthesiser presets, and audio-reactive shaders from the Infinite Library.

Honest limits: when a timeline DAW remains preferable

While a node-based architecture offers unmatched flexibility for modular synthesis, generative composition, and audiovisual integration, it is not always the most suitable tool for every project:

  • Large multitrack vocal and acoustic recording: Tracking forty live audio microphones, comping vocal takes, and editing audio phase alignments across multitrack drum kits is faster in a linear timeline DAW such as Logic Pro, Cubase, or Pro Tools.
  • Proprietary AAX ecosystem: Infinite does not support proprietary Avid AAX plugins. Pro Tools studio environments requiring AAX DSP hardware interfaces cannot run those plugins inside Infinite.
  • Headless mode hardware limits: While Infinite provides a headless command-line interface for automated rendering and batch validation, headless execution deliberately refuses patches containing live microphone capture or hardware MIDI inputs with exit code 4. Live interactive hardware inputs require running the graphical application interface.
  • Young ecosystem: Infinite is a modern, open-source project licensed under MIT. While rapidly expanding with regular updates, its library of third-party templates is still developing compared to software platforms that have existed for two decades.

For generative music, modular sound design, live algorithmic performance, and integrated audiovisual art, a node-based DAW provides an inspiring and unconstrained creative environment.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/node-based-daw-modular-audio-routing.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Every note node in Infinite: generative arpeggiators and algorithmic sequencing
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Explore all 24 note nodes in Infinite: algorithmic arpeggiators, scale quantizers, Markov chains, chord generators, humanizers, and generative note logic.
item.content:encoded:
In traditional music production environments, MIDI is treated as a static piano roll. Notes are clicked onto a grid, quantised rigidly, and routed through a single linear track directly into a virtual instrument.

Infinite re-imagines MIDI and musical timing as an open, modular stream of discrete note events. Notes are not passive rows in an arrangement; they are first-class signals that flow through cables, branch across splitters, undergo algorithmic transformations, and drive both sound engines and 3D visual geometry in real time.

Infinite provides twenty-four dedicated note processing nodes, spanning hardware input bridges, rhythmic arpeggiators, Markov-chain phrase predictors, physics-based trigger simulations, scale quantizers, and programmable algorithmic note generators.

Here is an architectural guide to every note node in Infinite, how they process musical events, and how to patch generative music systems on the canvas.

1. MIDI Notes: hardware controller & MPE input bridge

The MIDI Notes node connects physical MIDI keyboards, pad controllers, and MPE (MIDI Polyphonic Expression) devices to the Infinite canvas.

How it works

  • Multi-channel routing: Listens on all channels (Omni) or binds to a specific MIDI channel (1 to 16).
  • MPE support: Full per-note polyphonic pitch bend, slide, and pressure/aftertouch tracking.
  • Port activity visualization: Real-time visual LEDs displaying active note-on gates, polyphonic voice count, and pitch numbers.
  • Event stream outputs: Outputs polyphonic note events cleanly buffered for sample-accurate scheduling.

Try it

Connect a USB MIDI keyboard, wire MIDI Notes into an Analog synth, and route per-note MPE pressure into the filter cutoff knob.

MIDI Notes -> Analog -> Audio Out

2. Keyboard: interactive on-screen playable piano

The Keyboard node provides a playable virtual piano keyboard directly inside the node canvas, supporting mouse clicks, multi-touch, and computer QWERTY keyboard typing.

How it works

  • Octave range navigation: Configurable key span with quick octave shift controls.
  • Musical scale highlighting: Highlights active scale notes across white and black keys, preventing accidental off-key inputs during live performance.
  • Velocity sensitivity: Clicking near the bottom of a key triggers high velocity (up to 127), while clicking near the top triggers soft pianissimo notes.

Try it

Select the Dorian scale in the inspector, highlight the scale keys, and jam melodies using your computer keyboard without opening external controllers.

Keyboard -> FM -> Reverb -> Audio Out

3. Note Filter: range, channel, and velocity gate

The Note Filter node acts as a selective filter for incoming note streams, allowing only notes meeting specific musical criteria to pass downstream.

How it works

  • Pitch key zones: Set minimum and maximum note limits (e.g. C1 to B2 for bass, C3 to C6 for leads) to create multi-instrument keyboard splits.
  • Velocity window: Filters notes by dynamics, passing only ghost notes (low velocity) or accents (high velocity).
  • Channel filtering: Strips out or isolates specific MIDI channels from multi-timbral controllers.

Try it

Wire one MIDI Notes output into two Note Filters: set filter 1 to notes below C3 for a sub bass synth, and filter 2 to notes above C3 for a shimmering lead.

MIDI Notes -> Note Filter (Low) -> Analog (Bass)
MIDI Notes -> Note Filter (High) -> Wavetable (Lead)

4. Note Transpose: chromatic and scale-aware pitch shifting

The Note Transpose node shifts the pitch of incoming note events by octaves and semitones while optionally constraining the shifted notes to a selected musical scale.

How it works

  • Octave & semitone offsets: Shift notes up or down by up to 4 octaves and 12 semitones.
  • Modulatable transposition: The semitone parameter is modulatable, allowing an LFO or step sequencer to modulate chord progressions automatically.
  • Scale snapping: Forces transposed notes onto the nearest valid scale degree to prevent dissonant pitch clashes.

Try it

Modulate Note Transpose with a Slow Step Sequencer to shift an arpeggio across root, fourth, and fifth chords every four bars.

Arpeggiator -> Note Transpose -> Wavetable -> Audio Out

5. Pitch Bend: expressive pitch deflection router

The Pitch Bend node routes and scales continuous pitch bend wheel messages and modulation signals for connected synthesizers.

How it works

  • Configurable bend range: Adjust the pitch bend semitone window from 1 semitone to a full octave (-12 to +12 semitones).
  • Bipolar modulation input: Accepts LFO or envelope modulation to produce automatic vibrato and dive bombs.
  • Smoothing: Built-in 14-bit interpolation prevents audible stepping during aggressive wheel movements.

Try it

Wire a slow triangle LFO into Pitch Bend to add subtle, expressive pitch wander to vintage synth leads.

LFO -> Pitch Bend -> Analog -> Audio Out

6. Velocity Curve: dynamic touch and curve response

The Velocity Curve node remaps the velocity dynamics of incoming note events, tailoring keyboard touch response to performance preferences.

How it works

  • Curve profiles: Linear, Exponential (emphasising soft touches), Logarithmic (punchy and responsive), and S-curve (compressed dynamics).
  • Min/max clamping: Sets minimum velocity floor and maximum ceiling limits.
  • Fixed velocity mode: Locks all incoming notes to a single uniform velocity level (such as 100 for consistent organ or synth-pop lines).

Try it

Apply an Exponential velocity curve to a physical Karplus-Strong String synth for natural acoustic response when playing delicate arpeggios.

MIDI Notes -> Velocity Curve (Exp) -> String -> Audio Out

7. Gate: rhythmic duration and articulation shaper

The Gate node controls the duration of active note events, turning sustained chords into short staccato bursts or stretching short taps into legato drones.

How it works

  • Time and beat modes: Set gate length in milliseconds (5ms to 2000ms) or metric musical divisions (1/16, 1/8, 1/4).
  • Fixed gate vs proportional: Choose between fixed note lengths or proportional scaling (e.g. 50% staccato of incoming note length).
  • Legato tie mode: Automatically bridges notes together when consecutive keys overlap.

Try it

Feed an Arpeggiator into Gate set to 15% length to transform an arpeggio into tight, robotic 16th-note staccato plucks.

Arpeggiator -> Gate (15%) -> FM -> Audio Out

8. Humanizer: micro-timing shuffle and organic dynamics

The Humanizer node injects subtle, natural human imperfections into rigid, computer-quantized note streams.

How it works

  • Timing jitter: Introduces microscopic Gaussian time offsets (from 0ms to 35ms) to note onsets, simulating the slight imprecisions of live human performance.
  • Velocity spread: Randomizes note velocity around the played value by a customizable percentage window.
  • Pitch drift: Adds minute micro-tuning offsets for analog acoustic warmth.

Try it

Place Humanizer between a rigid 16-step Note Sequencer and a drum machine or piano synth to make programmed patterns breathe naturally.

Note Sequencer -> Humanizer -> Sampler (Piano) -> Audio Out

9. Quantizer: musical scale and modal pitch snapping

The Quantizer node forces arbitrary pitch numbers, microtonal frequencies, and random pitch modulators onto chosen musical scales and temperaments.

How it works

  • Over 40 musical scales: Major, Minor, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Locrian, Harmonic Minor, Melodic Minor, Pentatonic, Blues, Hirajoshi, Insen, Raga, and microtonal modes.
  • Root note transposition: Set the tonic key to any pitch (C through B).
  • Snap algorithms: Snaps to the nearest scale degree either upward, downward, or to the absolute closest interval.

Try it

Feed a Random Modulator or CV voltage into Quantizer set to Japanese Hirajoshi, and pipe the output into a Metallic resonator for generative gamelan melodies.

Random -> Quantizer (Hirajoshi) -> Metallic -> Delay -> Audio Out

10. Glide: monophonic portamento and polyphonic slide

The Glide node produces smooth pitch glides between consecutive notes, featuring both classic analog monophonic portamento and multi-voice polyphonic slide.

How it works

  • Glide time: Continuous portamento rate control (0ms to 3000ms).
  • Legato-only mode: Glides only when two notes overlap in time, leaving non-overlapping notes with instant attack.
  • Constant time vs constant rate: Select whether pitch transitions take the same amount of time regardless of distance, or glide at a fixed semitones-per-second velocity.

Try it

Enable Legato Glide on a bass synth patch, hold a low note while tapping octaves higher, and enjoy smooth analog pitch slides.

MIDI Notes -> Glide (Legato) -> Analog (Acid Bass) -> Audio Out

11. Note Echo: algorithmic MIDI delay and rhythmic repeats

The Note Echo node creates rhythmic echoing MIDI notes, repeating incoming note events across musical intervals with decay and transposition.

How it works

  • Tempo-synced delay time: Set delay intervals to standard, dotted, or triplet metric divisions (1/16, 1/8d, 1/4t).
  • Feedback & count: Controls the number of echo repeats (1 to 32).
  • Velocity decay: Gradually scales down the velocity of successive repeats for natural fading.
  • Semitone pitch transpose: Shifts each repeat up or down by a set semitone interval, turning a single key press into an ascending or descending staircase.

Try it

Set Note Echo to a dotted 8th note (1/8d) with a +7 semitones (fifth) pitch shift, and play single notes to create layered arpeggiated patterns.

MIDI Notes -> Note Echo (1/8d, +7) -> Wavetable -> Audio Out

12. Note Router: dynamic keyboard splitting and voice dispatching

The Note Router node directs incoming notes across up to four separate output ports based on pitch thresholds, velocity ranges, or voice allocation.

How it works

  • Split mode: Routes notes below a split point to Output 1, and notes above to Output 2.
  • Velocity dispatch: Sends soft notes to an intimate electric piano, and hard accents to a brass synth.
  • Round-robin voice allocation: Cycles notes sequentially across Outputs 1, 2, 3, and 4, allowing four distinct synthesizers to share parts of a polyphonic phrase.

Try it

Set Note Router to Round-Robin and connect three different synths (Analog, FM, and String) to play dynamic hocketing melodies where every note has a unique timbre.

Arpeggiator -> Note Router (Round Robin) -> [Analog, FM, String]

13. Note Merge: unified polyphonic stream combiner

The Note Merge node combines multiple independent note streams into a single unified polyphonic stream with intelligent collision handling.

How it works

  • Multi-input bus: Combines up to four note sources into one stream.
  • Duplicate note suppression: Prevents hanging notes and double-trigger clicks when two input streams send the same pitch simultaneously.
  • Voice priority: Option to prioritize higher or lower notes during polyphony overflow.

Try it

Merge an algorithmic Arpeggiator pattern with live keyboard playing so you can play expressive solo counter-melodies over automated sequences.

[Arpeggiator, Keyboard] -> Note Merge -> Analog -> Audio Out

14. Note Switcher: modulated phrase selector

The Note Switcher node selects which of several incoming note streams passes downstream, controlled via a macro knob or logic trigger.

How it works

  • Multi-channel selector: Seamlessly switches between alternate note patterns without dropping active note-off events.
  • Modulatable selection index: Switch patterns automatically using a slow square LFO or timeline automation track.
  • Smooth transition handling: Sends clean note-off messages to active voices before switching to prevent stuck notes.

Try it

Wire a verse bassline into Input 1 and a chorus bassline into Input 2, then automate the selector with a Macro Toggle for arrangement transitions.

[Pattern A, Pattern B] -> Note Switcher -> Analog -> Audio Out

15. Arpeggiator: algorithmic pattern and chord engine

The Arpeggiator node takes held chords and breaks them into rhythmic, tempo-synced melodic sequences.

How it works

  • Directional modes: Up, Down, Up/Down, Down/Up, Random, Chord Repeat, and As-Played.
  • Octave span: Sweeps arpeggios across 1 to 4 octaves with cyclical or ping-pong octave progression.
  • Gate & swing: Adjusts note duration percentage and metric shuffle.
  • Hold toggle: Latches played chords so the arpeggio continues cycling after keys are released.

Try it

Hold a minor ninth chord, set Arpeggiator to Up/Down across 3 octaves at 1/16th notes, and route through an analog filter sweep.

Keyboard -> Arpeggiator (Up/Down) -> Analog -> Audio Out

16. Note Sequencer: 16-step polyphonic pitch & gate grid

The Note Sequencer node is a classic 16-step grid sequencer with per-step pitch, velocity, octave shift, and gate tie controls.

How it works

  • Interactive step matrix: 16 dedicated pitch knobs with visual semitone displays.
  • Per-step ties & mutes: Tie steps together for long sustained bass notes, or mute steps for syncopated rests.
  • Variable step length: Set pattern length from 1 to 16 steps to create odd-meter polyrhythms (such as 5/16 or 7/16).
  • Direction modes: Forward, Reverse, Ping-Pong, and Brownian random walk.

Try it

Set the sequencer length to 7 steps over 16th notes to produce a shifting polyrhythmic ostinato that cycles across the 4/4 bar line.

Note Sequencer (7 Steps) -> FM -> Delay -> Audio Out

17. Random Note Generator: constrained generative melody engine

The Random Note Generator node creates constrained melodic phrases and basslines algorithmically in real time.

How it works

  • Key & scale constraints: Restricts generated notes strictly to a selected musical key and scale.
  • Interval jump weighting: Biases random generation toward small melodic steps (seconds and thirds) rather than wide, disjointed leaps.
  • Rhythmic density: Controls the probability of active note triggers per clock tick, introducing musical rests.
  • Seed repeatability: Freeze the random seed to loop an inspiring generated phrase indefinitely.

Try it

Set the scale to Minor Pentatonic, set density to 60%, and pipe the generated notes into a Wavetable pad for an endless generative ambient performance.

Random Note Generator -> Wavetable -> Reverb -> Audio Out

18. MIDI File: standard MIDI file canvas player

The MIDI File node loads and plays standard .mid sequence files directly on the canvas, locked to the global transport clock.

How it works

  • Drag and drop loading: Drop standard Type 0 or Type 1 MIDI files directly onto the node body.
  • Track isolation: Choose which MIDI track to output, or sum all tracks into one polyphonic stream.
  • Transport synchronization: Automatically tracks project tempo, loop markers, and timeline playhead location.

Try it

Drag a complex classical piano MIDI file onto the canvas, route note outputs to a String synth, and use note velocities to drive 3D particle bursts.

MIDI File -> String -> Audio Out
MIDI File (Velocity) -> Particle System (Speed)

19. Chorder: single-note harmonizer and chord voicings

The Chorder node converts single incoming note taps into rich multi-voice polyphonic chords.

How it works

  • Pre-configured chord types: Major, Minor, Sus2, Sus4, Dominant 7th, Major 7th, Minor 7th, 9th, and Diminished.
  • Custom chord editor: Define custom interval offsets (e.g. [0, +7, +12, +16]) for signature chords.
  • Root-relative transposition: Voicings transpose across the keyboard relative to the incoming note pitch.

Try it

Select Minor 9th voicing, set Arpeggiator downstream, and play single bass notes to trigger sweeping impressionist arpeggios.

Keyboard -> Chorder (Min 9) -> Arpeggiator -> Wavetable -> Audio Out

20. Note Stack: interval and octave voice layering

The Note Stack node layers harmonic interval copies on top of played notes to thicken synth leads and basslines.

How it works

  • Up to 4 interval layers: Add octave below (-12), fifth above (+7), octave above (+12), or custom intervals.
  • Per-voice detuning: Applies subtle pitch detuning between stacked voices for rich chorus effects.
  • Velocity scaling: Scales the velocity of stacked intervals relative to the primary note.

Try it

Add an octave below (-12) and a fifth above (+7) to an analog saw lead to produce a classic vintage stadium rock synth sound.

MIDI Notes -> Note Stack (-12, +7) -> Analog -> Audio Out

21. Note Capturer: live performance buffer recorder

The Note Capturer node acts as a live MIDI scratchpad, recording incoming performances into a circular memory buffer for playback or loop export.

How it works

  • Retrospective recording: Keeps a continuous rolling buffer of your recent playing, allowing you to capture spontaneous improvisation after it occurs.
  • Bar quantization: Trims captured phrases cleanly to musical bar boundaries.
  • Loop playback: Plays captured takes in a continuous loop while leaving the keyboard free for additional layers.

Try it

Improvise freely on your keyboard, press Capture to grab the last 4 bars, and immediately loop the phrase while designing synth patches.

MIDI Notes -> Note Capturer (Loop) -> Analog -> Audio Out

22. Bouncing Balls: physics-based rhythmic trigger generator

The Bouncing Balls node runs an internal physics simulation where virtual spheres bounce inside a gravity well, triggering note events whenever a ball collides with the floor.

How it works

  • Gravity & elasticity: Balls bounce with physically realistic gravitational acceleration, bouncing rapidly as they reach the floor.
  • Multi-ball polyphony: Simulate up to 8 independent bouncing spheres with differing drop heights and restitution coefficients.
  • Collision pitch mapping: Map collision velocity to note velocity, and bounce frequency to musical pitch.

Try it

Route Bouncing Balls into a Metallic resonator or physical String synth to hear organic, accelerating acoustic impacts mimicking raindrops or dropped marbles.

Bouncing Balls -> Metallic Resonator -> Reverb -> Audio Out

23. Note Strum: realistic acoustic chord strumming

The Note Strum node emulates guitar and harp playing by staggering the onset times of notes in a polyphonic chord.

How it works

  • Strum speed: Sets the time delay between consecutive notes (2ms to 150ms).
  • Direction control: Down-strum (low notes to high notes), Up-strum (high notes to low notes), or Alternating.
  • Velocity decay: Gradually tapers velocity across the strum to emulate natural hand dynamics.

Try it

Place Note Strum between a Chorder and a String physical modeling synth for convincing nylon-string acoustic guitar chord strumming.

Keyboard -> Chorder -> Note Strum -> String -> Audio Out

24. Field Notes: programmable algorithmic note generation

The Field Notes node allows you to script custom generative algorithms, Markov-chain phrase models, and rhythmic logic directly in Infinite's bare-name Field language.

How it works

  • Event-driven execution: Executes on every clock tick or MIDI input trigger.
  • State registers: Retains history across steps to calculate Euclidean rhythms, Fibonacci sequences, or cellular automata.
  • Output note generation: Emits note pitch, velocity, and gate events directly to downstream synths.

Example: Fibonacci sequence arpeggiator

// registers: step_counter, prev_a, prev_b
state a = 1
state b = 1
state step = 0

// advance Fibonacci sequence modulo 12
let next_fib = (a + b) % 12
a = b
b = next_fib
step = step + 1

// map to minor pentatonic scale
let root = 60
let intervals = [0, 3, 5, 7, 10]
let note_out = root + intervals[next_fib % 5]

emit_note(note_out, 90, 120) // pitch, velocity, duration_ms

Try it

Drop a Field Notes node, enter your own algorithmic rules, and explore generative compositions impossible in conventional static DAWs.

Clock -> Field Notes -> FM -> Delay -> Audio Out

Modular note architecture

Because Infinite unifies note processing, audio synthesis, and visual rendering onto a single real-time execution graph, these note nodes can drive both sound and visual form simultaneously.

An Arpeggiator can trigger a synth lead while stepping through colors in an Audio Color Ramp, and the physical collisions of a Bouncing Balls node can displace 3D geometry meshes at the exact microsecond an acoustic chime rings out.

Drop any note node onto the canvas, cable it into an instrument, and build generative musical systems unconstrained by linear timelines.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/every-note-node-in-infinite-generative-sequencing-guide.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Every synthesizer node in Infinite: the complete sound design guide
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: The complete guide to all 20 synthesizer nodes in Infinite: subtractive, wavetable, FM, physical modeling, granular, spectral resynthesis, and DSP kernels.
item.content:encoded:
Most digital audio workstations isolate sound generation inside third-party plugins. You purchase an instrument, load a floating window, navigate vendor-specific preset systems, and route stereo audio into a rigid mixer channel.

Infinite approaches synthesis from a different foundation. Every synthesizer lives directly on the open canvas as a modular node. Notes, audio streams, modulation voltages, and visual textures share the same graph and memory space. A single LFO can sweep a wavetable position while warping a 3D geometry mesh, and a reaction-diffusion simulation can directly generate polyphonic audio timbre.

Infinite features twenty native synthesizer engines, spanning virtual analog, morphing wavetables, 4-operator frequency modulation, Karplus-Strong waveguides, granular cloud generators, extreme spectral time-stretchers, and per-sample programmable JIT kernels.

Here is an architectural breakdown of every synthesizer node in Infinite, how their sound engines work, and how to patch them.

1. Oscillator: dual-oscillator subtractive & FM engine

The Oscillator node is Infinite's foundational sound generator, built upon bandlimited anti-aliased wavetables with linear frequency modulation and phase synchronization.

How it works

  • Waveforms: Sine, Triangle, Sawtooth, and Square with variable Pulse Width (0.01 to 0.99).
  • Pitch controls: Coarse frequency (20 Hz to 8000 Hz), octave shift (-4 to +4), semitone offset (-12 to +12), and fine detune (-50 to +50 cents).
  • Linear FM input: An audio-rate fm_in pin enables modulation from a secondary oscillator, producing rich sidebands for metallic chimes, FM brass, and aggressive growls.
  • Portamento: Continuous glide parameter (0 to 2 seconds) providing constant-rate pitch transitions between notes.

Try it

Patch a secondary Oscillator set to a high octave into the fm_in port, modulate FM Depth with an Envelope, and route through an Audio Filter for crisp metallic bells.

Random Note Generator -> Oscillator -> Audio Filter -> Audio Out

2. Wavetable: 64-table morphing synth with unison

The Wavetable node is Infinite's flagship polyphonic wavetable instrument, featuring 64 factory wavetables that morph smoothly across eight distinct single-cycle frames.

How it works

  • 2D table scanning: Continuous position interpolation across 8 frames per table, eliminating step clicks or boundary artifacts.
  • Unison detune & stereo spread: Stacks up to 8 voices per note with adjustable frequency detuning and wide stereo placement.
  • Sub-oscillator: Integrated sub-harmonic generator providing dedicated low-end weight independently of table morphing.
  • Modulatable position: The position parameter can be cabled directly to LFOs, envelope followers, or hand tracking modulators.

Try it

Wire an LFO into the table position input so the waveform continually evolves, then layer chorus for a lush cinematic pad.

Arpeggiator -> Wavetable -> Chorus -> Reverb -> Audio Out

3. Analog: polyphonic virtual analog with nonlinear filters

The Analog node models the physical circuit behaviour of vintage analog synthesizers, complete with subtle oscillator drift, saturation stages, and four distinct nonlinear filter topologies.

How it works

  • Twin drift-stabilized oscillators: Dual oscillators with saw, square, triangle, and sine options, pulse width modulation, sub-oscillator, and a pink/white noise source.
  • Circuit-modeled filters: Switchable between a 4-pole Moog transistor ladder, Korg MS-20 resonant lowpass, diode ladder, and state-variable filter (SVF).
  • 4x oversampling: Drives and non-linear filter stages run at 4x internal oversampling to keep aliasing strictly under -80 dB across all octaves.
  • Dual ADSR envelopes: Dedicated amplitude and filter envelopes with exponential decay curves.

Try it

Stack three detuned unison voices, select the MS-20 filter model with medium resonance, and sweep cutoff with an envelope for an authentic acid bassline.

MIDI Notes -> Analog -> Delay -> Audio Out

4. FM: 4-operator frequency modulation synthesizer

The FM node delivers classic frequency modulation synthesis using four sine operators configured across eleven classic routing algorithms.

How it works

  • 11 routing algorithms: Ranging from a pure vertical cascade (4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1) for complex harmonic teeth, to parallel carriers for additive electric pianos.
  • Harmonic frequency ratios: Per-operator integer and fractional frequency multipliers (0.5x to 32x).
  • Feedback loop: Operator 4 includes self-modulation feedback, transitioning from smooth sines to saw waves and broadband noise.
  • Per-operator envelopes: Individual envelope generators shaping the modulation index over time.

Try it

Select algorithm 5 (two parallel carrier-modulator stacks), tune operator 2 to a 3.5x non-harmonic ratio, and add a brief decay envelope for a crystalline mallet sound.

Arpeggiator -> FM -> Reverb -> Audio Out

5. Partials: 64-harmonic additive formant resynthesis

The Partials node performs real-time additive resynthesis, tracking harmonic partials and reproducing acoustic instruments and voices without pitch artifacts.

How it works
