  • Formant preservation: When transposing incoming audio across octaves, Partials keeps the spectral formant envelope locked in place, avoiding the unnatural "chipmunk" timbre common to conventional samplers.
  • Spectral tilt & odd/even balance: Continuous control over harmonic roll-off slope and the ratio between even and odd harmonics.
  • Inharmonic stretching: Stretches partial frequencies away from integer multiples for bell and metallic timbres.
  • Residual noise tracking: Models the turbulent air and breath left behind by harmonic analysis.

Try it

Load a vocal syllable or acoustic cello sample into Partials, trigger it across three octaves, and hear natural vocal character preserved across the entire keyboard.

MIDI Notes -> Partials -> Convolution Reverb -> Audio Out

6. String: Karplus-Strong physical modeling waveguide

The String node models the physical acoustics of vibrating strings stretched over a resonating wooden body using Karplus-Strong waveguide synthesis.

How it works

  • Physical waveguide loop: A delay line length tuned exactly to the note's fundamental frequency, coupled with an internal lowpass reflection filter.
  • Three exciter modes:
  • Pluck: Impulse burst simulating a guitar plectrum or finger pick.
  • Bow: Continuous friction noise simulating a violin or cello bow.
  • Strike: Felt hammer excitation simulating an acoustic piano or hammered dulcimer.
  • Body resonance & pickup position: Configurable acoustic body model and spatial pickup location along the string length.

Try it

Set the exciter mode to Bow, slow the attack time slightly, and play sustained chords for a lush acoustic string ensemble.

Chorder -> String -> Reverb -> Audio Out

7. Wave Terrain: topographic image-to-sound synthesis

The Wave Terrain node turns any 2D image, video capture, reaction-diffusion simulation, or procedural texture into a continuous 3D acoustic terrain surface z = T(u, v).

How it works

  • Audio-rate orbital paths: An oscillator traces a closed orbital trajectory (u(t), v(t)) across the image (circle, ellipse, Lissajous curve, or lemniscate).
  • Surface height as amplitude: As the orbital scan travels across pixels, the image luminance z becomes the instantaneous audio amplitude.
  • 10-level Fourier MIP antialiasing: Sampling raw image pixels causes harsh aliasing; Infinite computes an internal Real Discrete Fourier Transform (RDFT) MIP pyramid across 10 octaves, ensuring pristine, alias-free polyphonic synthesis across all 8 octaves.

Try it

Feed a live Reaction Diffusion texture into Wave Terrain, route an LFO to orbit radius, and listen to the sound morph as the organic visual pattern blooms.

Reaction Diffusion -> Wave Terrain -> Saturator -> Audio Out

8. Equation Synth: Desmos-style mathematical synthesis

The Equation Synth node evaluates custom mathematical expressions y = f(x, a, b, c, d) directly at 48kHz audio rates, turning formulas into playable instruments.

How it works

  • Inline formula parsing: Type formulas directly using standard mathematical functions (sin, cos, tan, pow, abs, tanh, floor).
  • Real-time parameter knobs: Four continuous parameters (knobA, knobB, knobC, knobD) exposed as modulation pins.
  • Compile-time bandlimiting: Evaluated curves are compiled into bandlimited wavetable mipmaps, preventing mathematical sharp edges from creating audible foldback distortion.

Try it

Type sin(x) + a * sin(x * 3) + b * sin(x * 5), wire an LFO to knobA, and listen to third and fifth harmonics fade in and out with algebraic purity.

MIDI Notes -> Equation Synth -> Formant Filter -> Audio Out

9. Spectral Synth: real-time spectrogram resynthesis

The Spectral Synth node scans an image or visual canvas horizontally as a spectrogram, converting visual pixels into audible frequencies.

How it works

  • Horizontal scan line: A playhead travels across the texture from left to right at tempo-synced rates.
  • Vertical frequency mapping: The vertical $y$-axis maps to acoustic frequency (low frequencies at the bottom, high frequencies at the top), while pixel brightness sets partial amplitude.
  • Spectral freeze: Freeze the playhead at any point along the image to produce an indefinite, unmoving spectral chord.

Try it

Draw three horizontal brush strokes in a Draw node at low, mid, and high positions, patch the texture into Spectral Synth, and hear your sketch played back as a triad.

Draw Canvas -> Spectral Synth -> Delay -> Audio Out

10. Metallic: modal physical resonator for bells and plates

The Metallic node models the physical vibrations of acoustic metal and glass objects struck by hard or soft mallets using a bank of coupled two-pole bandpass resonators.

How it works

  • 8 material presets: Steel, Brass, Bell Bronze, Aluminium, Glass, Wood, Ceramic, and Titanium.
  • Modal dispersion: Modes follow non-integer frequency ratios corresponding to the physical vibration equations of circular plates and rectangular bars.
  • Stiffness & decay: Stiffness controls modal frequency clustering, while decay adjusts the acoustic damping rate across high versus low modes.
  • Strike hardness: Blends from a soft felt mallet impulse to a sharp metal point impact.

Try it

Trigger Metallic from the Bouncing Balls note generator for an acoustic gamelan performance where notes ring and decay naturally in space.

Bouncing Balls -> Metallic -> Reverb -> Audio Out

11. Sampler: polyphonic multisample engine

The Sampler node provides polyphonic sample playback with precision loop boundaries, pitch tracking, and real-time live audio recording.

How it works

  • Playback modes: One-Shot, Forward Loop, Reverse Loop, and Ping-Pong bidirectional loop.
  • Live buffer recording: An audio record_in port allows capturing incoming microphone feeds, guitar inputs, or synth stems straight into memory.
  • Root pitch tracking: Tracks MIDI keyboard pitch relative to a configurable base key with crossfade loop smoothing.
  • Envelope shaping: Built-in ADSR envelope for smooth sample transitions.

Try it

Record an ambient field recording through record_in, set the loop mode to Ping-Pong with a 100ms crossfade, and play rich chords across the keyboard.

Microphone -> Sampler (Record In) -> MIDI Notes -> Sampler -> Audio Out

12. Slicer: transient-detecting beat chopper

The Slicer node analyzes incoming audio loops, detects transient attacks, and slices the recording into individual hits mapped across MIDI notes.

How it works

  • Onset detection: High-precision transient peak detection algorithm automatically finding drum hits and percussive transients.
  • Metric grid fallback: Option to slice by strict musical divisions (1/8, 1/16, or 1/32 notes) locked to transport BPM.
  • Per-slice control: Individual start/end offsets, pitch offsets, and reverse triggers per slice.
  • MIDI pad mapping: Slices automatically map upward from MIDI note C1 for instant pad controller performance.

Try it

Feed a drum break into Slicer, connect an Arpeggiator with a random pattern, and generate an endless supply of breakbeat permutations.

Drum Loop -> Slicer -> Arpeggiator -> Slicer -> Audio Out

13. PaulStretch: extreme spectral time-stretching

The PaulStretch node implements the legendary Paul Nasca spectral time-stretch algorithm, expanding audio recordings from 10x to 1000x their original length without pitch shifts.

How it works

  • Windowed FFT analysis: Deconstructs incoming audio into heavily overlapping spectral windows (typically 0.25 to 2.0 seconds wide).
  • Phase randomization: Completely randomizes the phase angle of every frequency bin while preserving original magnitude, eliminating comb filtering and phase cancellation.
  • Extreme stretch factors: Stretches a 3-second vocal sample into a 5-minute ambient drone that retains acoustic warmth.
  • Unison & detune: Adds multi-voice spectral unison for shimmering cinematic textures.

Try it

Load a short acoustic piano chord into PaulStretch, set Stretch to 50x, open the FFT window to 1.5 seconds, and send the result into a Limiter for an ambient soundscape.

Piano Sample -> PaulStretch (50x) -> Limiter -> Audio Out

14. Molder: harmonic partial decomposition and waveshaping

The Molder node decomposes incoming audio into tracked sinusoidal partials and residual noise, then applies nonlinear wavefolding and dynamic mutation curves.

How it works

  • Sinusoidal tracking: Extracts frequency tracks and energy envelopes from any incoming sample.
  • Mutation roll: The Roll button mutates frequency tracks, introducing harmonic permutations and metallic shifts.
  • Nonlinear folding: Compresses partial amplitudes through polynomial folding curves, producing grit and analog saturation.

Try it

Send a clean acoustic vocal recording into Molder, trigger the Roll parameter via a macro button, and listen to the voice transform into alien harmonic drones.

Sampler -> Molder -> Chorus -> Audio Out

15. Grain Molder: granular feature sorting and risers

The Grain Molder node chops an audio buffer into thousands of overlapping micro-grains, analyzes their acoustic properties (loudness, spectral centroid, or pitch), and sorts them in ascending or descending order.

How it works

  • Micro-grain slicing: Deconstructs buffers into grains between 20ms and 150ms with Hann window envelopes.
  • Acoustic feature classification: Measures root-mean-square (RMS) energy, brightness, and pitch density for every grain.
  • Sorting engine: Reorders grains along the playback timeline according to the chosen metric.
  • Amount slider: Morphs continuously from original chronological playback to fully sorted granular order.

Try it

Load a busy drum break, set Sort Mode to Level, and automate the Amount slider from 0% to 100% over four bars to produce a natural granular riser.

Drum Loop -> Grain Molder (Amount) -> Audio Filter -> Audio Out

16. Granular: real-time polyphonic granular cloud engine

The Granular node shreds recorded or live audio into micro-sound grains (10ms to 500ms), scattering them across space and time to produce granular clouds, textures, and pitch-shifted shimmers.

How it works

  • Grain density & size: Generates up to 64 simultaneous overlapping grains with customizable duration and emission rate.
  • Position scrub & spray: Controls the center read head position in the buffer, while Spray introduces random time offsets.
  • Pitch randomization: Randomly scatters grain playback speeds across customizable semitone windows.
  • Freeze toggle: Instantly locks the read head to sample an infinitesimal sliver of sound indefinitely.

Try it

Pipe a live guitar input into Granular, hit Freeze during a sustained chord, and widen Pitch Spray to turn a single strum into an ethereal cloud of sound.

Audio In -> Granular (Freeze) -> Stereo Delay -> Audio Out

17. Field Synth: programmable per-sample JIT DSP kernel

The Field Synth node is Infinite's most flexible sound engine: a polyphonic synthesizer whose entire voice algorithm is written in Infinite's bare-name Field language and compiled directly into native machine code.

How it works

  • Bare-name syntax: Write DSP code with plain algebraic expressions (freq, phase, out) without sigils or boilerplate.
  • Per-sample execution: Runs on the audio thread at 48kHz with zero garbage collection or allocation overhead.
  • Dynamic user knobs: Define custom parameters in code that automatically expose modulatable pins on the node body.
  • Polyphonic voice architecture: The engine handles note allocation, voice stealing, and per-voice registers automatically.

Example: resonant dual-oscillator kernel

// inputs: f (frequency), t (time), gate (0..1)
state p1 = 0.0
state p2 = 0.0

// phase accumulators
let inc = f * (6.2831853 / 48000.0)
p1 = p1 + inc
if p1 > 6.2831853 { p1 = p1 - 6.2831853 }

p2 = p2 + inc * 1.005 // slight detune
if p2 > 6.2831853 { p2 = p2 - 6.2831853 }

// soft-clipped sum
let raw = sin(p1) * 0.5 + sin(p2) * 0.5
out = tanh(raw * 1.5) * gate

Try it

Drop a Field Synth, paste the kernel above, connect MIDI Notes, and immediately enjoy a clean, detuned analog lead with zero external dependencies.

MIDI Notes -> Field Synth -> Limiter -> Audio Out

18. Drum Sequencer: 16-step polyphonic drum engine

The Drum Sequencer node is an integrated 8-track, 16-step drum machine combining analog drum synthesis circuits with an intuitive pattern grid.

How it works

  • 8 synthesized drum voices: Dedicated circuits for Kick, Snare, Closed Hat, Open Hat, Clap, Low Tom, High Tom, and Percussion.
  • Individual audio outputs: Includes a master stereo mix output plus eight individual audio outs (1 to 8) for per-channel external processing and mixing.
  • Step velocity & swing: Per-step velocity sliders with configurable shuffle percentage.
  • Transport lock: Automatically locks to Infinite's global BPM and timeline transport.

Try it

Wire individual output 1 (Kick) to an Audio Analyze node, and use its bass energy output to drive the scale of a 3D Sphere in sync with the beat.

Drum Sequencer (Kick Out) -> Audio Analyze -> 3D Sphere (Scale)

19. MPC: 16-pad vintage sampling groovebox

The MPC node captures the tactile immediacy and groove feel of classic 16-pad hardware samplers.

How it works

  • 16 dynamic sample pads: Drag and drop audio files onto any of the 16 pads.
  • 16-level velocity mode: Spreads either volume or pitch across all 16 pads for expressive melodic playing of a single sample.
  • Note repeat: Hold a pad while pressing Note Repeat to generate rhythmic rolls quantized to 1/8, 1/16, or 1/32 triplets.
  • Choke groups: Assign pads to mutually exclusive mute groups (such as open and closed hi-hats).

Try it

Load a vocal chop onto pad 1, turn on 16-Level Tuning, and play pitched vocal melodies straight from a MIDI keyboard or pad controller.

MIDI Notes -> MPC -> Saturator -> Audio Out

20. Looper: multi-layer live performance phrase looper

The Looper node is designed for live improvisation, enabling bar-quantized audio phrase recording, seamless overdubbing, and speed manipulation.

How it works

  • Bar-quantized punch-in: Automatically rounds start and stop commands to the nearest bar boundary (1, 2, 4, 8, or 16 bars).
  • Non-destructive overdubbing: Layer takes indefinitely with an adjustable decay feedback control to prevent buildup.
  • Reverse & half-speed: Instant reverse toggle and half-speed playback for tape-style pitch drop effects.
  • Boundary crossfades: Applies 5ms micro-crossfades across loop seams, eliminating clicks on imperfect takes.

Try it

Record a 2-bar guitar or vocal loop, hit Dub to add counter-melodies, and toggle Reverse for an immediate backwards psychedelic texture.

Audio In -> Looper -> Stereo Delay -> Audio Out

Synthesis on a unified graph

Because Infinite shares a single execution graph across audio, 2D compositing, and 3D geometry, these twenty synthesizers are not confined to traditional DAW audio tracks.

You can drive a Wavetable position from a particle system's average kinetic energy, strike a Metallic resonator whenever a 3D bouncing sphere collides with a floor plane, or scan a generative reaction-diffusion texture through Wave Terrain at 48kHz.

Drop any synthesizer onto the canvas, wire it up, and explore sound design unconstrained by plugin windows.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/every-synthesizer-node-in-infinite-sound-design-guide.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Raymarching signed distance fields in real-time GLSL
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How to build a real-time raymarcher in GLSL: sphere tracing algorithm, primitive distance functions, smooth blending, normals, and audio-reactive scenes.
item.content:encoded:
Building a system for raymarching signed distance fields in real-time GLSL provides a powerful alternative to traditional polygonal rasterisation. While standard 3D rendering pipelines rely on vertex buffers, index arrays, and triangle meshes, raymarching computes three-dimensional surfaces procedurally inside a fragment shader. Every geometric volume, smooth Boolean blend, and fractal surface is evaluated mathematically for every individual pixel on the screen.

In modern audiovisual software such as Infinite, raymarching allows visual artists and audio producers to bridge the gap between mathematical graphics and low-latency audio synthesis. Because signed distance fields are defined purely through mathematical equations, parameters such as scale, repetition, twisting, and morphing can be cabled directly to live audio frequency bands, envelope followers, and LFO modulators without regenerating vertex buffers or stalling the graphics pipeline.

Here is an architectural walkthrough of how sphere tracing works, how to construct signed distance functions (SDFs) for common 3D primitives, how to blend geometry organically with polynomial smooth minimums, and how to wire a complete audio-reactive raymarching pipeline inside Infinite.

What is sphere tracing and how the ray steps

Traditional raymarching steps through 3D space along a view ray using small, uniform increments. While simple to implement, uniform stepping suffers from severe trade-offs: if the step size is too large, the ray can skip thin geometry entirely, producing visual holes and aliasing artifacts; if the step size is too small, performance drops precipitously.

Sphere tracing, introduced by John C. Hart in 1996, solves this inefficiency by exploiting the fundamental mathematical property of a signed distance field.

A signed distance function f(p) takes any point p in three-dimensional space and returns the shortest Euclidean distance from that point to the nearest surface in the scene:

f(p) > 0  : The point p is located outside the object.
f(p) = 0  : The point p lies exactly on the boundary surface.
f(p) < 0  : The point p is located inside the object.

Because f(p) yields the absolute minimum distance to the closest boundary, a sphere of radius R = f(p) centred at p is guaranteed to be completely empty of any geometry. Therefore, a view ray starting at p can safely advance along its direction vector by the full distance R in a single step without any risk of overshooting or penetrating a surface.

To construct the view ray for each pixel, we map normalised screen coordinates uv into a camera origin ro and a normalised direction vector rd:

vec3 rayDirection(vec2 uv, vec3 eye, vec3 target, float fov) {
    vec3 forward = normalize(target - eye);
    vec3 right = normalize(cross(forward, vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)));
    vec3 up = cross(right, forward);
    return normalize(uv.x * right + uv.y * up + forward * fov);
}

With the ray direction established, the sphere tracing loop evaluates the scene's signed distance function iteratively:

float raymarch(vec3 ro, vec3 rd, float minDistance, float maxDistance) {
    float distanceTravelled = minDistance;
    
    for (int step = 0; step < 128; step++) {
        vec3 currentPosition = ro + rd * distanceTravelled;
        float distanceToSurface = map(currentPosition);
        
        // Surface hit detected within threshold epsilon
        if (distanceToSurface < 0.001) {
            return distanceTravelled;
        }
        
        distanceTravelled += distanceToSurface;
        
        // Ray escaped into empty background
        if (distanceTravelled >= maxDistance) {
            break;
        }
    }
    
    return -1.0; // Miss
}

Notice how this algorithm naturally adapts to the spatial complexity of the scene: in vast regions of open space, the distance to the nearest surface is large, allowing the ray to take massive strides across thousands of units in a handful of steps. Near surfaces and delicate geometric silhouettes, the steps automatically shrink to sub-millimetre precision, capturing razor-sharp edges.

Primary SDF geometric primitives

Every scene evaluated in a raymarcher is described by an overall distance function, typically named map(vec3 p). Complex scenes are constructed by combining simple mathematical primitives.

Here are the canonical signed distance functions for fundamental 3D solids:

1. Sphere

The sphere is the simplest primitive in distance field mathematics. The distance from point p to the surface of a sphere centred at the origin with radius r equals the Euclidean length of p minus r:

float sdSphere(vec3 p, float r) {
    return length(p) - r;
}

2. Box

An axis-aligned box with half-dimensions b requires computing the component-wise distance outside the boundary and combining it with the internal signed distance:

float sdBox(vec3 p, vec3 b) {
    vec3 q = abs(p) - b;
    return length(max(q, 0.0)) + min(max(q.x, max(q.y, q.z)), 0.0);
}

3. Torus

A torus lying on the XZ plane with major radius t.x and minor tube radius t.y is derived by projecting p onto the circular core:

float sdTorus(vec3 p, vec2 t) {
    vec2 q = vec2(length(p.xz) - t.x, p.y);
    return length(q) - t.y;
}

4. Cylinder

A vertical cylinder centred along the Y axis with radius h.x and half-height h.y:

float sdCylinder(vec3 p, vec2 h) {
    vec2 d = abs(vec2(length(p.xz), p.y)) - h;
    return min(max(d.x, d.y), 0.0) + length(max(d, 0.0));
}

Spatial domain operations

One of the great advantages of signed distance fields over triangle meshes is that geometric transformations are performed by transforming the input coordinate space p before evaluating the primitive, rather than modifying millions of stored vertices:

  • Translation: Evaluating sdSphere(p - offset, r) moves the sphere to position offset.
  • Rotation: Multiplying p by a rotation matrix rotates the geometry. For example, rotating around the Y axis by angle theta:

``glsl vec3 rotateY(vec3 p, float theta) { float c = cos(theta); float s = sin(theta); return vec3(c * p.x + s * p.z, p.y, -s * p.x + c * p.z); } ``

  • Infinite domain repetition: By wrapping coordinates with modulo arithmetic, an artist can duplicate an object infinitely across 3D space with zero memory cost:

``glsl vec3 repeatDomain(vec3 p, vec3 cellSpacing) { return mod(p + 0.5 * cellSpacing, cellSpacing) - 0.5 * cellSpacing; } ``

Constructive solid geometry and polynomial smooth blending

Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) combines multiple primitive distance fields using Boolean logic. In signed distance fields, Boolean operations map directly to basic arithmetic functions:

float opUnion(float d1, float d2)        { return min(d1, d2); }
float opIntersection(float d1, float d2) { return max(d1, d2); }
float opSubtraction(float d1, float d2)  { return max(-d1, d2); }

While standard CSG produces hard, sharp seams where surfaces intersect, creative coding and natural forms frequently demand organic, continuous transitions.

The polynomial smooth minimum, formulated by Inigo Quilez, creates an organic fillet between two distance fields. The smoothing factor k controls the radius of the organic bridge:

float opSmoothUnion(float d1, float d2, float k) {
    float h = clamp(0.5 + 0.5 * (d2 - d1) / k, 0.0, 1.0);
    return mix(d2, d1, h) - k * h * (1.0 - h);
}

float opSmoothSubtraction(float d1, float d2, float k) {
    float h = clamp(0.5 - 0.5 * (d2 + d1) / k, 0.0, 1.0);
    return mix(d2, -d1, h) + k * h * (1.0 - h);
}

When two spheres or geometric shapes pass through one another with opSmoothUnion, they blend seamlessly like drops of liquid mercury or metaballs. In live audiovisual performance, modulating the parameter k with audio amplitude causes sharp geometric structures to dissolve into fluid organic masses on heavy musical accents.

Surface normals and Blinn-Phong lighting

Because signed distance fields do not carry pre-computed vertex normals, we estimate the surface normal vector directly from the spatial gradient of the distance field.

The gradient ∇f(p) points in the direction where the distance increases most rapidly. On a surface boundary where f(p) = 0, this gradient vector points directly perpendicular to the surface. We approximate the gradient using finite differences with a tiny offset e:

vec3 calculateNormal(vec3 p) {
    vec2 e = vec2(0.001, 0.0);
    return normalize(vec3(
        map(p + e.xyy) - map(p - e.xyy),
        map(p + e.yxy) - map(p - e.yxy),
        map(p + e.yyx) - map(p - e.yyx)
    ));
}

This central differences technique samples the scene six times around point p and yields a smooth, accurate unit normal.

Shading and illumination

With the surface normal normal and view direction viewDir calculated, we compute standard Blinn-Phong shading:

vec3 computeLighting(vec3 p, vec3 normal, vec3 viewDir, vec3 lightPos, vec3 baseColour) {
    vec3 lightDir = normalize(lightPos - p);
    vec3 halfwayDir = normalize(lightDir + viewDir);
    
    // Ambient illumination
    vec3 ambient = 0.15 * baseColour;
    
    // Diffuse Lambertian reflection
    float diff = max(dot(normal, lightDir), 0.0);
    vec3 diffuse = diff * baseColour;
    
    // Specular highlight
    float spec = pow(max(dot(normal, halfwayDir), 0.0), 32.0);
    vec3 specular = vec3(0.8) * spec;
    
    // Soft shadow attenuation
    float shadow = computeSoftShadow(p + normal * 0.002, lightDir, 0.02, 10.0, 16.0);
    
    return ambient + (diffuse + specular) * shadow;
}

Raymarched soft shadows

Raymarching offers an elegant way to compute realistic penumbra soft shadows with zero shadow maps. As a secondary shadow ray travels from surface point p toward the light source, we record the minimum ratio of distance to travel distance:

float computeSoftShadow(vec3 ro, vec3 rd, float mint, float maxt, float k) {
    float res = 1.0;
    float t = mint;
    
    for (int i = 0; i < 48; i++) {
        float h = map(ro + rd * t);
        if (h < 0.0005) {
            return 0.0; // In full shadow
        }
        res = min(res, k * h / t);
        t += clamp(h, 0.02, 0.25);
        if (t >= maxt) {
            break;
        }
    }
    
    return clamp(res, 0.0, 1.0);
}

The parameter k controls shadow softness: smaller values yield wide, blurry penumbras resembling diffuse studio lighting, while larger values produce crisp direct sunlight.

Building an audio-reactive raymarcher in Infinite

To run this pipeline inside Infinite, we write our complete GLSL kernel inside a Field Pixel node. Infinite's built-in Field language compiles short text kernels into native GPU fragment shaders without extra wrapper boilerplate.

1. Declaring modulatable parameters

In Field, parameters are declared directly at the top of the kernel script. Each parameter automatically turns into an interactive knob on the node and exposes an input pin on the canvas:

param float u_bass = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0]
param float u_morph = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0]
param float u_twist = 0.5 [0.0, 2.0]
param float u_smooth = 0.3 [0.05, 1.0]

2. Defining the scene distance map

We define a dynamic scene combining a central sphere, a rotating torus, and an organic twist distortion:

float map(vec3 p) {
    // Audio-reactive spatial twist
    float angle = p.y * u_twist + t * 0.4;
    float cosA = cos(angle);
    float sinA = sin(angle);
    p.xz = mat2(cosA, -sinA, sinA, cosA) * p.xz;
    
    // Primitive 1: Central pulsing sphere driven by bass
    float sphereRadius = 1.0 + u_bass * 0.45;
    float dSphere = sdSphere(p, sphereRadius);
    
    // Primitive 2: Outer torus morphed by midrange frequencies
    vec2 torusDims = mix(vec2(1.8, 0.35), vec2(2.2, 0.15), u_morph);
    float dTorus = sdTorus(p, torusDims);
    
    // Smooth organic blend
    return opSmoothUnion(dSphere, dTorus, u_smooth);
}

3. Assembling the canvas patch

The visual half of the patch connects as follows:

  1. Add a Field Pixel node and paste the raymarching kernel.
  2. Cable the image output pin of Field Pixel into a Bloom node to introduce subtle optical glow on high specular reflections.
  3. Cable the output of Bloom into the Output node to send the rendered picture to your display or projector.

The audio half of the patch provides the real-time modulation streams:

  1. Add an Analog or Wavetable synth node, or connect live audio through an Audio In node.
  2. Route the audio signal to an Audio Out node for playback and into an Audio Analyze node.
  3. The Audio Analyze node decomposes the audio stream into frequency bands: low, mid, and high.
  4. Cable the low pin of Audio Analyze to the u_bass input pin of Field Pixel. When a kick drum hits, the central sphere expands dynamically.
  5. Cable the mid pin of Audio Analyze to u_morph. Snare hits and synth melodies cause the torus geometry to morph in radius and thickness.
  6. Add an LFO node configured to a slow sine wave and cable its output into u_twist. This guarantees that the geometric lattice continually drifts and rotates even during quiet musical breakdowns.

For ready-to-use patch setups, browse the free templates in the Library.

Performance optimisation for real-time framerates

Evaluating up to 128 distance queries for every pixel at 1080p or 4K resolution requires careful attention to GPU execution:

  1. Bounding volume tests: Before evaluating an expensive geometric calculation or infinite repetition array, wrap the object in a simple bounding sphere. If the ray step indicates that the distance to the bounding sphere is positive, return that distance immediately, bypassing complex inner math.
  2. Step budget constraints: In a live performance setting running at 60 FPS, cap ray iterations between 64 and 96 steps. This prevents GPU thermal throttling while maintaining clean visual results.
  3. Avoid branch divergence: Avoid placing conditional branching statements (if/else) inside distance functions. Instead, prefer arithmetic blending functions like mix(), step(), and clamp().
  4. Over-relaxation: Standard sphere tracing steps by exactly f(p). Over-relaxation techniques scale each step by a relaxation factor omega (typically around 1.2 to 1.5), speeding up ray travel through long open corridors without skipping boundaries.

To explore further techniques in real-time shader authoring, read our audio-reactive GLSL shaders guide.

Summary and where to experiment next

Raymarching signed distance fields transforms the fragment shader into a full 3D geometric engine. By replacing stored polygon meshes with analytic distance functions, artists gain complete procedural control over form, repetition, lighting, and soft shadows.

When integrated into Infinite's unified audiovisual node canvas, these distance fields become reactive physical instruments. Kick drums displace space, melodies morph geometric topology, and LFOs twist coordinate domains in real time, all running on the GPU with zero audio-thread latency.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/raymarching-signed-distance-fields-in-real-time-glsl.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Real-time fluid simulation in GLSL: Navier-Stokes and dye advection
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How to implement real-time Eulerian fluid simulation in GLSL: velocity advection, multigrid pressure solves, vorticity confinement, and audio reactivity.
item.content:encoded:
Implementing real-time fluid simulation in GLSL provides creative coders and visual artists with an organic medium for live performance, interactive installations, and audiovisual synthesis. Unlike particle-based systems or static procedural distortions, a Navier-Stokes fluid solver models the conservation of mass and momentum across a continuous vector field. When applied to visual media, live video feeds and generative graphics become dynamic dyes that swirl, fold, and disperse according to physical laws.

In real-time audiovisual software such as Infinite, fluid dynamics can be driven directly by incoming sound and camera motion. Because audio frequency bands and optical flow vectors can be mapped to velocity injection points, the fluid reacts with zero perceptible delay to live musical performance.

This guide walks through the complete mathematical and architectural implementation of an Eulerian fluid solver on the GPU: the staggered Marker-and-Cell (MAC) grid layout, unconditionally stable semi-Lagrangian advection, geometric multigrid Poisson solvers for incompressibility, vorticity confinement for preserving turbulence, and live audio-reactive modulation.

What is real-time fluid simulation in GLSL

Computer graphics divides fluid simulation into two primary paradigms: Lagrangian and Eulerian.

The Lagrangian approach treats the fluid as a discrete collection of moving particles, commonly implemented via Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH). Each particle carries its own position, velocity, and mass. While intuitive, particle methods require expensive spatial hashing and neighbour search routines on the GPU, making high-resolution simulations computationally heavy.

The Eulerian approach fixes the coordinate frame in space and observes fluid quantities flowing through a stationary grid of cells. Each cell tracks local velocity, pressure, and passive dye concentration. Because GPU fragment shaders and framebuffers operate natively on two-dimensional pixel grids, the Eulerian formulation maps directly to hardware textures:

  1. Velocity field: a two-component floating-point texture storing horizontal velocity u and vertical velocity v.
  2. Pressure field: a single-component scalar texture storing local hydrostatic pressure p.
  3. Dye field: an RGBA colour texture storing graphic media, video, or synthetic pigmentation carried passively by the flow.

By executing successive rendering passes across offscreen framebuffer objects (FBOs), the graphics card computes each phase of the fluid equations in parallel for millions of cells at sixty frames per second.

The Navier-Stokes equations and grid discretisation

Incompressible fluid flow is governed by the Navier-Stokes equations:

∂u/∂t = -(u · ∇)u - (1/ρ)∇p + ν∇²u + f
∇ · u = 0

Here:

  • u is the velocity vector field (u, v).
  • -(u · ∇)u represents advection, the transport of velocity along itself.
  • -(1/ρ)∇p is the pressure gradient force that accelerates fluid from high to low pressure regions.
  • ν∇²u accounts for kinematic viscosity, causing momentum to diffuse across adjacent layers.
  • f denotes external body forces, such as gravity, user mouse stirrers, or audio impulses.
  • ∇ · u = 0 enforces incompressibility, meaning the volume of any parcel of fluid remains strictly constant over time.

Solving these partial differential equations on a discrete grid requires careful cell alignment. In a naive collocated grid, both velocity components (u, v) and pressure p are stored at the exact centre of each cell. When central differences are computed to evaluate pressure gradients and velocity divergence, adjacent cells skip their immediate neighbours:

∂p/∂x ≈ (p[i+1, j] - p[i-1, j]) / (2 * Δx)

This causes an odd-even decoupling known as the checkerboard instability, where high-frequency oscillatory pressure fields register a false divergence of zero.

To eliminate this artifact without artificial damping, production solvers employ a staggered Marker-and-Cell (MAC) grid layout:

  • The horizontal velocity component u is stored on the vertical cell faces between cell (i-1, j) and (i, j).
  • The vertical velocity component v is stored on the horizontal cell faces between cell (i, j-1) and (i, j).
  • The pressure p and passive dye c are stored at the geometric centre of cell (i, j).

On a staggered grid, divergence is evaluated across immediate face values:

div[i, j] = (u_face[i+1, j] - u_face[i, j]) / Δx + (v_face[i, j+1] - v_face[i, j]) / Δy

Every face velocity couples directly to the pressure of the two cells sharing that face. The resulting discretisation guarantees that when the pressure Poisson equation converges, the velocity field leaves zero divergence behind.

Semi-Lagrangian advection and velocity transport

Advection describes how moving fluid transports both external properties (such as colour and temperature) and its own velocity. Standard explicit finite-difference schemes suffer from the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) stability condition: if the fluid velocity multiplied by the time step exceeds the cell width (|u| * Δt > Δx), the numerical scheme explodes into floating-point infinities.

In 1999, Jos Stam introduced unconditionally stable semi-Lagrangian advection to computer graphics. Rather than asking where a parcel of fluid will travel in the future, semi-Lagrangian advection looks backward in time.

For every grid cell x, the solver traces a virtual particle backward along the current velocity field to determine its origin point x_prev at the previous time step:

x_prev = x - u(x) * Δt

The new value at cell x is then sampled from the previous state at position x_prev using bilinear interpolation:

// GLSL fragment shader for semi-Lagrangian advection
#version 150

uniform sampler2D uVelocity;
uniform sampler2D uSource;
uniform float uDeltaTime;
uniform vec2 uTexelSize;

in vec2 vUv;
out vec4 fragColor;

void main()
{
    // Sample the current velocity at this location
    vec2 vel = texture(uVelocity, vUv).xy;

    // Backtrack along the velocity vector
    vec2 prevPos = vUv - vel * uDeltaTime * uTexelSize;

    // Sample the transported quantity with bilinear hardware filtering
    fragColor = texture(uSource, prevPos);
}

Because bilinear texture sampling on modern graphics hardware is executed directly inside fixed-function texture units, semi-Lagrangian advection runs with minimal shader cost. Even under extreme velocities and large time steps, the algorithm cannot diverge, as the interpolated value is always bounded by the minimum and maximum values of the surrounding texels.

The inherent trade-off of semi-Lagrangian advection is numerical dissipation. Repeated bilinear interpolation acts as an unintended low-pass filter, gradually smoothing out sharp velocity gradients and subtle eddies over time.

Making the flow divergence-free with pressure projection

After advection and the application of external forces, the provisional velocity field w is generally divergent (∇ · w ≠ 0). Compressible fluid would bunch up or create vacuums; an incompressible liquid must satisfy ∇ · u = 0.

The Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition theorem states that any smooth vector field w can be uniquely resolved into the sum of a divergence-free vector field u and the gradient of a scalar potential p:

w = u + ∇p

Taking the divergence of both sides yields the Poisson equation for pressure:

∇ · w = ∇ · u + ∇²p
∇²p = ∇ · w    (since ∇ · u = 0)

Once the scalar pressure field p is obtained by solving this Poisson system, the final divergence-free velocity field is calculated by subtracting the pressure gradient:

u = w - ∇p

Multigrid V-cycles versus standard Jacobi relaxation

On a discrete two-dimensional grid, the Laplacian operator ∇²p is approximated by a five-point stencil:

(p[i+1, j] + p[i-1, j] + p[i, j+1] + p[i, j-1] - 4 * p[i, j]) / (Δx²) = div[i, j]

Rearranging this formula yields the standard Jacobi relaxation step:

p_new[i, j] = 0.25 * (p[i+1, j] + p[i-1, j] + p[i, j+1] + p[i, j-1] - Δx² * div[i, j])

Simple Jacobi iteration dampens high-frequency error quickly, but eliminates low-frequency, long-wavelength pressure differences very slowly. Resolving pressure across a 1920x1080 grid using Jacobi relaxation alone requires between 80 and 150 render passes per frame, which places severe strain on GPU memory bandwidth.

Infinite solves this bottleneck using a geometric multigrid V-cycle solver across five hierarchical grid levels (kMaxLevels = 5):

  1. Pre-smoothing: two Jacobi relaxation passes are performed on the finest simulation grid (Level 0).
  2. Residual calculation: the remaining error r = div - ∇²p is computed.
  3. Restriction: the residual and obstacle masks are downsampled to a half-resolution grid (Level 1).
  4. Recursive descent: this restriction repeats down through Level 4, where the entire screen is represented by a coarse 120x68 grid.
  5. Coarse solve: at the lowest level, long-wavelength pressure modes span only a handful of pixels, allowing ten Jacobi iterations to propagate pressure across the entire domain.
  6. Prolongation: the coarse correction is bilinearly upsampled, added back to the finer level, and followed by two post-smoothing Jacobi passes.

A single five-level multigrid V-cycle with twenty total iterations achieves tighter divergence-free convergence than 120 brute-force Jacobi iterations, leaving ample GPU headroom for real-time video compositing and audio DSP.

Preserving turbulence with vorticity confinement

Because semi-Lagrangian advection introduces numerical dissipation, fine vortices and turbulent swirls tend to decay quickly. In creative coding and visual effects, this loss of rotational energy makes fluids look like thick syrup rather than water or air.

To restore this lost turbulence without destabilising the solver, Infinite employs vorticity confinement, originally formulated by Steinhoff and Underhill and adapted for graphics by Ronald Fedkiw.

Vorticity measures the local rotation or spin of the fluid:

ω = ∇ × u = (∂v/∂x - ∂u/∂y)

In two dimensions, vorticity is a scalar quantity. The gradient of the absolute vorticity points toward the centre of local vortices:

η = ∇|ω| / (|∇|ω| + 1e-5)

The normal vector η is perpendicular to the vortex axis. The confinement force is calculated as the cross product of η and the vorticity vector:

f_vort = ε * (η × ω) * Δx

In GLSL, this evaluates to:

// GLSL fragment shader for vorticity confinement
#version 150

uniform sampler2D uVelocity;
uniform float uVorticityStrength;
uniform vec2 uTexelSize;

in vec2 vUv;
out vec4 fragColor;

void main()
{
    // Compute local curl (vorticity)
    float uT = texture(uVelocity, vUv + vec2(0.0, uTexelSize.y)).x;
    float uB = texture(uVelocity, vUv - vec2(0.0, uTexelSize.y)).x;
    float vR = texture(uVelocity, vUv + vec2(uTexelSize.x, 0.0)).y;
    float vL = texture(uVelocity, vUv - vec2(uTexelSize.x, 0.0)).y;
    
    float curl = 0.5 * ((vR - vL) - (uT - uB));

    // Sample curl magnitude in neighbouring cells
    float cT = abs(texture(uVelocity, vUv + vec2(0.0, uTexelSize.y)).z);
    float cB = abs(texture(uVelocity, vUv - vec2(0.0, uTexelSize.y)).z);
    float cR = abs(texture(uVelocity, vUv + vec2(uTexelSize.x, 0.0)).z);
    float cL = abs(texture(uVelocity, vUv - vec2(uTexelSize.x, 0.0)).z);

    // Find the gradient of curl magnitude
    vec2 eta = 0.5 * vec2(cR - cL, cT - cB);
    float len = length(eta);
    if (len < 1e-5) {
        fragColor = vec4(0.0);
        return;
    }
    eta /= len;

    // Confinement force: F = epsilon * (eta_y, -eta_x) * curl
    vec2 force = uVorticityStrength * vec2(eta.y, -eta.x) * curl;
    fragColor = vec4(force, curl, 1.0);
}

Applying this corrective force before the pressure projection step injects angular momentum back into emerging eddies. Fine rotational details remain crisp and swirling indefinitely without causing instability.

Solid boundaries and obstacle interaction

To allow fluid to flow naturally around visual elements, text, or logos, the solver must handle solid obstacles.

In Infinite, obstacles are provided as a single-channel luminance texture where bright pixels represent solid barriers. Two physical boundary conditions must be satisfied at obstacle surfaces:

  1. No-penetration condition: fluid cannot flow through a solid wall. The velocity normal to the wall must be zero (u · n = 0).
  2. Free-slip or no-slip tangential condition: for low-viscosity aesthetic fluids, free-slip boundaries (where tangential velocity slides unhindered) produce clean, non-sticky circulation.

In the staggered MAC grid, wall boundaries are enforced during the divergence and pressure solve passes. When evaluating the divergence of cell (i, j), any face touching a solid cell or the outer boundary of the texture is flagged as a wall:

bool solidAt(sampler2D obs, ivec2 q, ivec2 sz) {
    if (q.x < 0 || q.y < 0 || q.x >= sz.x || q.y >= sz.y) return true;
    return texelFetch(obs, q, 0).r > 0.5;
}

float faceU(sampler2D vt, sampler2D obs, ivec2 p, ivec2 sz) {
    bool wall = solidAt(obs, p, sz) || solidAt(obs, p - ivec2(1, 0), sz);
    return wall ? 0.0 : texelFetch(vt, p, 0).x;
}

In the pressure solve, the pressure gradient across a solid face is set to zero (∂p/∂n = 0), ensuring that the projection pass does not reintroduce flow into solid barriers. The fluid cleanly wraps around obstacle contours, creating realistic wake patterns and stagnation points.

Audio-reactive forces and optical flow injection in Infinite

A fluid simulation becomes truly compelling in creative performance when connected to sound and real-time motion.

In Infinite, the node canvas combines audio synthesis, DSP analysis, 3D graphics, and 2D GLSL compositing within a single executable timeline. The Fluid node exposes three primary inputs:

  • image: the passive dye carried by the flow. Video clips, generative Shader nodes, or live webcam streams can be cabled here.
  • force: a two-component velocity vector field that stirs the fluid each frame.
  • obstacles: an image mask defining impenetrable solid surfaces.

Coupling with the Optical Flow node

One of the most expressive ways to drive the fluid is through the Optical Flow node. Based on pyramidal Lucas-Kanade feature tracking (Bouguet 2001), Optical Flow computes the instantaneous motion between consecutive video frames across multiple resolution levels.

When set to raw output mode, Optical Flow writes horizontal motion into the red channel and vertical motion into the green channel as floating-point pixels per frame. Cabled into the force pin of the Fluid node, dancer movements, camera gestures, or animated geometric shapes physically push and stir the fluid dye with zero manual calibration.

Modulating fluid physics with audio analysis

To synchronise fluid dynamics with electronic music, audio frequency content is extracted via the Audio Analyze node:

[Audio In / Synth] ---> [Audio Analyze (8-Band FFT)]
                             |
                             +---> band 0 (sub-bass) ---> [Fluid].forceGain
                             |
                             +---> band 3 (snare/mid) ---> [Fluid].vorticity
                             |
                             +---> band 7 (high hat)  ---> [Fluid].stirrerStrength
  1. Sub-bass punch: cabling the lowest FFT band into forceGain amplifies the velocity response on kick drum transients, causing sudden outward explosive bursts.
  2. Vorticity modulation: connecting the snare or mid-frequency transient band to vorticity triggers intricate curling smoke patterns on snare hits, which relax back into smooth laminar flow during quiet passages.
  3. Built-in stirrer automation: the Fluid node includes built-in rotational stirrers (Orbit, Pulse, Spin). By modulating stirrerStrength with a tempo-synced LFO or Envelope node, the entire fluid volume sustains an organic ambient circulation even when external forces pause.

Because Infinite computes parameter modulation, audio DSP, and GPU frame rendering synchronously within the same tick loop, there is zero buffer latency between audio peaks and graphical reaction.

Building the real-time node network in Infinite

Setting up this audiovisual pipeline in Infinite requires five nodes cabled together on the canvas:

  1. Add a Video or Shape node to provide visual content. Connect its output to the image pin of a Fluid node.
  2. Add a Video In node receiving a live camera stream. Cable its output into an Optical Flow node.
  3. Set Optical Flow parameter view to 0 (Raw motion vectors) and cable its output into the force pin of Fluid.
  4. Add an Audio In node patched into an Audio Analyze node.
  5. In the modulation matrix or by dragging modulation cables:
  • Map FFT Band 0 (sub-bass) to Fluid parameter forceGain (range 0.5 to 3.0).
  • Map FFT Band 2 (low-mids) to Fluid parameter vorticity (range 0.1 to 0.6).
  • Map an LFO node running at a 1/2-bar division to Fluid parameter stirrerStrength.
  1. Add an Output node and connect Fluid's output to project the final rendered artwork.

To view alternative internal states during rehearsal, the Fluid node's view parameter allows switching the display from Dye to Velocity (visualised as colour hue and brightness), Pressure gradients, or Obstacles.

The resulting patch and dozens of related creative coding templates are available to explore in the Infinite patch library.

Honest technical limits and GPU performance

While real-time Eulerian fluid simulation in GLSL produces striking visuals, practical production environments have distinct constraints:

  1. Memory bandwidth and fillrate: Eulerian simulations are memory-bandwidth bound. A full-resolution 4K (3840x2160) grid requires reading and writing tens of gigabytes per second across multiple FBO passes. In practice, setting the resolution parameter to 1 (half-resolution simulation grid) allows the velocity and pressure solves to run at 960x540 while the passive dye advection pass remains at full 1080p, preserving sharp visual edges while cutting GPU compute cost by 75 percent.
  2. Two-dimensional planar flow: A 2D simulation does not account for vortex stretching, a three-dimensional physical phenomenon responsible for the energy cascade from large eddies down to microscopic scales. While 2D fluids produce convincing swirling sheets and marbling effects, they cannot simulate three-dimensional smoke plumes or tumbling spherical vortices.
  3. Incompressible assumption: The solver assumes the medium has uniform, constant density. Sound waves (acoustic compression waves) do not propagate through the simulated fluid itself. The audio reactivity described here is achieved by external parametric coupling rather than physical acoustic simulation.

Summary and patch architecture

Real-time fluid simulation in GLSL transforms standard video feeds and generative graphics into dynamic, physics-based audiovisual instruments.

By combining the staggered MAC grid layout with unconditionally stable semi-Lagrangian advection, geometric multigrid Poisson projection, and vorticity confinement, high-resolution fluid dynamics can run smoothly at sixty frames per second on modern hardware. When modulated by live optical flow vectors and audio frequency analysis, the fluid responds organically to music and motion with zero latency.

To experiment with native fluid dynamics, real-time shaders, and modular sound design, download Infinite and explore our detailed guides on raymarching signed distance fields and audio-reactive GLSL shaders.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/real-time-fluid-simulation-in-glsl.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Reaction-diffusion simulation in real-time GLSL
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How to build a reaction-diffusion simulation in real-time GLSL shaders and nodes, creating generative Turing patterns with audio-reactive parameter modulation.
item.content:encoded:
A reaction-diffusion simulation in real-time GLSL brings the organic complexity of natural morphogenesis directly into creative coding and live visual performance. From the spots on a leopard and the stripes on a zebrafish to coral formations and cellular colonies, biological patterns are rarely drawn with static geometry. Instead, they grow out of non-linear chemical interactions where substances spread, react, and compete across space.

In audiovisual environments like Infinite, reaction-diffusion simulations can run entirely on the GPU, updating at high frame rates while reacting to incoming sound. By coupling partial differential equations to real-time audio analysis, artists can guide chemical morphogenesis with musical rhythm, using bass frequencies to seed new matter and high frequencies to trigger cell division.

Here is how the underlying chemistry works, how to discretise the equations for GLSL execution, and how to patch an audio-reactive reaction-diffusion pipeline using both native nodes and custom Field kernels.

The morphogenesis equations of Alan Turing and Gray-Scott

The mathematical foundation of biological pattern formation was introduced in 1952 by Alan Turing in his paper The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis. Turing demonstrated that a system of two reacting chemicals with different diffusion rates, initially distributed almost uniformly, can spontaneously break symmetry and produce stable spatial patterns: spots, stripes, and whorls.

The most widely adopted model in computer graphics and creative coding is the Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion formulation, developed in 1983. In this model, two hypothetical chemical substances, chemical A and chemical B, diffuse across a two-dimensional grid while undergoing an autocatalytic reaction.

Chemical A represents a nourishing substrate that is constantly replenished at a feed rate F. Chemical B represents an active catalyst that consumes chemical A to duplicate itself through the reaction:

2B + A -> 3B

As chemical B reproduces, it also decays and is removed from the system at a kill rate k. The continuous system is governed by two coupled partial differential equations:

dA / dt = D_a * ∇²A - A * B² + F * (1.0 - A)
dB / dt = D_b * ∇²B + A * B² - (F + k) * B

Here:

  1. D_a and D_b are the spatial diffusion rates of substances A and B. For pattern formation to occur, substance A must diffuse significantly faster than substance B, typically with D_a = 1.0 and D_b = 0.5.
  2. ∇² is the Laplacian operator, which computes the second spatial derivative of chemical concentration: measuring whether a point has a higher or lower concentration than its surrounding neighbourhood.
  3. A * B² is the non-linear reaction term representing the conversion of substrate A into catalyst B in the presence of two units of B.
  4. F * (1.0 - A) represents the replenishment of chemical A toward its maximum saturation level of 1.0.
  5. (F + k) * B represents the depletion of chemical B through natural decay and dilution.

The delicate balance between the feed rate F and the kill rate k determines the resulting morphological pattern. Small changes in these two numbers move the simulation between distinct visual regimes:

  • Coral growth (F = 0.054, k = 0.062): slender dendritic branches that expand outward and weave together.
  • Mitosis and dividing cells (F = 0.036, k = 0.065): individual circular spots that grow, deform into dumbbells, and divide into autonomous pairs.
  • Soliton waves (F = 0.030, k = 0.062): pulsating spots and traveling ripples that interact elastically.
  • Labyrinthine maze (F = 0.029, k = 0.057): dense fingerprint-like ridges and interconnected loops that fill the canvas.

Discretising the continuous Laplacian on a GPU pixel grid

To execute the Gray-Scott model on modern graphics hardware in real time, the continuous spatial derivatives must be discretised onto a discrete two-dimensional grid of texels.

The Laplacian operator ∇² measures the divergence of the gradient: the net flow of chemical into or out of a local area. On a discrete square grid with texel spacing Δx = 1.0, we compute the Laplacian using a two-dimensional convolution kernel evaluated over each pixel and its eight immediate neighbours:

∇²U(x, y) ≈ 
    0.05 * U(x - 1, y - 1) + 0.20 * U(x, y - 1) + 0.05 * U(x + 1, y - 1) +
    0.20 * U(x - 1, y)     - 1.00 * U(x, y)     + 0.20 * U(x + 1, y) +
    0.05 * U(x - 1, y + 1) + 0.20 * U(x, y + 1) + 0.05 * U(x + 1, y + 1)

Notice the arithmetic structure of this 9-point stencil:

  • The orthogonal direct neighbours (top, bottom, left, right) each receive a weight of +0.20.
  • The diagonal corner neighbours receive a weight of +0.05.
  • The central pixel receives a weight of -1.00.
  • The sum of all nine weights equals exactly 0.0.

This zero-sum constraint guarantees that in an area of uniform concentration where all neighbouring pixels have identical values, the Laplacian evaluates to zero: no spurious chemical diffusion is created out of nothing.

Because the numerical simulation must feed its own output back into its input on subsequent time steps, real-time GPU implementations allocate two 32-bit floating-point textures (an RG32F ping-pong framebuffer pair). Channel R stores the concentration of chemical A, while channel G stores the concentration of chemical B.

In each rendering pass, the fragment shader samples the current state texture, computes the discrete Laplacian, evaluates the reaction equations, and writes the updated (A, B) values to the secondary texture. On the next step, the roles of the two textures are swapped.

To maintain temporal stability while avoiding spatial aliasing, multiple integration substeps are evaluated per displayed video frame: typically between 4 and 16 iterations per frame with a time step dt = 1.0.

Simulating reaction-diffusion with the native node

Infinite provides a native GPU-accelerated compositing node designed specifically for this physical process: the Reaction Diffusion node.

The node runs an optimised multi-pass fragment shader pipeline on the graphics card, giving access to the full Gray-Scott parameter space without requiring manual framebuffer setup or ping-pong buffer management.

The node exposes several key controls:

  • preset: quick access to canonical Morphogenesis regimes including Coral, Mitosis, Maze, Spots, Worms, and Holes.
  • feed: the replenishment rate of substrate A (ranging from 0.01 to 0.09).
  • kill: the decay rate of catalyst B (ranging from 0.03 to 0.08).
  • diffuse A: spatial propagation speed of substrate A (default 1.0).
  • diffuse B: spatial propagation speed of catalyst B (default 0.5).
  • steps / frame: number of numerical substeps executed per video frame (ranging from 1 to 32, defaulting to 8).
  • source influence: blends incoming image or video frames directly into chemical concentrations, allowing live cameras or video clips to deposit catalyst B onto the grid.

When wired into an output chain, the scalar concentration of chemical B represents the biological pattern. By connecting the output of Reaction Diffusion to a Color Ramp node, artists can map the continuous chemical gradients onto rich palettes, from iridescent oceanic hues to high-contrast monochrome prints.

Writing custom reaction-diffusion in Field Pixel

For artists and developers who require complete control over the mathematical formulation, Infinite includes Field, a domain-specific kernel language that compiles directly to GLSL.

Using a Field Pixel node, you can write the full reaction-diffusion kernel in concise code. The state keyword declares persistent frame-to-frame memory cells that automatically allocate ping-pong GPU textures under the hood.

Here is a complete, self-contained Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion kernel written in Field:

// Field Pixel: Gray-Scott Reaction-Diffusion Kernel
param float feed = 0.037 [0.01, 0.08]
param float kill = 0.060 [0.03, 0.08]
param float diffA = 1.0  [0.2, 1.5]
param float diffB = 0.5  [0.1, 1.0]

// Declare persistent chemical concentration buffers
state vec2 chem = vec2(1.0, 0.0)

// 1. Initialise small central seed perturbations
if (frame < 2) {
    vec2 p = uv - vec2(0.5);
    if (dot(p, p) < 0.002) {
        chem = vec2(0.5, 0.25);
    } else {
        chem = vec2(1.0, 0.0);
    }
} else {
    // 2. Sample 9-point Laplacian from previous frame state
    vec2 texel = 1.0 / resolution;
    
    vec2 lap = -1.0 * chem;
    lap += 0.20 * chem_prev(uv + vec2(-texel.x, 0.0));
    lap += 0.20 * chem_prev(uv + vec2( texel.x, 0.0));
    lap += 0.20 * chem_prev(uv + vec2(0.0, -texel.y));
    lap += 0.20 * chem_prev(uv + vec2(0.0,  texel.y));
    lap += 0.05 * chem_prev(uv + vec2(-texel.x, -texel.y));
    lap += 0.05 * chem_prev(uv + vec2( texel.x, -texel.y));
    lap += 0.05 * chem_prev(uv + vec2(-texel.x,  texel.y));
    lap += 0.05 * chem_prev(uv + vec2( texel.x,  texel.y));
    
    // 3. Evaluate non-linear reaction terms
    float a = chem.x;
    float b = chem.y;
    float reaction = a * b * b;
    
    float da = (diffA * lap.x) - reaction + feed * (1.0 - a);
    float db = (diffB * lap.y) + reaction - (feed + kill) * b;
    
    // 4. Update concentrations and clamp within physical bounds
    chem = clamp(vec2(a + da, b + db), vec2(0.0), vec2(1.0));
}

// 5. Output chemical B mapped to visual colour
col = vec3(chem.y * 2.8, chem.y * 1.4, chem.y * 3.5);

To explore more examples of shader development in Field, refer to the guide on audio-reactive GLSL shaders and the comprehensive Field language manual.

Modulating feed and kill rates with live audio spectrum bins

The most compelling aspect of running physical simulations in a unified audiovisual workstation is modulation. In Infinite, modulation is not an afterthought handled over slow network bridges: audio analysis, visual synthesis, and parameter controls share one lock-free evaluation graph.

To build an audio-reactive reaction-diffusion system:

  1. Insert an audio source, such as an Oscillator, Analog synth, or Audio File node.
  2. Connect the audio signal to an Audio Analyze node. The node splits the incoming sound into eight isolated frequency bands: sub-bass, bass, low-mid, mid, high-mid, presence, brilliance, and air.
  3. Patch the sub-bass pin directly into the feed parameter of the Reaction Diffusion node. As heavy kick drums or bass notes trigger, the feed rate temporarily spikes upward. This floods the grid with fresh substrate A, stimulating aggressive outward branch growth and pattern expansion.
  4. Patch the high-mid or presence pin into the kill parameter with an inverted modulation amount. When sharp snare hits or hi-hats land, the kill rate momentarily drops, allowing catalyst B to survive in regions where it would normally decay. This causes solid labyrinth ridges to fracture into clusters of dividing mitotic cells in step with the beat.
  5. Alternatively, patch the Audio Analyze output into a Noise node, and connect the resulting texture to the input pin of Reaction Diffusion. By setting source influence to 0.2, transient acoustic energy injects localized bursts of catalyst directly onto the canvas, nucleating new self-replicating organisms at the sound of each musical event.

Mapping chemical concentrations to 3D surfaces and shaders

Reaction-diffusion is not restricted to flat two-dimensional video planes. The chemical density field can serve as a procedural displacement map, roughness texture, or volumetric density function for three-dimensional geometry.

In Infinite, you can wire the output of Reaction Diffusion directly into the input of a Displacement node. When applied to a high-density primitive such as a Sphere, Torus Knot, or subdivided Plane:

  1. The scalar concentration of chemical B drives vertex displacement along the surface normal vectors. Labyrinthine ridges rise out of the geometry like organic coral reefs or carved bone.
  2. The same texture is routed into a Material node to control roughness and metallic sheen. Valleys where catalyst B is depleted remain glossy and smooth, while displaced ridges take on tactile matte finishes.
  3. Placing directional and point lights with subtle ambient occlusion transforms the abstract mathematical output into realistic, physical sculptures that appear to breathe and morph in real time.

A selection of ready-to-use procedural patches and generative templates is available in the free Infinite Library.

Headless validation and batch rendering

Because Infinite features a robust headless command-line interface, reaction-diffusion patches can be verified, inspected, and rendered to lossless ProRes or MP4 video without ever opening a graphical window.

Here is a minimal, complete patch file defining an audio-reactive reaction-diffusion network. Save this plain text as reaction_diffusion.inf:

infinite-patch 1
rev 2
node 1 Source Audio File
  id audio
  s path "drums.wav"
end
node 2 DSP Audio Analyze
  id analyze
end
node 3 Compositing Reaction Diffusion
  id rd
  i preset 2
  f feed 0.037
  f kill 0.060
  i stepsPerFrame 8
end
node 4 Compositing Color Ramp
  id ramp
end
node 5 Utility Output
  id out
end
cable analyze 0 audio
cable rd 0 analyze
cable ramp 0 rd
cable out 0 ramp
mod rd feed analyze 0 0.01 0.08 0.4
mod rd kill analyze 4 0.04 0.07 -0.3

You can validate the patch syntax and ensure all cable connections are strictly legal using the command line:

Infinite --validate reaction_diffusion.inf

To render stills at specific time stamps and inspect the organic pattern evolution:

Infinite --frame reaction_diffusion.inf 1.0,2.5,5.0 output/ --contact-sheet sheet.png

To render the finished audiovisual composition to a video file:

Infinite --render reaction_diffusion.inf render.mp4 --duration 15.0 --fps 60

Detailed instructions on command-line flags, render automation, and CI integration can be found in the Headless User Guide.

By uniting non-linear differential equations, GPU fragment pipelines, and zero-latency audio modulation, reaction-diffusion in Infinite turns abstract biochemical morphogenesis into an expressive, interactive instrument for generative art.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/reaction-diffusion-simulation-in-real-time-glsl.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Audio-reactive GLSL shaders: writing real-time visuals in Infinite
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Learn how to write real-time audio-reactive GLSL shaders in Infinite, map FFT frequency bands to shader uniforms, and generate responsive visuals on the GPU.
item.content:encoded:
Writing audio-reactive GLSL shaders gives creative coders and visual artists the power to render responsive geometric worlds directly on the graphics processor. By connecting live sound analysis to GPU fragment programs, visual elements can pulse, distort, and morph in tight synchronisation with incoming music.

In Infinite, shaders and audio live on the same canvas. Rather than relying on separate applications communicating over Spout or NDI with variable latency, the audio engine and the GPU render pipeline share memory and clock timing. This article explains how to build custom audio-reactive GLSL shaders using the Field Pixel node, map fast Fourier transform frequency bands to shader uniforms, and maintain solid frame rates during live performance.

The architecture of audio-reactive shaders

A conventional graphics pipeline draws frames by calculating colour values for each pixel coordinate on the screen. In standard GLSL fragment shaders, coordinates arrive as normalized screen positions ranging from zero to one. To make these coordinates move with music, the shader requires numerical inputs that reflect acoustic energy across time.

In Infinite, this bridge is formed by two native nodes:

  1. Audio Analyze: An audio-rate sink that continuously computes an 8-band FFT spectrum, root-mean-square amplitude, and transient onset energy from any incoming sound signal.
  2. Field Pixel: A GPU shader node that compiles high-level Field kernel code directly into GLSL 150 fragment programs, exposing declared parameters as modulatable pins.

Because the audio engine runs on dedicated real-time worker threads while the rendering engine operates on the main display loop, modulation values pass through lock-free ring buffers. This prevents audio dropouts or graphics stutter, ensuring that modulation data reaches shader uniforms at full monitor refresh rates.

Extracting frequency bands with Audio Analyze

Before writing shader logic, the patch needs an acoustic signal. You can route an audio file, a live microphone input, a synthesizer such as Analog, or a third-party VST3 instrument into an Audio Analyze node.

The Audio Analyze node inspects incoming 48 kHz audio buffers and separates the frequency spectrum into distinct musical bands:

  • low: Energy below 250 Hz, capturing kick drums and sub-bass weight.
  • mid: Energy between 250 Hz and 4 kHz, covering vocals, synth leads, and snare bodies.
  • high: Energy above 4 kHz, capturing hi-hats, cymbals, and transient attacks.
  • level: The overall instantaneous RMS volume of the combined signal.

Each of these four measurements appears as an output pin on the node. When a cable is drawn from one of these pins to a shader parameter, Infinite updates the corresponding uniform before each frame render.

Writing GPU shaders in the Field Pixel node

The Field Pixel node allows you to author shader kernels directly in the node inspector. The Field compiler translates bare mathematical expressions into vectorised GLSL instructions.

Every pixel kernel in Infinite provides built-in coordinates:

  • uv: Normalized coordinates across the canvas from (0, 0) at bottom-left to (1, 1) at top-right.
  • aspect: The ratio of canvas width to height (res.x / res.y), essential for preventing circular shapes from stretching into ovals.
  • t: Elapsed time in seconds.
  • col: The final output RGB vector assigned at the end of the kernel.

To accept modulation values from outside the node, declare parameters using the param keyword. For example:

param float bass = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0];
param float treble = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0];
param float speed = 1.0 [0.1, 5.0];

Each declared param line automatically creates an input pin on the Field Pixel node. When you connect the low pin of Audio Analyze to bass, the value updates continuously as the bassline plays.

Constructing an audio-reactive radial pulse

To demonstrate how frequency data reshapes pixel geometry, consider a concentric wave pattern centered on the screen:

param float bass = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0];
param float treble = 0.0 [0.0, 1.0];

# Centre coordinates and correct aspect ratio
vec2 p = (uv - 0.5) * vec2(aspect, 1.0);
float r = length(p);

# Calculate dynamic rings influenced by time and bass
float rings = sin(r * 32.0 - t * 4.0);
float core = smoothstep(0.02, 0.0, abs(r - 0.25 - bass * 0.2) - rings * 0.015);

# Palette tinting with British colour notation
vec3 bg = vec3(0.05, 0.06, 0.12);
vec3 warm_ring = vec3(1.0, 0.42, 0.15) * core;
vec3 shimmer = vec3(0.65, 0.70, 1.0) * treble * (1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.8, r));

col = bg + warm_ring + shimmer;

In this kernel:

  1. p centers the origin at (0, 0) and scales the horizontal axis by aspect, ensuring symmetrical geometry on widescreen displays.
  2. r = length(p) computes the Euclidean distance from the centre.
  3. The radius of the main ring expands proportionally with bass * 0.2, creating a visible expansion whenever a kick drum hits.
  4. The high frequencies modulate shimmer, illuminating the central region with a cool tint whenever hi-hats sound.

Connecting the output of Field Pixel to an Output node displays the result on screen, which can be previewed inside the workspace or routed to an external projector.

Smoothing signals and preventing visual jitter

Raw audio analysis signals can oscillate abruptly from frame to frame. If mapped directly to high-contrast geometric boundaries, rapid fluctuations can produce visual harshness.

To achieve fluid, organic motion:

  • Interpolation in the shader: Use GLSL smoothstep or mix functions rather than hard conditional branches (if/else), allowing the GPU vector units to evaluate both branches without divergence stalls.
  • Node-based smoothing: Place a Smoothing node between Audio Analyze and Field Pixel. A rise time of 5 ms combined with a fall time of 60 ms provides an immediate rhythmic attack while letting the visual decay gently between musical beats.
  • Modulator layering: Combine the audio signal with a slow periodic LFO node using an inline math expression or a Math node. This ensures the canvas maintains subtle visual movement even during quiet breakdowns in the track.

For a ready-to-use project demonstrating these connections, explore the starter templates available in the Infinite Library.

Real-time performance and GPU execution

Because GLSL fragment programs execute once for every pixel on screen, writing efficient kernels is crucial for sustaining high frame rates. At 1920x1080 resolution and 60 frames per second, a fragment shader executes over 124 million times each second.

Infinite compiles Field kernels directly to native OpenGL shaders when a patch loads or when code is edited. The compilation runs in the background, avoiding audio glitches or frame hitches. When authoring complex signed distance fields or raymarched volumes:

  1. Avoid dynamic loop bounds: Keep loop counts constant so the GPU driver can unroll loops where advantageous.
  2. Minimise dependent texture reads: Compute math procedurally using sinusoidal or noise approximations rather than sampling oversized image textures.
  3. Inspect cook times: The inspector on the Field Pixel node reports cook duration in milliseconds. A clean fragment shader typically cooks in less than 0.5 milliseconds on modern integrated or discrete GPUs.

Taking shaders to the stage and export

Once your audio-reactive shader is dialed in, you can route the output to multiple destinations:

  • Live performance: Enable full-screen mode on a secondary display or beam video to stage visual software via Syphon on macOS or Spout on Windows using the Syphon Out and Spout Out nodes.
  • Offline high-resolution video render: Render the complete audiovisual composition to disk without dropping a single frame using Infinite's headless command-line interface. For a step-by-step guide to command-line automation, read our article on how to render video and audio from a text file.
  • Template sharing: Patches are saved as lightweight .inf text files that store the complete node graph, parameter bindings, and Field shader kernels. You can share your files with other artists or download community examples from the Infinite Library.

To begin building your own responsive graphics, download Infinite and experiment with the beginner walkthrough on how to make your first audio-reactive visual.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/audio-reactive-glsl-shaders.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Lorenz attractor interactive simulation in creative coding
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How to build a Lorenz attractor interactive simulation in real time using differential equations, interactive Sketch code, and audio modulation.
item.content:encoded:
A Lorenz attractor interactive simulation brings the non-linear elegance of deterministic chaos into modern creative coding and live audiovisual performance. In traditional generative art, procedural movement often relies on periodic functions like sine waves or pseudorandom noise fields. While periodic functions offer predictable repetition and noise fields produce uncorrelated drifting, neither captures the natural tension of complex physical systems: structured form that evolves continuously without ever repeating.

In modular workstations like Infinite, the Lorenz attractor bridges mathematics, real-time computer graphics, and modular sound design. By evaluating its three coupled differential equations inside a programmable canvas, artists can project intricate three-dimensional phase space paths, modulate attractor dynamics live with audio frequencies, and sonify chaotic coordinates into synthesiser parameters.

Here is how the underlying non-linear mathematics work, how to implement the simulation inside a Sketch node, and how to patch chaotic variables across visual and audio nodes on a single canvas.

The geometry of deterministic chaos

The Lorenz system was introduced in 1963 by mathematician and meteorologist Edward Lorenz. While studying a simplified twelve-variable mathematical model of atmospheric convection, Lorenz reduced the convective fluid flow between warm lower and cool upper boundaries to a minimal system of three autonomous ordinary differential equations:

dx / dt = sigma * (y - x)
dy / dt = x * (rho - z) - y
dz / dt = x * y - beta * z

Here, the state variables describe idealized physical properties:

  1. x is proportional to the rate of convective fluid circulation.
  2. y is proportional to the horizontal temperature variation between ascending and descending currents.
  3. z measures the distortion of the vertical temperature profile from pure linearity.

The three system parameters govern the physical regime:

  • sigma (the Prandtl number) represents the ratio of kinematic viscosity to thermal diffusivity. In standard simulations, this is fixed at 10.0.
  • beta represents the geometric aspect ratio of the convective roll cells, traditionally set to 8.0 / 3.0 (approximately 2.667).
  • rho (the Rayleigh number) measures the normalized temperature difference driving the fluid convection. It serves as the primary bifurcation parameter.

When rho is less than 1.0, the system has only one stable equilibrium at the coordinate origin (0, 0, 0), representing pure conduction where fluid motion dissipates. As rho exceeds 1.0, two symmetric convective fixed points emerge, labelled C+ and C-:

C+, C- = (+-sqrt(beta * (rho - 1)), +-sqrt(beta * (rho - 1)), rho - 1)

At the canonical threshold rho = 28.0, both equilibrium points become unstable spirals. Instead of settling into a fixed point or a simple limit cycle, the trajectory enters bounded deterministic chaos. The path orbits one fixed point, spirals outward as its radius expands, and then crosses the saddle point at the origin to loop around the opposing lobe. Because the trajectory never intersects itself in three-dimensional phase space, it traces a fractal structure with a Hausdorff dimension of approximately 2.06.

Numerical integration and step resolution

To compute the attractor trajectory in a real-time computer graphics pipeline, we discretise the continuous derivatives over a small forward time step dt.

In offline scientific research, higher-order integrators such as the fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) method are preferred because they minimise local truncation error. However, in real-time creative coding and interactive visual performance, the forward Euler integration scheme provides an ideal balance of speed, simplicity, and visual stability:

x_next = x + sigma * (y - x) * dt
y_next = y + (x * (rho - z) - y) * dt
z_next = z + (x * y - beta * z) * dt

The key to visual clarity is selecting an appropriate time step. If dt is set too high (for example, greater than 0.02), numerical instability causes coordinates to expand rapidly towards infinity. If dt is set too low (less than 0.001), the trajectory moves sluggishly, requiring tens of thousands of iterations per frame to reveal the dual-lobe geometry.

A time step between 0.005 and 0.008 produces stable integration. In interactive environments running at 60 or 120 frames per second, computing between 600 and 1,800 steps per frame generates a continuous glowing ribbon that showcases both the fast orbital motion around each lobe and the broader global butterfly structure.

Real-time simulation in a Sketch node

In Infinite, you can write JavaScript creative coding routines directly inside a Sketch node. The node exposes a lightweight drawing API with vector mathematics, colour utilities, and parameter reflection on the node body.

The official Lorenz Attractor Sketch available in the Infinite Library implements this simulation with live interactive parameter controls:

// Lorenz Attractor - Infinite Library (Sketch)
// Differential equations: dx=s(y-x), dy=x(r-z)-y, dz=xy-bz
param("rho", 28, 10, 40);
param("trail", 1400, 200, 4000);
param("zoom", 1, 0.5, 2);
