function draw(t) {
  background(0.04, 0.04, 0.08);
  const s = 10, b = 8 / 3, dt = 0.006;
  let x = 0.1, y = 0, z = 0;
  const steps = floor(t * 120) + 400;
  const pts = [];

  for (let i = 0; i < steps; i++) {
    const dx = s * (y - x), dy = x * (rho - z) - y, dz = x * y - b * z;
    x += dx * dt; y += dy * dt; z += dz * dt;
    pts.push([x, y, z]);
  }

  const from = max(0, pts.length - trail);
  const k = min(width, height) / 60 * zoom;
  noFill();
  strokeWeight(2.2);

  for (let i = from + 1; i < pts.length; i++) {
    const a = pts[i - 1], p = pts[i];
    const f = (i - from) / (pts.length - from);
    stroke(hsl(0.58 - 0.5 * f, 0.8, 0.35 + 0.35 * f));
    line(width / 2 + a[0] * k, height * 0.9 - a[2] * k, width / 2 + p[0] * k, height * 0.9 - p[2] * k);
  }
}

The script declares three interactive controls using param():

  1. rho: Controls the Rayleigh bifurcation value, ranging from 10.0 to 40.0. Modulating this changes the size of the lobes and the switching frequency between attractor wings.
  2. trail: Determines how many historical trajectory vertices are retained in the drawing buffer, shaping the visible tail length.
  3. zoom: Adjusts the projection scale so the attractor fits comfortably inside different viewport resolutions.

Each frame, the script advances the numerical integration from the initial perturbation coordinate (0.1, 0.0, 0.0). As the trail vertices accumulate, the script calculates a normalised depth ratio f for each line segment and applies an HSL colour ramp. Older segments fade into deep indigo and purple tones, while the leading head glows with bright cyan and orange strokes.

Audio-reactive modulation of system parameters

Because parameters declared with param() in a Sketch node are automatically registered with the application modulation system, you can connect audio analysis outputs directly into the chaotic equations.

To construct an audio-reactive chaos pipeline:

  1. Add an Audio Analyze node to the canvas to extract spectral energy across eight frequency bands.
  2. Connect the low-frequency bass output pin into a Math node configured with a scale function, mapping input amplitudes between 0.0 and 1.0 into a target rho range between 14.0 and 34.0.
  3. Patch the scaled output cable into the rho input pin of the Sketch node.
  4. Add an LFO node running a slow sine shape at 0.05 Hz and cable its output into the zoom parameter to add subtle camera breathing.

This patch produces compelling behavioural shifts during live music playback:

  • During quiet ambient passages where bass energy is low (rho < 20), the attractor collapses into gentle, tightly wound elliptical spirals around one of the fixed points.
  • When a kick drum or sub-bass transient hits, the sudden jump in rho forces the trajectory across the bifurcation threshold. The ribbon flings outward into wide sweeping arcs and switches lobes aggressively in rhythm with the musical beat.
  • Because the underlying differential equations maintain mathematical continuity, the visual transition is fluid and organic, avoiding the jerky threshold snapping typical of simple amplitude-triggered graphics.

Sonification and 3D visual geometry

In addition to driving visuals from sound, the chaotic coordinates generated by the Lorenz equations can be routed back into sound synthesis and three-dimensional spatial rendering.

Direct chaotic sonification

The three state variables possess distinct temporal signatures that map naturally into synthesiser controls:

  • Connect the x coordinate into the frequency modulation input of an Oscillator or the pitch modulation pin of an Analog synth. Because x oscillates back and forth between positive and negative lobes with sudden transitions, it generates expressive vibrato and gliding pitch contours.
  • Connect the z coordinate into the cutoff frequency pin of an Audio Filter. Since z remains strictly positive and pulses upward during lobe transitions, it sweeps filter cutoffs upwards on every cross-over.
  • Connect the y coordinate to a stereo balance or pan parameter. As the attractor moves between left and right wings in phase space, the sound sweeps smoothly across the stereo field.

Three-dimensional point cloud deformation

While the Sketch node renders a clean 2D projection using Canvas drawing commands, you can also compute the attractor in a Field node to deform true 3D meshes:

  1. In a Field geometry kernel, evaluate the Lorenz integration loop across thousands of parallel GPU threads.
  2. Store the resulting coordinates in a vertex buffer and pass them into an Instance on Points node.
  3. Feed the instanced points into Render 3D, applying realistic lighting, specular highlights, and depth of field blur.

You can inspect working real-time examples of procedural geometry and audio-reactive shaders in the interactive embeds showcase.

Creative workflows and live performance

Deterministic chaos offers creative coders and visual performers a versatile toolkit for generative design. Unlike purely random systems that can feel disjointed, or strictly periodic loops that can become monotonous, a strange attractor retains recognizable geometric structure while providing continuous variation.

When building live audiovisual performance sets, consider these practical techniques:

  1. Dampen incoming audio signals: Audio transients can exhibit high-frequency jitter. Inserting a subtle smoothing filter or using an Envelope follower between Audio Analyze and your Sketch parameters ensures the attractor responds to musical dynamics without visual stutter.
  2. Explore neighbouring attractor systems: The same integration loop can be adapted to simulate other chaotic regimes, such as the Rössler attractor, the Aizawa spherical flow, or the Clifford attractor.
  3. Automate parameter orbits: Connecting multi-stage envelope generators (MSEG) or chaotic modulators to both audio filters and visual projection scales creates unified audiovisual compositions where sound and form evolve together.

By uniting non-linear differential equations with modular audio routing and real-time graphics rendering, the Lorenz attractor demonstrates how classical mathematical physics can enrich modern creative coding.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/lorenz-attractor-interactive-simulation.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: PaulStretch on Mac: extreme spectral time stretching in Infinite
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Explore PaulStretch on Mac with Infinite. Learn how real-time spectral time stretching, phase randomisation, and FFT analysis turn audio into ambient drones.
item.content:encoded:
Finding a reliable version of paulstretch free mac users can run on modern Apple Silicon hardware has historically proved difficult. The original PaulStretch application created by Nasca Octavian Paul became an essential tool for sound designers, film composers, and electronic producers aiming to turn everyday field recordings and acoustic phrases into infinite, luminous drone textures. However, because the legacy standalone software was compiled as a 32-bit binary, newer versions of macOS can no longer run it without third-party audio editor plug-ins or terminal emulators.

In Infinite, extreme spectral time stretching is implemented as a first-class native node: the Paul Stretch node. Built from scratch with 64-bit precision, hardware-accelerated Apple vDSP fast Fourier transforms, and full real-time modulation on the canvas, it brings the iconic PaulStretch algorithm into a responsive audiovisual environment.

This article walks through the mathematics of spectral time stretching, explains how phase randomisation prevents flutter, explores the internal architecture of the Paul Stretch node in Infinite, and outlines practical patching techniques for ambient music production.

Why time-domain stretching fails at extreme ratios

Standard digital audio workstations rely on time-domain techniques for tempo manipulation. Algorithms such as waveform similarity overlap-add (WSOLA) or granular pitch shifting slice an incoming audio buffer into tiny grains, repeating or dropping fragments to stretch duration without shifting pitch.

While these time-domain algorithms work well for modest tempo adjustments of five or ten percent, they disintegrate when stretched by factors of 10x, 50x, or 1000x:

  1. Transient flutter: Grains repeated thousands of times produce rapid comb filtering and an artificial buzzing sound.
  2. Phase cancellation: Splicing non-continuous waveforms results in phase interference across mid and high frequencies.
  3. Discontinuous harmonics: Long sustained tones lose their acoustic coherence, turning orchestral chords into static chatter.

To achieve genuine ambient expansion, where a four-second piano chord blooms into a lush twenty-minute harmonic cloud, the processing must take place entirely within the frequency domain.

The mathematics of the PaulStretch algorithm

The PaulStretch algorithm solves the extreme duration problem through Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) analysis, complete phase randomisation, and overlap-add synthesis.

1. Windowing and the forward transform

The algorithm extracts overlapping segments of audio from a source buffer. Each segment is multiplied by a symmetrical Hann window function:

w(n) = 0.5 * (1.0 - cos(2.0 * pi * n / (N - 1)))

Here, N represents the window length in samples. The windowed segment is then transformed into complex frequency bins using the forward fast Fourier transform (FFT):

X[k] = FFT(x(n) * w(n))

Each bin X[k] contains a real component and an imaginary component, encoding the amplitude and phase of that specific frequency band.

2. Spectral magnitude extraction and phase randomisation

In conventional phase vocoders, the algorithm must track and calculate the exact phase progression across consecutive frames to preserve pitch. When audio is stretched by 100x or 800x, phase tracking accumulates floating-point errors, creating hollow, metallic ringing.

Paul Nasca discovered that for extreme ambient textures, the exact temporal phase relationship of individual partials is largely irrelevant to the human ear. What matters is the spectral envelope: the distribution of energy across frequency bins.

The algorithm extracts the magnitude of each frequency bin:

M[k] = sqrt(real(X[k])^2 + imag(X[k])^2)

The original phase information is discarded entirely. In its place, the synthesiser assigns a fresh, uniformly distributed random phase angle between -pi and +pi:

theta[k] = uniform_random(-pi, +pi)

By reconstructing the complex spectrum from the original magnitude and the random phase angle:

Y[k] = M[k] * (cos(theta[k]) + i * sin(theta[k]))

the algorithm diffuses temporal transients into continuous acoustic energy. Attack transients such as drum strikes, vocal plosives, and string plucks are smeared evenly across the duration of the analysis window, transforming percussive impacts into warm, diffuse spectral pads.

3. Inverse transform and overlap-add accumulation

The modified spectrum Y[k] is converted back into the time domain using the inverse FFT (IFFT):

y(n) = IFFT(Y[k])

The resulting time-domain block is windowed a second time by the Hann curve and accumulated into an overlap-add output buffer. The playback pointer steps forward through the source sample by a hop size determined by the chosen stretch factor:

hop_size = (window_size / 2) / stretch_factor

When stretch_factor is set to 100.0, the hop size becomes tiny, allowing the synthesiser to continuously re-analyse and diffuse virtually identical slices of the source audio over extended periods of time.

Inside the Paul Stretch node in Infinite

In Infinite, the Paul Stretch node (src/nodes/PaulStretchNode.cpp) is engineered for low-latency live performance and audio thread reliability.

Zero allocation audio thread

Standard implementations often allocate memory buffers dynamically when changing window sizes or loading audio files. In Infinite, the node preallocates all necessary arrays during the initialization phase:

  • On macOS, the node allocates an optimised Apple vDSP FFT setup (vDSP_create_fftsetup) using radix-2 acceleration.
  • On Linux and Windows, it employs Infinite's portable FFT library (PortableFft.h), maintaining identical bit-level spectral parity across operating systems.
  • Work arrays for split complex storage (mSplitReal, mSplitImag), magnitude calculation, and overlap-add ring buffers are allocated ahead of time.
  • Phase angles are generated using an inlined, lock-free XorShift32 pseudorandom number generator, executing in nanoseconds per bin without thread contention.

Discrete window size selection

The node offers seven discrete power-of-two window sizes:

IndexWindow size (samples)Duration at 44.1 kHzMusical character
0204846 msFast response, subtle granular texture
1409693 msCrisp harmonic definition
28192186 msBalanced vocal and melodic expansion
316384372 msClassic PaulStretch pad density
432768743 msDeep orchestral and choral wash (default)
5655361.49 sImmense ambient decay, crystalline partials
61310722.97 sMonolithic drones, near-stationary spectra

Selecting an appropriate window size involves balancing time resolution against frequency resolution. Shorter windows (such as 4096 samples) track chord progressions and pitch changes with minimal lag, but retain slight granular flutter. Longer windows (such as 65536 samples) resolve individual low-frequency harmonics with microscopic precision, yielding smooth, glassy textures where individual note transitions blend like watercolours.

Real-time modulation and frequency transformation

Unlike traditional offline tools where you render a stretched file to disk and re-import it into your session, Infinite's Paul Stretch node runs continuously on the audio canvas. Every parameter can be controlled in real time using cables from modulators, LFOs, and MIDI sources.

Spectral pitch shifting and fine tuning

The node provides dedicated pitch transposition:

  • pitch: Transposes the spectrum up or down by plus or minus 24 semitones.
  • fine: Fine-tunes the transposition by plus or minus 100 cents.

Because transposition occurs by scaling spectral bin indices during frequency reconstruction rather than altering playback speed, changing pitch does not alter the playback duration or the stretch ratio.

Linear frequency shifting

In addition to musical pitch shifting, the node features a linear shift control ranging from -1000 Hz to +1000 Hz. Adding a constant frequency offset to all harmonics destroys harmonic integer ratios, yielding metallic, bell-like inharmonic resonances reminiscent of ring modulation.

Unison detuning in the frequency domain

For expansive stereo imaging, the node includes a unison control supporting up to 8 voices with a modulatable detune spread (0 to 50 cents).

Instead of running multiple redundant FFT instances across parallel audio threads, Infinite calculates unison layering directly in the frequency domain. Additional voice spectra are derived and accumulated into complex accumulator buffers before executing the inverse FFT, delivering wide, chorused drone textures with minimal processor load.

Live sampling via the record pin

The Paul Stretch node includes an audio input pin labeled slot 0 (record in). Sound designers can route any audio source: such as an acoustic microphone input, a drum machine, or the output of an Analog synthesiser: directly into the node.

Triggering the record control captures up to 30 seconds of live sound into an internal circular buffer. Once recorded, the playhead begins scrubbing and stretching the freshly captured material immediately, turning fleeting acoustic gestures into permanent ambient soundscapes.

Building an ambient sound design patch

To experience the musical depth of spectral time stretching, construct this foundational patch in Infinite:

[ Sample / Live Mic ] ---> [ Paul Stretch ] ---> [ Delay ] ---> [ Reverb ] ---> [ Audio Out ]
                                ^      ^
                                |      |
                             [ LFO ] [ Random ]
  1. Load a source sample: Drop an acoustic guitar phrase, vocal harmony, or piano chord into the Paul Stretch node.
  2. Configure the stretch factor: Set stretch to 32.0 and select window size 32768 (743ms).
  3. Add playhead modulation: Connect a slow sinusoidal LFO node (running at 0.02 Hz) to the pos input pin. This gently sweeps the analysis point back and forth across the recording, ensuring the timbre continually shifts.
  4. Modulate the texture: Connect a subtle Random modulator to the detune pin to introduce gentle microtonal drifting.
  5. Spatial finishing: Cable the stereo outputs of Paul Stretch through a stereo Delay and an algorithmic Reverb node before connecting to Audio Out.

To examine more advanced configurations featuring polyphonic modulators and frequency analysis, explore the downloadable project templates in the Infinite Library.

Headless automation and batch processing

Because Infinite features a comprehensive command-line interface, you can automate spectral sound design pipelines without opening the graphical interface.

You can save your patch as a .inf document, modify sample paths or stretch parameters programmatically using Python or the terminal, and render pristine 24-bit audio files to disk. For detailed instructions on headless rendering and scripting, consult our guide on how to render video and audio from a text file.

Furthermore, if you are synchronising visuals with your stretched audio, you can route the output of Paul Stretch into an Audio Analyze node to extract frequency bands, subsequently driving real-time GPU graphics as described in our tutorial on audio-reactive GLSL shaders.

Summary

The PaulStretch algorithm remains one of the most expressive audio processing techniques ever conceived for ambient music and experimental sound design. By implementing this iconic process natively in 64-bit C++ with hardware-accelerated FFTs, Infinite gives musicians on macOS, Windows, and Linux instant access to extreme spectral time stretching on an open, modular canvas.

Download Infinite from the homepage to explore the Paul Stretch node and begin creating your own evolving drone environments.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/paulstretch-extreme-spectral-time-stretching.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Euclidean rhythm sequencer algorithms for modular music
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How to generate Euclidean rhythm sequencer algorithms using Bjorklund integer distribution, modular arithmetic, and audio-reactive triggers in Infinite.
item.content:encoded:
A Euclidean rhythm sequencer algorithm distributes a fixed number of active musical pulses as evenly as possible across a discrete timeline of metric steps. First identified in computer science by E. Bjorklund in 2003 for timing neutron accelerators at Los Alamos, and brought into music theory by Godfried Toussaint in 2005, Euclidean rhythms revealed a startling truth: the mathematical distribution of pulses on a circle generates the foundational rhythmic structures of traditional music worldwide.

In modern modular synthesis and creative coding environments like Infinite, Euclidean sequencers provide an elegant alternative to static step grids. Because the pattern emerges directly from two integer parameters, pulse count and step length, composers can morph complex groove structures live without editing step arrays by hand.

Here is how the mathematics work, how to implement the algorithm in a single line of procedural code, and how to patch Euclidean triggers into synthesizers and 3D geometry simultaneously.

From nuclear accelerators to world rhythms

The core challenge of rhythmic distribution can be stated simply: given $n$ available steps in a bar and $k$ active beats, how can we space the beats so the interval between any two consecutive hits differs by at most one step?

Bjorklund originally developed an iterative algorithm based on Euclid's greatest common divisor method. Starting with a set of $k$ ones (active hits) and $n - k$ zeros (rests), the algorithm repeatedly distributes the smaller group into remainder sequences until no division remains. When applied to musical intervals, Toussaint observed that this mechanical reduction produces virtually every major non-Western and folk timeline pattern:

  • E(3, 8) produces [X . . X . . X .], the Cuban tresillo and Caribbean habanera rhythm.
  • E(5, 8) produces [X . X X . X X .], the Cuban cinquillo and Spanish tango.
  • E(5, 12) produces [X . . X . X . . X . X .], the Venda clapping pattern from South Africa.
  • E(7, 12) produces [X . X . X X . X . X . X], the West African bell pattern (Bembe), which is also geometrically isomorphic to the diatonic major scale on a twelve-tone chromatic circle.
  • E(5, 16) produces [X . . X . . X . . . X . . X . .], the Brazilian bossa nova necklace.
  • E(7, 16) produces [X . . X . X . . X . X . . X . .], a fundamental Brazilian samba rhythm.

Because each pattern can be rotated around the circular step circle, a single pair of integers yields multiple distinct syncopations simply by advancing the starting step index.

The closed-form integer Bresenham formula

While Bjorklund's recursive array partitioning works well for static sequence generation, running recursive string manipulations inside a real-time audio thread or graphics shader is inefficient.

Fortunately, Euclidean distribution can be expressed in closed form as a one-dimensional Bresenham line-drawing algorithm. Imagine drawing a continuous line from coordinate (0, 0) to (n, k) on a 2D integer grid. Each time the line crosses an integer threshold on the vertical axis, an active hit occurs.

For any discrete step index $s \in [0, n - 1]$, the state of the trigger is calculated directly by comparing two consecutive floor evaluations:

on(s) = floor((s + 1) * k / n) - floor(s * k / n)

This mathematical identity possesses several vital properties for modular audio workstations:

  1. Constant time complexity: The evaluation takes $O(1)$ operations with zero loops, making it suitable for per-sample DSP evaluation at 48,000 Hz.
  2. Deterministic boundary precision: Because integer multiplication precedes division, no floating-point rounding errors accumulate across long performances.
  3. Instantaneous parameter morphing: Changing $k$ or $n$ on the fly immediately recalculates the current step without clearing internal buffers or causing audio clicks.

To introduce pattern rotation, we add a phase offset parameter $r$ before taking the modulo of the sequence length:

step_rotated = (s + r) % n
on = floor((step_rotated + 1) * k / n) - floor(step_rotated * k / n)

Implementing Euclidean algorithms in Field Notes

In Infinite, you can write procedural note generation directly using the Field Notes node. Unlike fixed piano roll clips, Field Notes compiles real-time mathematical expressions into sample-accurate MIDI event streams.

Here is the complete implementation of a parameterised Euclidean rhythm sequencer kernel:

param float hits = 5 [1, 16]
param float steps = 16 [1, 32]
param float rotate = 0 [0, 31]
param float pitch = 60 [24, 96]
state float step = 0

if (tick(1/16) > 0.5) {
   s = (step + floor(rotate + 0.5)) % steps
   k = clamp(floor(hits + 0.5), 1, steps)
   n = floor(steps + 0.5)
   
   on = floor((s + 1) * k / n + 0.001) - floor(s * k / n + 0.001)
   
   if (on > 0.5) {
      note(pitch, 0.85, 1/16)
   }
   
   step = (step + 1) % n
}

In this kernel, tick(1/16) synchronises with the workstation transport clock, firing a pulse on every sixteenth note. The state variable tracks the playback position, while param exposes hits, steps, and rotate as live modulatable controls on the node canvas. You can patch an LFO or Random node directly into rotate to create evolving rhythmic variations that stay locked to the metric grid.

If you want to explore pre-built musical patches and procedural devices, check the interactive devices in the Infinite Library.

Polyrhythms, phase shifting, and polymetre

The true compositional depth of Euclidean sequencing emerges when combining multiple independent generators running in parallel.

When two sequencers share the same step resolution (for example, sixteenth notes) but use coprime total step counts, they produce polymetric phasing. Consider patching three distinct Field Notes instances into separate lanes of a Drum Sampler or Analog synth:

  • Voice 1 (Kick drum): $E(4, 16)$, a steady four-on-the-floor pulse.
  • Voice 2 (Snare / Rim): $E(5, 12)$, a five-beat pattern looping every twelve sixteenth notes.
  • Voice 3 (Hi-hat / Bell): $E(7, 15)$, a seven-beat pattern looping every fifteen sixteenth notes.

Because 16, 12, and 15 have a lowest common multiple of 240 steps, the combined rhythm will play for fifteen bars of 4/4 time before ever repeating identical downbeat alignments. The music feels continuously evolving and organic, yet remains strictly locked to a shared mathematical grid.

Furthermore, by applying subtle phase modulation to the rotate input with a slow triangle LFO, the patterns gently slip against one another, creating Steve Reich style phase-shifting textures.

Simultaneous audio transients and 3D visual geometry

Because Infinite hosts audio synthesis, procedural shaders, and 3D rendering on a single unified execution graph, Euclidean triggers are not restricted to sound design. The same trigger pulse that drives an audio envelope can simultaneously deform procedural geometry in the viewport.

To build an audio-reactive visual installation driven by Euclidean rhythms:

  1. Connect the event output of Field Notes into an Analog synth or Drum Sampler to produce the audible transient.
  2. Split the trigger velocity into an Envelope or Formula node to generate a smoothed modulation envelope.
  3. Patch the modulation cable into an Instance on Points node, scaling concentric rings of geometry in a Render 3D scene whenever a Euclidean pulse fires.
  4. Route the sound output through Audio Filter for warmth, and observe how the 3D particles expand and contract in sample-locked synchronisation with the audio transient.

By evaluating both domains in the same execution cycle, there is zero communication latency, zero MIDI jitter, and zero frame mismatch between the kick drum transient and the on-screen geometric displacement.

You can inspect working interactive visualisers and audio-reactive shaders directly in the Infinite embeds collection.

Creative applications in your music

Euclidean rhythm sequencer algorithms strip away the manual labour of clicking individual grid squares in a conventional timeline. By treating rhythm as a geometric problem of spacing pulses evenly across time, you can discover syncopations and polyrhythms that feel human, balanced, and compelling.

Whether you are designing polyrhythmic techno percussion, West African bell lattices, or live audio-reactive visual performances, Euclidean sequencing turns simple modular numbers into rich musical phrases.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/euclidean-rhythm-sequencer-algorithm.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Embedding interactive audio-reactive WebGL visuals on any website
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How to embed responsive, microphone-reactive 3D WebGL visualisers into portfolios, documentation, and blogs using self-contained HTML iframes.
item.content:encoded:
Adding an interactive audio visualizer embed to a technical portfolio, documentation page, or creative release announcement often sounds simpler than it turns out to be. In practice, embedding real-time generative computer graphics on the web usually means pulling in large third-party runtime bundles, wrangling WebAudio permission policies, managing asset loading cascades, and debugging WebGL canvas resize glitches across mobile viewports.

Infinite approaches web graphics from a different perspective. Because Infinite compiles procedural fragment shaders, JavaScript sketches, and per-sample audio DSP nodes into self-contained formats, its web export pipeline generates standalone HTML widgets that require zero external dependencies, zero CDN requests, and zero script frameworks.

Here is how these embeds are structured, how the microphone reactivity works, and how you can place one on any page with a standard iframe.

The problem with traditional web audio visualisers

Most web visualisers rely on heavy JavaScript libraries such as Three.js, Babylon.js, or complex bundling setups. When embedded inside an article or project portfolio, these libraries create three distinct friction points:

  1. Payload weight and cold starts: Loading megabyte-scale runtime libraries introduces layout shifts, slow paint times, and stuttering initial frames.
  2. Audio context locking: Modern web browsers block audio playback and microphone capture until an explicit user interaction occurs. If an embedded canvas tries to initialise WebAudio automatically, the browser mutes or rejects the audio stream.
  3. Cross-origin security restrictions: When hosting visual widgets in iframes, microphone access requires explicit permission delegation via the allow="microphone" attribute. Without this header, permission dialogues fail silently.

Infinite solves this by generating single-file HTML embeds where the entire WebGL vertex shader, fragment shader, audio analysis loop, and fallback UI live in under twelve kilobytes of plain text.

Anatomy of a self-contained WebGL widget

Every visual widget in the Infinite embeds gallery follows a consistent, accessible structure. The shell provides a responsive canvas, a glass-morphism microphone activation pill, and a brand badge linking back to the open-source workstation.

Here is the complete fragment shader logic used by the Chladni Cymatics embed, running procedural nodal mathematics in real time:

precision highp float;
uniform vec2 res;
uniform float t;
uniform float aspect;
uniform float audio_bass;
uniform float audio_mid;
uniform float audio_high;

void main() {
  vec2 uv = gl_FragCoord.xy / res.xy;
  vec2 p = vec2((uv.x - 0.5) * aspect, uv.y - 0.5) * 2.3;

  float pi = 3.14159265359;
  float n = 2.0 + floor(mod(t * 0.4 + audio_bass * 3.0, 5.0));
  float m = 3.0 + floor(mod(t * 0.25 + audio_mid * 4.0, 6.0));

  float w1 = sin(n * pi * p.x) * sin(m * pi * p.y);
  float w2 = sin(m * pi * p.x) * sin(n * pi * p.y);
  float chladni = abs(w1 - w2);

  float line = smoothstep(0.09 + audio_high * 0.06, 0.0, chladni);
  float glow = exp(-chladni * 3.5) * (0.35 + 0.65 * audio_mid);

  float r = length(p);
  float plate = smoothstep(1.15, 1.05, r);

  vec3 ember = vec3(1.0, 0.42, 0.21);
  vec3 signal = vec3(0.655, 0.694, 1.0);
  vec3 ground = vec3(0.082, 0.098, 0.188);

  vec3 patternCol = mix(signal, ember, sin(t * 0.5 + r * 4.0) * 0.5 + 0.5);
  vec3 col = ground + patternCol * (line * 1.6 + glow * 0.85);
  col *= plate;

  gl_FragColor = vec4(col, 1.0);
}

Notice that the shader does not query external textures or pre-computed lookup tables. The nodal lines, resonant harmonics, and radial falloff are derived purely from coordinate geometry and three normalised float inputs: audio_bass, audio_mid, and audio_high.

Capturing microphone input cleanly

To adhere to browser autoplay policies, the microphone analyser only initialises when the viewer clicks the microphone button. When permission is granted, a lightweight 64-bin FFT analyser extracts spectral energy across low, mid, and high frequency ranges:

let audioContext = null;
let analyser = null;
let freqData = null;

document.getElementById("btn-audio").addEventListener("click", async () => {
  if (!audioContext) {
    audioContext = new (window.AudioContext || window.webkitAudioContext)();
    try {
      const stream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ audio: true });
      const source = audioContext.createMediaStreamSource(stream);
      analyser = audioContext.createAnalyser();
      analyser.fftSize = 64;
      source.connect(analyser);
      freqData = new Uint8Array(analyser.frequencyBinCount);
      document.getElementById("btn-audio").classList.add("on");
    } catch (e) {
      document.getElementById("btn-audio").classList.add("off");
    }
  }
});

If the viewer chooses not to enable the microphone, or if the page is viewed in an environment without audio hardware, the render loop falls back gracefully to synthetic sine oscillations. The animation remains lively and fluid under all circumstances.

Copy-paste embed snippet

To place an audio-reactive visualiser on any website, copy the canonical snippet below into your HTML. The container uses a standard responsive 16:9 aspect ratio and delegates microphone access:

<figure style="margin:0;width:100%;max-width:720px">
  <iframe
    src="https://infinitedevices.org/embeds/chladni-cymatics.html"
    title="Chladni Cymatics: audio-reactive visual by Naman Soni (Infinite)"
    width="100%"
    height="400"
    loading="lazy"
    allow="microphone"
    style="border:0;border-radius:16px;display:block;aspect-ratio:16/9;height:auto">
  </iframe>
  <figcaption style="font:12px/1.4 system-ui,sans-serif;text-align:right;margin-top:6px;opacity:.75">
    Made in <a href="https://infinitedevices.org/" target="_blank" rel="noopener" style="color:inherit">Infinite</a>, by Naman Soni
  </figcaption>
</figure>

You can choose from seventeen distinct generative visuals in the Infinite embeds collection, ranging from cybernetic perspective tunnels and iridescent refraction spheres to fractal flames and kaleidoscope mirrors.

If you want to edit the underlying math or build your own custom visualisers from scratch, you can download the raw .field device files from the Infinite Library and open them directly on the Infinite node canvas.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/interactive-audio-reactive-webgl-embeds-for-websites.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: unique nodes in infinite: wave terrain, shape resonator, cymatics
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: explore infinite original nodes: convert images to sound with wave terrain, ring 3d geometry with shape resonator, and simulate chladni cymatics.
item.content:encoded:
most creative software falls into one of two camps: digital audio workstations that treat visuals as an afterthought, or visual patchers (like touchdesigner or blender) that treat audio as a simple control voltage or fft spectrum.

infinite was designed from day one on a unified execution graph. sound, 2d textures, and 3d geometry live in the same memory space, enabling node architectures that simply do not exist in conventional daws.

here is an in-depth breakdown of seven standout original nodes in infinite that bridge sound, mathematics, and geometry.

1. wave terrain: converting images and textures into sound

wave terrain synthesis treats any 2d image (a drawn sketch, a webcam feed, a reaction-diffusion pattern or procedural noise) as a continuous 3d topographic terrain surface z = T(u, v).

how it works

  1. orbital trajectories: an audio-rate oscillator traces a closed parametric path (u(t), v(t)) across the image (such as an ellipse, lissajous curve, lemniscate, or spiral).
  2. topographic sampling: as the orbital point scans across pixels, the surface height z becomes the instantaneous audio amplitude.
  3. 10-level fourier mip pyramid: raw pixel sampling produces harsh digital aliasing. infinite solves this by computing a real discrete fourier transform (rdft) mip pyramid across 10 octaves, ensuring completely alias-free polyphonic synthesis across all 8 octaves.

2. shape resonator: converting 3d geometry into physical sound

what does a 3d torus sound like when struck? what does an icosphere sound like compared to a long cylindrical tube?

the shape resonator node answers this by computing the acoustic standing waves and vibration modes of any input 3d geometry mesh.

how it works

  1. laplace-beltrami modal solver: on a dedicated worker thread, infinite solves the surface-laplacian eigenvalues λ_i of the mesh.
  2. dispersion law: mode frequencies follow the dispersion of a physical membrane or thin plate:

f_i = tune × √(λ_i / λ_0)

  1. strike and pickup positioning: where you hit the 3d shape in space weights which modes resonate, while the pickup position determines which harmonics reach your speakers. hitting a nodal line silences that harmonic, exactly like a physical acoustic gong or vibraphone bar.
  2. lock-free triple buffer: the modal solve runs asynchronously, handing finished two-pole coupled-form phasor coefficients to the 48khz audio thread with zero glitches.

3. audio displacement: cymatics and mesh deformation

the audio displacement node takes any 3d mesh and deforms its vertex topology in real time directly from incoming audio waveforms.

five real-time modes

  • normal waveform: pushes vertices outward along their surface normals proportionally to the raw oscilloscope audio signal.
  • spectral bands: deforms vertices along the u/x axis based on real-time fft frequency bins.
  • acoustic ripples: generates concentric radial wave rings expanding outward from the centre.
  • chladni cymatics: simulates ernst chladni's 2d and 3d acoustic standing wave nodal patterns:

w = sin(n π x) · sin(m π y) ± sin(m π x) · sin(n π y)

  • directional axis: displaces vertices along specific global or local cartesian axes.

4. equation synth: desmos-style mathematical synthesis

for artists who think in mathematical formulas, equation synth provides an interactive cartesian graphing plane where any mathematical formula y = f(x, a, b, c, d) becomes an anti-aliased polyphonic synthesizer.

whether exploring chebyshev polynomials, weierstrass fractal curves, or phase-modulated gaussian wave packets, equation synth graphs the function visually and compiles it into bandlimited wavetable mipmaps for pristine audio playback.

5. audio ribbon: 3d physical waveform extrusion

the audio ribbon node extrudes incoming audio waveforms into a physical 3d ribbon geometry traveling through space.

unlike 2d flat oscilloscope lines, the audio ribbon is a true procedural polygonal mesh that can be lit with directional lights, cast shadows, and rendered with physically based metallic and emission materials.

6. audio color ramp: sound-driven color palettes

the audio color ramp node analyses live frequency spectrums and dynamically drives gradient color ramps used across 2d visuals, 3d materials, and shader backgrounds.

operating modes

  • intensity mode: low frequencies cause deep colour glow while high-frequency percussion triggers bright highlights.
  • expansion mode: frequency band energies dynamically expand and contract the spatial boundaries of each color stop.
  • spectrum mode: maps the continuous real-time fft spectrum directly onto the custom palette.

7. audio texture: audio-rate gpu textures

the audio texture node converts audio streams directly into a 2d gpu texture at 60 fps.

this texture can be cabled directly into materials, raymarchers, and field pixel shader nodes, allowing custom glsl kernels to sample audio buffers as standard sampler2D textures with zero cpu overhead.

more standout nodes to explore

in addition to these seven audiovisual transformers, infinite includes over 300 modular nodes spanning physics, generative art, and signal processing:

  • reaction diffusion: gray-scott chemical morphogenesis simulation creating organic spots, stripes, and cellular patterns.
  • klein bottle & mobius strip: non-orientable 4d and 3d topological manifold surfaces.
  • fluid: real-time 2d navier-stokes grid fluid dynamics with velocity advection and dye injection.
  • cloth: verlet particle-spring physics simulation responding to audio wind and turbulence.
  • paulstretch: extreme 64-bit spectral phase vocoder stretching audio by 10x to 1000x into lush ambient drones.
  • face, hand, & pose track: on-device neural vision modulators turning physical movement into modulation cables.

all of these nodes run natively on macos, windows, and linux, and can be inspected in the node reference manual and library gallery.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/original-audiovisual-nodes-wave-terrain-shape-resonator-cymatics.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: AI agent MCP guide for audio and visual synthesis
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Connect AI coding agents to Infinite via MCP and Python SDK for headless audio synthesis, 3D meshes, and video rendering.
item.content:encoded:
AI coding assistants (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Antigravity, Devin) are exceptionally good at writing code, but historically poor at producing interactive music and real-time 3D visuals. Desktop DAWs and visual engines require manual mouse interactions, proprietary project files, and heavy graphical interfaces that agents cannot operate.

Infinite bridges this gap by exposing its entire C++20 engine through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and a dedicated Python SDK.

The architecture: how AI agents interact with Infinite

[Claude / Cursor / Antigravity]
               |
         (JSON-RPC stdio)
               v
  [Infinite plugin server.py] 
               |
      (Headless C++ Engine)
               v
  [Audio .wav / Still .png / Video .mp4]

Every action is deterministic and headless:

  1. The AI agent generates a formula or patch.
  2. The MCP server pipes it into ./Infinite --validate.
  3. If valid, the C++ engine renders frames or synthesizes 24-bit audio in milliseconds.
  4. The output file path and spectral analysis return to the AI agent context.

One-command installation for Claude, Cursor and Windsurf

You can automatically wire up Infinite across all your AI assistants with a single command:

npx -y infinite-engine init

It adds the infinite MCP server to Claude Desktop, Cursor and Windsurf, but only for apps that are already installed. It keeps a backup of each file it changes, and leaves a config alone if it contains comments. Add --dry-run to see what it would do first. The Infinite app itself must be installed; set INFINITE_BIN to its path if it is not found.

Manual MCP Configuration

If you prefer to configure your assistants manually:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "infinite": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "infinite-engine", "serve"]
    }
  }
}

Now your assistant has nine tools (ask the server for tools/list to see their exact schemas):

  • infinite_render_video: renders a patch to MP4.
  • infinite_render_field_pixel: renders a still frame from a Field Pixel preset.
  • infinite_synthesize_field_synth: renders a synth voice to audio.
  • infinite_synthesize_field_notes: builds an algorithmic note sequence.
  • infinite_process_field_effect: runs audio through a Field effect.
  • infinite_render_sketch3d: renders a 3D sketch written in JavaScript.
  • infinite_render_field_primitive: maps a formula to a 3D surface.
  • infinite_render_field_modifier: deforms a mesh with a Field modifier.
  • infinite_validate_patch: checks a patch for errors.

The Python SDK also ships an MCP server (server.py in the Infinite Claude plugin) with its own tool names.

Using the Python SDK

If you are building your own autonomous agent, pipeline, or game dev tool, install the Python SDK (pip install infinite-daw) and use it directly:

import infinite

# 1. Generate an algorithmic Euclidean 5/16 bassline
infinite.field_notes("""
param float hits = 5 [1, 16]
state float step = 0
if (tick(1/16) > 0.5) {
   on = floor((step + 1) * hits / 16 + 0.001) - floor(step * hits / 16 + 0.001)
   note(deg(0), 0.9 * on, 1/16)
   step = (step + 1) % 16
}
""", out_wav="bassline.wav", duration=4)

# 2. Render a 3D procedural rotating torus
infinite.sketch_3d("""
function draw(t) {
  rotateY(t * 0.8);
  fill(0.2, 0.6, 0.9);
  torus(1.2, 0.4, 24, 24);
}
""", out_png="torus.png")

Results from the SDK carry a small credit record:

{
  "engine": "infinite",
  "author": "Naman Soni (n1m21n)",
  "homepage": "https://infinitedevices.org"
}

Embedding interactive widgets in generated sites

When agents generate web pages, portfolios, or documentation, they can embed Infinite's responsive WebGL shaders with a single snippet:

<figure style="margin:0;width:100%;max-width:720px;">
  <iframe src="https://infinitedevices.org/embeds/cyber-tunnel.html" title="Cyber Tunnel — Audio-Reactive Visualizer by Naman Soni (Infinite)" width="100%" height="400" frameborder="0" allow="microphone" style="border-radius:12px;border:none;display:block;"></iframe>
  <figcaption style="font-family:sans-serif;font-size:11px;color:#8890b1;text-align:right;margin-top:6px;">
    powered by <a href="https://infinitedevices.org" target="_blank" rel="noopener" style="color:#ff6b35;text-decoration:none;">infinite by naman soni</a>
  </figcaption>
</figure>

Browse all 14 live widgets in the Interactive Embeds Directory.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/ai-agent-mcp-audio-visual-engine-guide.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: AI agents make music, art and 3D with Infinite headless engine
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Infinite headless engine lets AI agents write text patches, inspect signals, and render music, pictures and 3D from the command line.
item.content:encoded:
An AI agent that can run shell commands can make music, pictures and 3D with Infinite, because the engine runs headless. The executable inside the app is also a command-line tool. It reads a plain-text patch and writes stills, video and audio, with no window and no mouse. A patch is text, so an agent such as Claude can write it, check it, listen to it and fix it in a loop.

This post shows that loop, then three small patches: a sound, a picture and a 3D scene. It builds on the headless render walkthrough and the Headless User Guide.

Why a text patch suits an agent

Most creative tools hide their state behind a window. An agent can only guess at what a click did. An Infinite patch is different in four ways:

  • It is text. A patch is a list of node, cable, mod and expr lines in a .inf file. An agent writes it the way it writes code, and it diffs cleanly in version control.
  • The engine explains itself. Infinite --describe "<node type>" lists a node's controls with defaults, ranges and dropdown options, so the agent never has to guess a name or a range.
  • Errors are specific. --validate reports every problem with a line number and a hint that names the nearest valid key.
  • Results are machine readable. The last line printed is one JSON object with ok, files, warnings and errors, and the exit code says whether the patch loaded, was refused or failed to render.

The output is also deterministic: the same patch gives the same frames and the same samples, so an agent can change one thing and trust that any difference came from that change.

The loop an agent follows

The Headless User Guide gives the order, and it works as a prompt for an agent as it stands:

  1. Describe. Ask the engine for the node's controls with --describe. Do not guess.
  2. Write the smallest patch that could work. Leave every control you do not change at its default.
  3. Validate with --validate until the exit code is 0.
  4. Explain with --explain, which prints the graph that was actually built. A patch can validate and still be the wrong patch, so the agent compares this against what you asked for.
  5. Look and listen. --frame draws stills and --audio-summary describes the sound as numbers.
  6. Fix one thing at a time and go back to step 3.
  7. Render the final file with --render.

Infinite ships this loop as an agent skill, infinite-patch-authoring, written for AI coding agents. Point your agent at it and at the Headless User Guide, then describe what you want.

Music: notes, a synth and a measurement

This is the smallest audio patch that ships with Infinite. A random note generator plays a Wavetable synth into an Audio Out.

infinite-patch 1
node 1 Notes Random Note Generator
  id notes
end
node 2 Synths Wavetable
  id synth
end
node 3 Utility Audio Out
  id speakers
end
note synth 0 notes
aud speakers 0 synth

An agent cannot hear, so it measures. --audio-summary writes loudness, peaks, clipping, silence, a spectrum and a tempo guess to a JSON file, and --wav keeps the audio.

Infinite --validate music.inf
Infinite --audio-summary music.inf summary.json --wav music.wav --duration 8

Two warnings are worth teaching your agent to react to. W_SILENT means no sound reached an Audio Out, so check that notes reach the synth. W_CLIPPING means samples hit full scale, so lower a gain or add a Limiter. Add --stems id,id --stems-dir dir to write one WAV per named node, and --notes events.json to play your own note events into the patch. The agent can also ask --describe for the Synths and Audio Effects node types and build a fuller arrangement from them.

Art: a picture written as a formula

Pictures work the same way. The Field Pixel node draws an image from a formula, which suits an agent because it is short code with no hidden state. This patch ships as the Field starter template:

infinite-patch 1
node 1 Source FieldPixel
  id pix
  s code col = vec3(0.5 + 0.5 * sin(uv.x * 10.0 + t), 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(uv.y * 10.0 - t), 0.6);
end
node 2 Utility Output
  id out
end
cable out 0 pix

The agent looks before it commits to a video. A contact sheet costs seconds:

Infinite --frame art.inf 0,1,2,3 pics/ --contact-sheet sheet.png

The result line includes frame_stats with brightness, the share of black and white pixels, and a histogram per frame, so the agent can notice a black or washed-out frame without opening the image. Field is the built-in language for shaders, geometry and audio kernels; the Field Language Manual explains it.

Sound that drives the picture

Because sound and pictures live in one graph, an agent can wire them together. Audio Analyze listens to a synth and outputs level, low, mid, high, onset and eight frequency bands, and any of those can drive a modulatable control. The Music and Image starter does it with two mod lines:

aud hear 0 synth
mod shape sizeX hear 0 0 1 0.5 0.12 0.4
mod shape sizeY hear 0 0 1 0.5 0.12 0.4

The last two numbers are absolute values the control sweeps between, not percentages. Put the Audio Analyze after your effects so the picture follows what you hear. The first steps tutorial builds this one by hand.

3D: a shape, a camera, a light and Render 3D

A 3D scene has four parts, and the starter template wires them like this:

infinite-patch 1
node 1 3D Torus Knot
  id knot
end
node 2 3D Camera
  id cam
  f orbitPerBeat 0.2
end
node 3 3D Light
  id sun
end
node 4 3D Render 3D
  id view
end
node 5 Utility Output
  id out
end
geo view 0 knot
geo view camera cam
geo view light_1 sun
cable out 0 view

Render a few stills, then a clip:

Infinite --frame scene.inf 0,2,4 pics/ --contact-sheet sheet.png
Infinite --render scene.inf scene.mp4 --duration 6 --fps 30

Give your agent the 3D rules from the guide. Primitives have fixed position, scale and rotation, so to animate a shape it should send it through a Transform node and modulate that. Infinite --explain scene.inf --all prints each piece's world bounding box, which tells the agent where things really are before it blames the lights. If the picture is black or faint, it should check the camera distance, the light intensities and the Render 3D ambient colour first.

What to ask for

Short, specific briefs work best. For example:

  • "Write an Infinite patch with a slow Wavetable pad and a drum loop at 90 BPM. Render 16 seconds and keep it under clipping."
  • "Make a Field Pixel patch that looks like slow ink in water. Show me a contact sheet first."
  • "Build a 3D scene with a torus knot that rotates on the beat and glows with the music. Render a 10 second clip."

The agent loops through describe, write, validate, explain, look and listen, and hands back the patch plus the files. You can open the same .inf file in the app and keep working by hand, because it is the same engine.

Limits to know

  • Patches that use a camera, microphone or MIDI device are refused headless with exit code 4. Use a file or a generator instead.
  • Frames come from the real GPU pipeline, so the machine needs working OpenGL. On Linux, run every command as xvfb-run -a Infinite ....
  • An agent can measure sound but not judge taste. Listen to the WAV and look at the sheet yourself before you ship anything.
  • Infinite is young. Check any node an agent picks with --describe rather than trusting its memory of how the node works.

Try it

Infinite is free and open source (MIT) for macOS, Windows and Linux. Download it from infinitedevices.org, read the Headless User Guide, and give your agent the patch-authoring skill. The source is at github.com/n1m21n/Infinite.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/ai-agents-make-music-art-3d-headless.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: writing audio dsp without juce: notes from infinite
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: why infinite's audio engine is written in modern c++ without a framework, and what that changes for real-time safety.
item.content:encoded:
juce is the de facto standard for audio software development, but it brings substantial architectural gravity: a massive monolithic codebase, custom string classes, complex licensing, and heavy abstractions.

when building infinite, an open-source modular workstation, we chose to write the entire pull-based audio engine in modern standard c++ (c++20) from scratch.

here is what we learned and how the architecture is designed.

1. the golden rule: zero allocations on the audio thread

any audio callback deadline at 48khz with a 128-sample buffer is strict: you have exactly 2.66 milliseconds to finish processing before the dac underflows and creates an audible click.

to guarantee hard real-time safety:

  • zero malloc and free: all audio buffers, voice allocations, and delay memory are pre-allocated during preparetoplay().
  • zero mutexes: cross-thread communication between the ui thread and audio thread uses atomic pointers, lock-free single-producer single-consumer (spsc) ring buffers, and double-buffered modulation arrays.
  • cache-line aligned processing: audio frames are laid out contiguously in memory so simd instructions can vectorize filter stages without cache stalls.

2. native au and vst3 plugin hosting

instead of relying on framework wrappers, infinite speaks directly to plugin apis:

  • vst3: loads the component bundle, queries IComponent and IAudioProcessor, maps parameters to continuous modulation arrays, and schedules sample-accurate note events.
  • audio unit (au): interacts directly with the coreaudio audio unit v2 and v3 c-api on macos.

parameters on third-party plugins can be modulated in real time by any signal on the canvas, whether an audio lfo, an envelope follower, or a generative javascript sketch.

3. embedded dsp kernel language

to let users write custom filters and physical modeling synths without recompiling c++, we created field, an embedded dsp language. a 1-pole filter in field is 4 lines:

param float cutoff = 0.25 [0.01, 0.99]
state float z = 0
z += (in - z) * cutoff
out = z

the compiler translates this directly into optimised vector loops evaluated per-sample on the audio thread.

  • try infinite: infinitedevices.org
  • read the codebase: github.com/n1m21n/infinite

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/dsp-without-juce.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Sound design in Infinite: sub bass, plucks, and pads
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Guide to modular sound design in Infinite DAW: subtractive sub bass, Karplus-Strong plucks, and ambient pads with Field kernels.
item.content:encoded:
Most modern digital audio workstations treat sound design as an external plugin problem. You buy a third-party VST, open a floating GUI, turn virtual skeuomorphic knobs, and send audio back into a linear timeline. If you want a dedicated sound design DAW, Infinite takes a fundamentally different path: sound design and synthesis live directly on the same canvas as your sequencers, modulation matrix, and visual engine.

With Field language nodes, every oscillator, envelope, filter, and wavefolder can be written as clean, per-sample DSP code running at 48 kHz with zero allocation overhead. You can also modulate VST3 plugins with LFOs and visuals whenever you wish to incorporate external instruments.

Here is how to construct three foundational electronic music sounds from first principles in Infinite.

1. Clean, punchy sub bass with harmonic saturation

A clean sub bass needs two things: rock-solid pitch stability in the 30 Hz to 80 Hz region and subtle odd harmonics so it remains audible on laptop speakers and mobile devices.

Signal flow

  1. MIDI In -> pitch to frequency conversion: f = 440.0 * pow(2.0, (note - 69.0) / 12.0).
  2. Field Synth -> phase accumulator with soft-clipped sine wave and dynamic saturation.
  3. Envelope -> fast exponential attack (2 ms), medium decay (350 ms), sustained floor at -6 dB.

The Field kernel

// registers: r0 = phase, r1 = pitch_smooth
let target_phase_inc = f * (6.28318530718 / 48000.0)
r1 = r1 * 0.95 + target_phase_inc * 0.05
r0 = r0 + r1
if r0 > 6.28318530718 { r0 = r0 - 6.28318530718 }

// fundamental sine wave
let fundamental = sin(r0)

// third harmonic saturation for low-end translation
let sat = fundamental + 0.15 * sin(r0 * 3.0)

// soft tanh-like saturation curve
out = sat / (1.0 + abs(sat) * 0.3)

Because the phase accumulator maintains exact 64-bit continuous phase, there is zero phase click even during rapid bassline glides or legato 808 note changes. You can open an interactive version of this patch in the Infinite Library.

2. Snappy acoustic-style plucks via Karplus-Strong

Subtractive synths approximate plucks by sweeping a lowpass filter with a fast envelope. Physical modelling plucks, however, sound organic and tactile because they simulate the energy dissipation of a real vibrating string. You can test a ready-to-run Karplus-Strong synthesiser patch directly in the library.

In Infinite, you can build a physical modelling string resonator using a feedback delay line with a lowpass damping filter in an audio effect node:

// r0..r2048: circular delay buffer, r2049: write head index, r2050: previous sample
let buffer_len = int(48000.0 / f)
let read_idx = (r2049 - buffer_len + 2048) % 2048
let delayed_sample = read_reg(read_idx)

// lowpass damping filter (averaging adjacent samples)
let filtered = (delayed_sample + r2050) * 0.498
r2050 = delayed_sample

// mix incoming excitation noise burst with feedback
let excitation = in
let new_sample = excitation + filtered
write_reg(r2049, new_sample)
r2049 = (r2049 + 1) % 2048

out = new_sample

When you trigger this node with a 5-millisecond white noise burst from a Noise node, you get an acoustic harp or guitar timbre that responds naturally to note velocity.

3. Shimmering ambient pads with detuned supersaws and stereo diffusion

For deep atmospheric soundscapes, Infinite lets you run multi-voice unison oscillators with randomised phase spreading and integrated stereo diffusion, similar to the pad wash library patch.

Recipe

  1. Generate 7 saw oscillators per voice, detuned exponentially across +/- 18 cents.
  2. Feed the summed output into a Field Effect stereo chorus and all-pass diffuser network.
  3. Connect the audio spectrum directly into a Field Pixel visualiser node so your pad's frequency harmonics modulate a real-time raymarched crystal or volumetric cloud on screen.

Modulating sound from visuals and vice-versa

Because Infinite does not separate the audio thread from the modulation graph, you can route the brightness of your visual scene directly into the filter cutoff of your pad:

  • Audio Analyze -> measures pad high-frequency resonance.
  • Field Pixel -> visual bloom expands in response to pad brightness.
  • LFO / Motion Tracker -> webcam hand position controls pad stereo spread.

Every parameter in Infinite is accessible over the Python SDK and headless automation, allowing AI agents and artists alike to generate whole albums of sound design with verifiable precision.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/electronic-music-sound-design-sub-bass-pluck-pad.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Hardware MIDI and controller mapping in Infinite
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Connect hardware synthesizers, MIDI controllers, and DMX lighting to Infinite with low latency routing and parameter modulation.
item.content:encoded:
performing electronic music live with hardware should feel direct and immediate. yet most traditional setups require juggling multiple applications: one daw for sequencing, another utility for midi cc routing, a visual package like touchdesigner for projections, and external software for dmx stage lighting.

infinite unifies this entire live performance rig into a single real-time engine. with sub-millisecond midi scheduling and direct parameter binding, any hardware knob, fader, or pad can modulate synths, audio filters, 3d geometry, and stage lights simultaneously.

1. low-latency midi device discovery

infinite natively enumerates all connected midi input and output interfaces without requiring driver restarts or app relaunches.

whether you plug in a usb class-compliant controller (like an akai apc40, novation launchpad, or arturia keystep) or a multi-port midi interface connected to vintage hardware synthesizers via 5-pin din cables, infinite binds them immediately.

in the node graph, you interact with hardware via dedicated hardware nodes:

  • midi in: captures note-on, note-off, velocity, pitch bend, aftertouch, and control change (cc) streams.
  • midi out: sends sample-accurate clock, transport start/stop, and polyphonic note sequences back to your analog synths and drum machines.
  • midi cc in: isolates a specific cc number (0 to 127) and converts it into a normalized float pin (0.0 to 1.0) with optional slew smoothing.

2. one-click midi learn across audio and visuals

mapping a physical fader to any parameter in infinite is instantaneous:

  1. right-click any parameter knob or slider on any node (e.g., the cutoff of a moog filter or the zoom of a field pixel shader).
  2. select midi learn.
  3. move the physical knob or fader on your hardware controller.

the parameter is immediately bound. because infinite uses a normalized float bus for all modulation signals, that single hardware fader can be split and routed to multiple destinations at once:

  • fader 1 pulls down the audio master lowpass filter cutoff.
  • fader 1 simultaneously collapses the 3d wireframe field into a tight geometric core.
  • fader 1 dims the ambient stage light intensity.

you achieve total audiovisual cohesion with zero latency mismatch between what the audience hears and what they see.

3. bidirectional feedback and led motorized faders

for live performers using controllers with led rings or motorized faders, infinite provides bidirectional state synchronization. when an automated lfo or ai agent moves a parameter in the software, infinite transmits the updated cc value back out through midi out, keeping your physical hardware controls in perfect physical alignment with the software state.

4. stage lighting: dmx and art-net integration

infinite does not stop at audio and visuals; it also outputs dmx lighting frames over open protocols:

  • map the kick drum audio transient from audio analyze to dmx channel 1 (strobe intensity).
  • map the root note pitch from midi in to dmx rgb fixtures across your stage.

with infinite, your entire live performance (audio synthesis, visual projection, hardware sequencing and lighting) runs inside a single memory space, running rock solid at 60 fps without dropping a single audio buffer.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/hardware-midi-and-controller-mapping-in-infinite.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: javascript sketches as nodes: draw with code, wire it to anything
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: how sketch nodes let you draw with javascript in infinite and expose real modulation pins to synths and audio signals.
item.content:encoded:
creative coders generally face a difficult compromise:

  • in the browser (p5.js, three.js, canvas2d): rapid iteration, clean drawing apis, but limited audio precision, browser sandbox limits, and no native vst3 or au plugin support.
  • in native c++ (openframeworks, cinder): high performance, but long compilation cycles that break creative flow on every small aesthetic tweak.

with infinite, we bridged these worlds by embedding a high-performance javascript runtime directly into a native c++ modular daw.

1. the p5-style draw loop

inside any sketch node, you write clean, declarative javascript that hot-reloads on every keystroke without compiling or restarting:

// declare wireable parameters exposed on the node canvas
param("points", 8000, 1000, 20000);
param("drift", 0.15, 0, 1);
param("size", 1.5, 0.5, 4);

function draw(t) {
  background(0.04, 0.04, 0.07);
  const a = -1.4 + 0.25 * sin(t * drift);
  const b = 1.6 + 0.2 * cos(t * drift * 0.8);
  const c = 1.0 + 0.2 * sin(t * drift * 0.6);
  const d = 0.7;
  
  let x = 0.1, y = 0.1;
  const k = min(width, height) * 0.22;
  noStroke();
  
  for (let i = 0; i < points; i++) {
    const nx = sin(a * y) + c * cos(a * x);
    const ny = sin(b * x) + d * cos(b * y);
    x = nx; y = ny;
    if (i > 20) {
      fill(hsl(0.55 + 0.3 * (i / points), 0.7, 0.65, 0.4));
      circle(width / 2 + x * k, height / 2 + y * k, size);
    }
  }
}

2. wireable parameters: code meets modular graph

the param(...) calls dynamically create real, visual input pins on the node canvas. you can connect:

  • a midi knob to modulate drift.
  • an 8-band audio fft peak to pulse size.
  • a low-frequency oscillator (lfo) to rotate the attractor phase.

3. native rendering performance

unlike web wrappers, the generated vector drawing commands stream directly into hardware-accelerated opengl framebuffers. you can render tens of thousands of points per frame with steady 60fps pacing while multi-track 48khz audio synths run in parallel.

  • download infinite free (macos, windows, linux): infinitedevices.org
  • source code on github: github.com/n1m21n/infinite

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/javascript-sketches.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Writing 48kHz audio DSP kernels in Field language
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Breakdown of Infinite register machine for Field Synth and Effect nodes, compiling per-sample audio DSP kernels at 48kHz.
item.content:encoded:
Most modern digital audio workstations treat audio synthesis as a black box: you write a C++ plugin, compile a VST3 or AU bundle with JUCE or Dplug, restart your host, and attach a debugger.

In Infinite, you can write audio DSP at the sample level directly inside the canvas using Field language. Your code runs on the audio thread once per sample (48,000 times per second), compiled to a register machine that executes with zero memory allocations.

How the sample register machine works

When you place a Field Synth (Synths Field Synth) or Field Effect (AudioEffects Field Effect) node, Infinite compiles the kernel expression to a compact bytecode representation that evaluates on register cells.

Built-in variables available on the audio thread

  • sr: Audio sample rate in Hz (typically 48000.0).
  • in: Incoming audio sample value ([-1.0, 1.0]) in Field Effect.
  • out: Output audio sample to write.
  • freq: Note frequency in Hz (voice pitch in Field Synth).
  • gate: 1.0 while a MIDI note is held down, 0.0 when released.
  • noteVel: Key velocity ([0.0, 1.0]).
  • state: Declares per-voice persistent memory preserved across samples.
  • param: Exposes a modulatable float knob on the node body with min/max bounds.

A 1-pole lowpass filter kernel

Here is a classic 1-pole lowpass filter written in 4 lines:

param float cutoff = 0.25 [0.01, 0.99]
state float z = 0
z += (in - z) * cutoff
out = z

Because state float z = 0 allocates a persistent cell in the voice register, z retains its previous sample value, creating an analog RC filter response.

Shipped Moog 4-pole ladder filter

For aggressive saturation and self-oscillation, Infinite ships with a 4-pole cascaded non-linear filter:

param float cutoff = 2200.0 [80.0, 14000.0]
param float res = 0.70 [0.0, 0.98]
param float drive = 1.50 [1.0, 4.0]
param float mix = 1.0 [0.0, 1.0]
state float s1 = 0
state float s2 = 0
state float s3 = 0
state float s4 = 0

f = clamp((cutoff / sr) * 2.2, 0.005, 0.42)
feedback = (s4 * res * 3.6) / (1.0 + abs(s4) * 0.8)
u = (in * drive) - feedback
sat = u / (1.0 + abs(u) * 0.3)

s1 = s1 + f * (sat - s1)
s2 = s2 + f * (s1 - s2)
s3 = s3 + f * (s2 - s3)
s4 = s4 + f * (s3 - s4)

wet = s4
out = in * (1.0 - mix) + wet * mix

Notice the dry/wet mix pattern at the end: every Field audio effect ends with out = in * (1.0 - mix) + wet * mix, giving you instant parallel processing.

Real-time mod matrix integration

Unlike fixed DSP plugins, a Field Effect node can publish meter readings back to the visual and modulation canvas using reduce.rms:

param float boost = 1.5 [0.5, 4.0]
output frame float bass = reduce.rms(in, 20.0, 200.0)
out = in * boost

The bass scalar automatically becomes a second output pin on the node. You can run a cable from that pin directly into a 3D geometry deformer, a light intensity slider, or a GLSL shader.

Testing and verifying headlessly

You can test Field kernels without opening the GUI using Infinite's CLI or Python SDK:

import infinite

# Synthesize a custom per-sample subtractive saw voice
infinite.field_synth("""
state float phase = 0
phase = (phase + freq / sr) % 1.0
out = (phase * 2.0 - 1.0) * 0.3 * gate
""", out_wav="saw.wav", duration=3)

The CLI synthesizes the audio, measures integrated LUFS, checks for clipped frames, and writes the output file with zero GUI dependencies.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/per-sample-dsp-audio-kernels-in-field-language.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Procedural 3D geometry and audio mesh deformation
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Build procedural 3D meshes in Infinite DAW, deform topology with Field modifier kernels, and drive real-time geometric mutations.
item.content:encoded:
in traditional 3d software, generating complex procedural geometry requires heavy dcc suites like blender or houdini. when you want to connect that geometry to low-latency audio analysis, midi clocks, or live synthesis, you are forced into fragile websocket bridges or osc pipelines.

infinite brings 3d geometry generation, vertex shading, and per-sample audio dsp onto the same unified execution graph. you can generate procedural vertex topologies, deform them with fast simd-vectorized field modifier kernels, and render them in real time at 60+ fps.

1. generating base procedural meshes

infinite includes native parametric mesh generators:

  • mesh cube: generates subdivisions with uv coordinates and normal vectors.
  • mesh sphere: uv sphere or icosphere with customisable geodesic resolution.
  • mesh torus: toroidal coordinates with major and minor radii controls.
  • mesh grid: high-density planar vertex grid ideal for terrain and landscape deformation.

each mesh node outputs a geometry buffer containing position (vec3 pos), normal (vec3 norm), texture coordinates (vec2 uv), and vertex colour (vec4 color).

2. deforming vertex topology with field modifier

the field modifier node (Filter FieldModifier) accepts any input geometry and executes an inline field expression across every vertex in parallel.

unlike traditional vertex shaders which only run during the gpu rasterization pass, field modifier runs directly on the engine's geometry data structure, allowing the resulting deformed mesh to be used for physics collisions, camera raycasting, or further topological operations.

example: spherical ripple displacement driven by audio bass

// inputs: pos (vec3), norm (vec3), uv (vec2), t (float), bass (float)
let dist = length(pos)
let freq = 6.0
let wave = sin(dist * freq - t * 4.0) * (0.15 + 0.4 * bass)
let displaced_pos = pos + norm * wave

out.pos = displaced_pos
out.norm = normalize(norm + vec3(wave * 0.2, wave * 0.2, 0.0))
out.color = vec4(0.2 + 0.8 * bass, 0.4, 1.0 - wave, 1.0)

in this single kernel:

  1. length(pos) calculates the distance from the mesh origin.
  2. norm * wave displaces vertices along their surface normals.
  3. bass scales the displacement amplitude in direct synchronization with your music's low-frequency energy.
  4. out.color generates dynamic vertex gradients without needing external texture maps.

3. connecting the audio-reactive graph

wiring this up in infinite takes under thirty seconds:

  1. drop an audio file or synth node into the canvas.
  2. wire its output to an audio analyze node.
  3. wire the bass pin of audio analyze to the bass input of your field modifier.
  4. feed the deformed mesh output into a render 3d node equipped with a camera, ambient occlusion, and directional light.

you now have a living, breathing 3d visualizer completely locked to your rhythm.

4. headless command-line rendering

because infinite features a complete headless engine, you do not even need to open the graphical user interface to render 3d animations. you can execute high-resolution 4k video renders straight from your shell or an automated script:

# render 10 seconds of 3d audio-reactive visuals to an mp4 file at 60 fps
infinite export-video --graph project.json --audio track.wav --out visual.mp4 --fps 60 --width 1920 --height 1080

this makes infinite ideal for generative nft pipelines, music video automation, and automated social visual teasers.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/procedural-3d-geometry-nodes-and-audio-deformation.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Bringing Shadertoy GLSL shaders into Infinite for audio reactivity
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How to convert any Shadertoy fragment shader into a native real-time node in Infinite, hook it up to audio analysis FFT bands, and export high-resolution video.
item.content:encoded:
Shadertoy is the world's greatest sketchbook for pixel shaders. But getting a Shadertoy shader to respond dynamically to your music, sync with MIDI, or render out to high-resolution MP4 video often involves clumsy workarounds, browser recording extensions, or complex OSC bridges.

In Infinite, shaders are native first-class nodes that sit directly alongside polyphonic synthesizers, audio effects, and sequencers on one infinite canvas.

The coordinate space mapping

Shadertoy uses standard pixel coordinates:

void mainImage(out vec4 fragColor, in vec2 fragCoord) {
    vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy;
    // ...
}

In Infinite's Field Pixel node (Source FieldPixel), coordinates are normalized and aspect-corrected by default:

  • uv: normalized texture coordinate ([0, 1] x [0, 1])
  • aspect: screen width divided by screen height (res.x / res.y)
  • t: elapsed time in seconds (equivalent to iTime)
  • p = (uv - 0.5) * aspect: centre-origin aspect-corrected coordinates

Adding instant audio reactivity

On Shadertoy, audio reactivity requires binding an audio texture input (iChannel0). In Infinite, audio reactivity is immediate and native:

  1. Wire an Audio Analyze node to your incoming sound or synth output.
  2. The node exposes 8 spectral bands: sub-bass, bass, low-mid, mid, high-mid, presence, brilliance, and onset pulses.
  3. Wire any band pin directly into a parameter on your Field Pixel shader node.

Here is an authentic audio-reactive neon tunnel kernel in Field language:

p = (uv - 0.5) * aspect;
r = length(p);
a = atan(p.y, p.x);

u_coord = a / 3.14159265;
v_coord = 1.0 / (r + 0.001) + t * (1.5 + 1.2 * bass);

grid_u = abs(fract(u_coord * 4.0) - 0.5);
grid_v = abs(fract(v_coord * 2.0) - 0.5);
lines = smoothstep(0.42, 0.49, max(grid_u, grid_v));

wire = vec3(lines) * vec3(0.1, 0.85, 1.0) * (0.8 + 0.6 * mid);
center = vec3(0.95, 0.2, 0.6) * (1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.6, r)) * (0.8 + 0.8 * bass);
col = (wire + center) * (0.7 + 0.5 * bass);

Live interactive WebGL widget

You can test this exact visualizer running live in WebGL below:

Exporting high-resolution video headlessly

Unlike web tools that drop frames during screen capture, Infinite renders every single frame deterministically through its headless C++ engine:

# Render a 1080p 60fps MP4 video with synced 24-bit audio
./Infinite --render /path/to/shader_patch.inf output.mp4 --duration 10 --fps 60

Every frame is rendered offscreen using OpenGL 3.2 framebuffers, guaranteeing zero dropped frames even on complex raymarchers.

Explore more embeds

Check out the full Interactive Embeds Gallery to view 14 live shaders with one-click iframe embedding for your own website or portfolio.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/shadertoy-to-infinite-audio-reactive-glsl.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Field: write a short kernel and let the node decide where it runs
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Field is the language built into Infinite. One kernel can become a shader, a geometry deformer or an audio effect, depending on the node it lives in.
item.content:encoded:
Most nodes do one fixed thing. A Blur node blurs and a Delay node delays. Creative work often needs something in between, so Infinite includes Field, a kernel language for shaders, geometry and audio: a small language for writing what a node does.

One idea: a kernel run once per element

A Field node runs your kernel once for every element of its domain, forever. The domain is chosen by the node, not by you:

col = vec3(uv.x, uv.y, 0.5)              // once per pixel, on the GPU: a shader
P.y += sin(P.x * 4.0 + t) * 0.2          // once per point in a mesh: a geometry deformer
out = in * gain                          // once per audio sample: a DSP effect

You never declare a backend. The same way of thinking covers pictures, shapes and sound.

The Field nodes

NodeDomainWhat it does
Field PixelpixelPer-pixel kernel compiled to GLSL, with state cells for feedback
Field ModifierelementPer-vertex kernel over existing geometry
Field PrimitiveelementGenerates point geometry such as spirals, lattices and torus knots
Field EffectsamplePer-sample audio effect with in, out, state and param
Field SynthsampleA polyphonic synth voice driven by freq and gate
