Field NotessampleSends notes with note(pitch, vel, len) and reads the transport
Field GraphgraphRuns at edit time and builds real nodes and cables

Knobs that become pins

A kernel can declare parameters in its own code, and each one becomes a real input on the node:

param float cutoff = 0.25 [0.01, 0.99]
state float z = 0
z += (in - z) * cutoff
out = z

That is a one-pole low-pass filter. The cutoff pin can be wired to an LFO, a MIDI knob or the output of an Audio Analyze node like any other control, and it survives save and load.

Why a language, not another plugin format

A kernel is short enough to read in one go and to share as a text file. The Library has a growing set of free Field devices to start from, and the language reference is available as a PDF manual.

To see where a kernel's numbers can come from, read how sound and pictures share one graph. Infinite is free and open source for macOS, Windows and Linux.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/field-language-write-what-a-node-does.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: A free TouchDesigner alternative for audio-reactive visuals?
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: An honest look at where Infinite fits next to TouchDesigner for audio-reactive visuals and VJ work, and where TouchDesigner is still the better choice.
item.content:encoded:
If you make audio-reactive visuals, you have probably met TouchDesigner. It is powerful, mature and has a large community. It is also a visual tool first: sound comes in through operators, and a full music setup usually means a second program next to it.

Infinite starts from the other side. It is a DAW and a visual tool on one canvas, free and open source. This page is a practical comparison, including the places where TouchDesigner is the better pick.

What Infinite does well for this job

  • Audio and visuals share a canvas. Synths, sequencers and plugins sit next to shaders and 3D, wired with cables. There is no OSC bridge to set up.
  • Audio analysis is a node. Audio Analyze gives an 8-band FFT and onset detection that you can wire to any control.
  • It hosts plugins. AU (macOS) and VST3 (macOS, Windows, Linux) plugins load into the graph, and their parameters can be modulated by visuals.
  • It is free and open source. No licence tier, and the source is on GitHub.
  • Video out to other tools. Syphon (macOS), Spout (Windows) and NDI carry the picture to a projector tool or a streaming setup.

Where TouchDesigner is stronger

  • It has been around for years, so the amount of tutorials, forum answers and shared networks is far larger.
  • Python scripting and a deep set of operators cover installations and data work that Infinite does not aim at.
  • Many venues and teams already have TouchDesigner in their pipeline.

If your show depends on that ecosystem, stay there. If you want sound and picture designed together, with a synth and a shader in the same patch, Infinite is worth an afternoon.

A quick way to judge it

  1. Download Infinite for your platform.
  2. Open the Moves with the music template from the Library.
  3. Press play, then replace the shape with something of your own.

You can also experiment directly inside the browser using the Samples page or browse the audio-reactive GLSL shader guide to see how shader uniforms bind to audio bands. For numbers, the site has a benchmarks page that states its method and its limits.

Bringing a shader over

If you already write GLSL, the Field Pixel node accepts a per-pixel kernel and compiles it for the GPU. Audio values arrive as ordinary inputs, so a shader that reacts to sound is a few lines. The Field language post explains how it works.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/free-touchdesigner-alternative-for-audio-reactive-visuals.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Infinite v0.6 benchmarks: where it is fast and where it is not
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Infinite benchmarks on a base MacBook Air M2 against Blender, Vital, Serum 2 and popular DAWs, with the results published, including where Infinite is slower.
item.content:encoded:
These are the Infinite v0.6 benchmarks: Infinite measured against the tools you already use, on one ordinary laptop, with the same tests for everyone. We publish the numbers that are good for us and the ones that are not. The full report is on the benchmarks page, with a PDF and the raw data as JSON.

How we tested

Everything ran on a base MacBook Air with an Apple M2 and 8 GB of memory, on macOS, between 12 and 17 October 2026. That is the cheapest model on purpose: if it is fast there, it is fast on yours. Nothing was measured on Windows or Linux.

The tests treat every product as a black box. Notes or a test signal go in, and what comes out is measured. Competitor plugins run inside Infinite's own plugin host, with default settings and no hand-picked presets, and the same code measures them as measures Infinite's own nodes. The tools are in the repository under tools/re-survey, so you can repeat any of it.

The good news

  • Launch: 0.34 seconds from launch to first frame. Opening a 400-node patch takes 6 ms.
  • Footprint: 244 MB of memory with the app open and idle, and a 45 MB download. That is less memory than Ableton Live (672 MB), Blender (693 MB), Bitwig (1,392 MB) and TouchDesigner (1,396 MB) in the same idle test.
  • Synth accuracy: The Wavetable synth has a worst pitch error of 0.2 cents across the keyboard. Vital and Serum 2 measure the same. Off-note energy stays between about -81 and -85 dB, even at the top of the keyboard where cheap synths alias.
  • Synth cost: The Wavetable synth uses 1.45 ms of CPU per second of audio for each voice. Vital uses 2.82 ms and Serum 2 uses 3.23 ms.
  • Video export: On matched test scenes, Infinite exported ProRes 4444 at 170 frames a second at 720p and 44 at 4K. Blender managed 1.6 and 0.5. These are different renderers, so this compares throughput, not image style.
  • Plugins: 97.6 % of the plugins installed on the test machine load and pass audio in Infinite's plugin host.
  • Live use: zero audio dropouts and zero missed screen refreshes in the standard live-performance test.

Where Infinite is behind

We list these on the report as below target:

  • Idle CPU: With nothing loaded, Infinite sits at 12.3 % of one core. Logic, Blender and Vital sit under 4 %.
  • Built-in effects: The EQ, Limiter, Drive and Chorus cost more CPU than the plugin equivalents.
  • Instancing: 10,000 instanced objects cost 3.1 ms a frame in Infinite and 1.3 ms in Blender.
  • Heavy projector scenes: The heaviest test (four 4K videos, three output windows, a camera and Syphon at once) drops frames. Normal and 1080p scenes do not.
  • Default levels: Reverb, Delay, Chorus and Flanger come out louder than they go in at their default settings.

What the numbers do not say

One laptop is one data point. The comparisons are about throughput and cost under a fixed test, not about taste: a faster export does not make a better picture, and equal pitch accuracy does not make two synths sound alike. Windows and Linux numbers will come later.

Check it yourself

Everything is repeatable. Read the benchmark report, download the raw JSON, or run the scripts in tools/re-survey on your own machine and tell us where your numbers differ. For how the headless renderer works, see render video and audio from a text file.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/infinite-v0-6-benchmarks.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Make your first audio-reactive visual in Infinite
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: A beginner walkthrough from a free template to a shape that moves with your music, using the Audio Analyze node and a single cable.
item.content:encoded:
This is the shortest path from nothing to a picture that follows your music. You need Infinite and about ten minutes. No plugins or extra software.

1. Start from a template

Open the Library and download Moves with the music. It is a small patch where a shape grows with the sound. Open the file from File, Open in Infinite and press play.

A template is a normal patch, so everything in it can be changed.

2. Follow the cable

The patch has two halves, and the template labels them with comments on the canvas.

  • The sound. A Random Note Generator plays an Analog synth into Audio Out.
  • The picture. A Shape goes through a Bloom effect to the Output node.

What joins them is an Audio Analyze node. It listens to the sound and turns it into moving numbers: level, low, mid and high. Those numbers drive the shape's Size X and Size Y. Controls that are driven by the music show an orange dot.

That is the whole trick. Any number can move any control.

3. Change what moves

Try these one at a time:

  1. Switch the source of Size X from level to low or high. Low reacts to bass, high to the bright parts of the sound.
  2. Change the Depth of a driven control to make it move more or less.
  3. Raise the Intensity on Bloom for a stronger glow.
  4. Add an LFO and connect it to a colour control, so the picture drifts even when the music is quiet.

4. Bring your own sound

Replace the template's synth with a Sampler or an audio file, or load a VST3 or AU plugin and play it from your MIDI keyboard. The Audio Analyze node listens to whatever you connect to it.

5. Save and share

Patches are plain-text .inf files. Send the file to a friend and they get exactly your setup. If you make something you like, the Discord is a good place to post it.

Where to go next

  • Read how sound and pictures share one graph.
  • Learn to write your own effect with Field.
  • Browse the other templates in the Library: Modulators, Synths, 3D and Compositing are good second stops.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/make-your-first-audio-reactive-visual.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Modulate any VST3 or AU plugin with LFOs, audio and visuals
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: How to modulate VST3 parameters in Infinite DAW using modular LFOs, audio envelopes, webcam feeds and real-time visual movement.
item.content:encoded:
Most digital audio workstations treat third-party plugins as static black boxes. You insert a synthesiser or effect into an audio track, open its bespoke window, and rely solely on the modulators the plugin developer chose to include. If your favourite compressor lacks sidechain filtering, or your preferred synthesiser lacks an extra complex LFO, you are normally out of options.

Infinite takes a modular approach where every hosted plugin becomes an open node on a shared canvas. When you host a plugin, you can modulate VST3 parameters directly with virtual patch cables, routing numbers from procedural LFOs, envelope followers, sound generators, and interactive graphics straight into plugin knobs.

What plugins can be hosted

Infinite hosts Audio Unit (AU) plugins on macOS and VST3 plugins across macOS, Windows and Linux. When you add a plugin node to the canvas:

  • The plugin opens in its native editor window for tactile preset selection.
  • Every automated parameter exposed by the plugin is registered as an addressable control port.
  • Input ports receive audio, MIDI note events, and continuous control values (CV).
  • Output ports deliver processed audio back into the master bus, a spatialiser, or an audio analysis node.

This architecture works with modern instruments like Vital, Surge XT and Serum, as well as creative effects from Valhalla, FabFilter, and native open-source audio tools.

Four ways to modulate plugin parameters

Because parameter inputs accept standard continuous signals from any other node, you are not restricted to traditional DAW automation lanes.

1. Multi-waveform LFOs

Add an LFO node, select a waveform (sine, triangle, ramp, square, or random sample-and-hold), and connect its output to the desired parameter port. You can dial in the modulation depth and baseline offset independently. By combining two LFOs through a Math node, you can create evolving, non-repeating modulation curves for filters and chorus rates.

2. Audio signals and envelope followers

An Envelope Follower converts the instantaneous amplitude of an audio stream into a continuous control signal. If you route the kick drum bus into an Envelope Follower and patch the output to the wet mix or cutoff of a reverb plugin on a synth lead, you get precise, transparent ducking without setting up sidechain routing menus.

3. Visuals and video analysis

In Infinite, audio and visuals operate on the same canvas engine. An Image Analyze node evaluates visual luminance, edge density, or optical flow motion vectors from a camera or a generative shader. When wired to a plugin parameter, physical movement in your studio or rhythmic pulses on the screen directly modulate synthesiser resonance, delay feedback, or distortion drive.

4. Custom Field kernel modulators

When standard LFO shapes are not enough, the Field Language node lets you write custom per-sample math. A single expression can compute chaotic attractors, Euclidean step sequences, or stochastic noise formulas running at audio rate.

A step-by-step modular patch

Here is a practical patch you can build in two minutes:

  1. Press Tab, type Plugin, and load your favourite VST3 synthesiser.
  2. Route a Note Sequencer node into the plugin's MIDI input port.
  3. Add a second Plugin node and load an external delay or reverb effect. Cable the audio outputs from the synthesiser into the effect.
  4. Add an LFO node set to a slow sine wave (around 0.15 Hz) and connect it to the reverb mix parameter.
  5. Add an Envelope Follower after the synthesiser and connect its modulation output to the cutoff of the reverb.
  6. Add an Audio Analyze node and pipe its spectral output into a real-time shader, so your sound and visual geometry evolve in lockstep.

Why modular plugin hosting matters

Traditional automation ties parameter movements to a static horizontal timeline. In contrast, modular parameter modulation makes sound design generative and reactive. For related routing workflows, explore the modular VST3 host audio routing guide and our breakdown of node-based DAW signal paths. If you are crafting basslines and plucks from scratch, see the electronic music sound design tutorial.

Infinite is free and open source. The Node Reference Manual documents every available modulator, math operator, and CV routing node.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/modulate-vst3-plugins-with-visuals-and-lfos.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Free motion tracking for music and visuals in Infinite
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Hand Track, Face Track and Pose Track turn a camera or picture into modulators, so a pinch, a smile or a raised arm can drive any parameter in your patch.
item.content:encoded:
Free motion tracking software is built into Infinite as an optional pack: it turns a camera image into numbers you can wire to anything: a shader's size, a filter cutoff, a synth note. There are three tracking nodes, Hand Track, Face Track and Pose Track, and each one outputs modulators the same way an LFO does. This post explains what they give you, how to set them up, and where they work well.

What you need

  • Infinite 0.5.0 or later.
  • The free Tracking pack (26 MB). Open Settings, then Extensions, and press Install next to Tracking. It installs while the app runs, with no restart. If you are offline, download the pack for your platform from the Extensions page and use Install from file.
  • A video source: a camera, a video file or a still image.

The pack is optional on purpose. If you never track anything, you never download it.

The three nodes

All three live in the Modulators category. Each has a present output that says whether a subject was found, followed by the values below.

Hand Track gives you palm x, palm y, index x, index y, thumb x, thumb y, then pinch, open, roll and size. It also has six gesture flags: fist, point, peace, thumbs up, ok and rock.

Face Track gives you head x, head y, yaw, pitch and roll, then eye L, eye R, brows, mouth, smile, gaze x and gaze y.

Pose Track gives you body x, body y, head x, head y, both wrists as wrist L x, wrist L y, wrist R x, wrist R y, then arm L, arm R, spread, lean and size.

Because these are ordinary modulator outputs, you connect them the same way as any other: drag a modulation cable to a parameter. Nothing about the destination needs to know it is being driven by a body.

Smooth, hold and mirror

Raw tracking jitters, and a hand leaving the frame for a moment should not make a visual snap to zero. Each tracking node has three settings for this:

  • mirror, on by default, so that moving your right hand moves things to the right on screen, like a mirror.
  • smoothing, 0.5 by default. At 0 the values are raw. Towards 1 they are very smooth. The filter is speed adaptive (One-Euro), so slow movements are smoothed hard while fast movements stay responsive.
  • holdMs, 150 by default. After the subject is lost, the node keeps the last values for that many milliseconds before reporting that nothing is there.

The gesture flags and present skip the smoothing, since a gesture is either on or off. The node body shows a live landmark overlay and slider-style meters, so you can see what the tracker sees before you wire anything.

Three patches to try

A pinch that controls a filter. Add a Hand Track node, then wire pinch to a filter cutoff on a synth or a hosted plugin. Closing your fingers closes the filter. If you want a different range, put a Range to Range node between them.

A head that steers the picture. Wire Face Track yaw and pitch to a shape's rotation or to a shader's offset, and smile to colour or brightness. For a gallery piece this is enough: a screen that leans towards the person looking at it.

Arms as a conductor. Wire Pose Track arm L and arm R to two different parameters, for example the level of two instruments, and spread to the amount of an effect. Stand back from the camera so the whole upper body is in frame.

Tips from how the trackers work

  • Light the subject from the front. A bright window behind you makes the face and hands harder to find.
  • Keep the whole hand in view. size tells you how close it is to the camera, which is a useful modulator on its own.
  • Use the gesture flags as switches and the continuous outputs as knobs. A fist that mutes and a pinch that sweeps feels natural.
  • If you want motion without identifying a person or body part, the Image Analyze node can measure luminance and motion in a region of any image, with no pack needed.
  • Tracking nodes report present as off when the input is unplugged, instead of freezing the last pose.

Combine it with sound

Tracking is most fun when it is one part of a larger patch. Because the same graph holds audio and visuals, a hand can drive a plugin while the plugin's output drives the picture. See modulating VST3 and AU plugins for the plugin side, and one graph for sound and pictures for why the two share a clock.

Try it

Download Infinite free from infinitedevices.org, install the Tracking pack from Settings, add a Hand Track node and watch the landmarks appear. The full parameter list is in the Node Reference Manual.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/motion-tracking-hand-face-pose-modulators.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: One graph for sound and pictures: how Infinite keeps them in step
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Infinite runs a pull-based audio graph and a GPU texture pipeline off one BPM transport, so audio can drive visuals and visuals can drive audio.
item.content:encoded:
Video tools and audio tools usually live in separate programs. You wire them together with OSC, MIDI clock or a texture-sharing protocol, and you accept a little latency and jitter on the way. Infinite takes a different route: audio and visuals are two parts of one engine that share a transport.

Two graphs, one clock

The engine has two sides, and each one follows the rules of its own medium.

  • Audio is a pull-based, sample-accurate graph. If a buffer is late, you hear a click, so it is built around a deadline.
  • Visuals are a GPU texture pipeline on GLSL and OpenGL 3.2 Core. A dropped frame is far less noticeable, but throughput matters.

Both sides are tied to a global BPM transport, so a beat means the same moment in the sound and in the picture.

Modulation crosses the boundary

The useful part is what happens between the two. Any signal can modulate any control:

  • an Audio Analyze node gives an 8-band FFT and onset detection;
  • an LFO, Envelope Follower, Random or Pattern CV gives a moving number;
  • an Image Analyze node reads luminance or motion from a picture.

Wire the output of one of those to a control and it moves. That control can be a shader parameter, a 3D transform, a synth knob or the slider of a hosted plugin. Sound drives pictures, and pictures drive sound.

Why one canvas helps

When both live on the same canvas, the connection is a cable you can see. There is no second application to launch, no port to configure and no project that has to be kept in sync by hand. A patch is also a plain-text .inf file, so it can be versioned, diffed and rendered without a window.

Try it

Open the Moves with the music template from the Library. It is a shape that grows with the sound, and it is the smallest example of the idea above.

Infinite is free and open source for macOS, Windows and Linux.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/one-graph-for-sound-and-pictures.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.

item.title: Render video and audio from a text file with no window open
item.dc:creator: Naman Soni
item.description: Infinite's headless mode turns a plain-text patch into stills, video and a loudness report from the command line. Here is the five-minute workflow.
item.content:encoded:
A headless DAW is one that renders with no window open. Most DAWs and visual tools only run with a window and a mouse. Infinite's engine does not need either. The executable inside the app is also a command-line tool, so a patch can be validated, drawn and rendered from a terminal, a script or a CI job.

This post walks through the loop from the Headless User Guide: describe, write, validate, explain, look and listen, render.

What you need

  • The Infinite app. There is no separate package; the executable inside the app is the tool.
  • A machine with working OpenGL, because frames are drawn by the real GPU pipeline.
  • On Linux, a virtual display. Run each render as xvfb-run -a Infinite ....
  • A text editor. Patches are plain text files ending in .inf.

Patches that use a camera, microphone or MIDI device are refused in headless mode (exit code 4), since there is no hardware to read. Swap them for a file or a generator.

A complete patch in a dozen lines

Save this as hello.inf:

infinite-patch 1
node 1 Source Shape
  id shape
  i shapeType Star
end
node 2 Modulators LFO
  id lfo
end
node 3 Utility Output
  id out
end
cable out 0 shape
mod shape sizeX lfo 0 0 1 0.5
expr shape rotation sin(t) * 90

That is one shape, one LFO and an output. The LFO drives the shape's width, and an expression spins it.

Validate, draw, render

Infinite --validate hello.inf
Infinite --frame hello.inf 0,1,2 pics/ --contact-sheet sheet.png
Infinite --render hello.inf hello.mp4 --duration 4 --fps 30

--validate loads the file strictly and lists every problem with its line number. --frame draws stills at 0, 1 and 2 seconds plus one labelled contact sheet. --render writes the video.

Ask the engine, do not guess

Two commands save a lot of trial and error:

  • Infinite --describe "<node type>" lists a node's controls with their defaults, ranges and dropdown options.
  • Infinite --explain hello.inf prints the graph that was actually built, so you can check every wire. A patch can validate and still be the wrong patch.

Measure the sound

--audio-summary describes the audio as numbers: loudness, peaks, clipping, silence, a spectrum and a tempo guess.

Infinite --audio-summary hello.inf summary.json --wav out.wav --duration 4

Add --stems id,id --stems-dir dir to write one WAV per named node, or --output node to measure a single Audio Out instead of the whole mix.

Reading the result

The last line printed is always one JSON object with ok, mode, frames, fps, size, audio, elapsed_ms, files, warnings and errors. A script can parse that line and branch on ok without scraping log text.

Where this is useful

  • Regression tests for sound and picture. Render a corpus of patches on every commit and compare the summaries.
  • Batch exports. Produce a hundred variations of a piece from one patch with --set node.param=value.
  • Bots and servers. Take a patch from a chat message and send back a video.

Want to see what a patch looks like before scripting it? Start with the first steps tutorial. Infinite is free and open source for macOS, Windows and Linux. The full flag list is in the Headless User Guide, and the patch format is documented in the repository.

Originally published at https://infinitedevices.org/blog/render-video-and-audio-from-a-text-file.html. Infinite is a free, open-source DAW for visuals, music and code: infinitedevices.org.
